docs.title: Wybthon
docs.text:
Wybthon is SolidJS for Python: a client-side single-page application (SPA) framework with SolidJS 2.0's fine-grained reactive model, a Pythonic API, and a runtime that lives in the browser through Pyodide.

If you can write Python, you can build interactive web apps with Wybthon. There's no JavaScript build pipeline and no JSX: markup is HTML in a Python template string.

docs.title: What is Wybthon?
docs.text:
You write function components in Python and return HTML written as Python 3.14 template strings: html(t"<p>Count: {count()}</p>"). Like Solid's, Wybthon's compiler turns every dynamic expression in that markup into a getter, and each template literal into a native <template> that the browser clones per instance, so the expressions you interpolate are its only moving parts. Components run once. When a signal changes, only the text nodes, attributes, and reactive holes that read it update, and the renderer batches the resulting DOM mutations into a single crossing of the Python-to-JavaScript bridge.

The framework ships with everything you need to build a real app:

  • Templates: html takes a t-string of ordinary HTML, with interpolations for text, attributes, events, refs, spreads, and component tags. h is the programmatic layer.
  • The compiler: {count() * 2} and {props.title} stay reactive without being wrapped, and production builds never parse a template at run time.
  • Reactive primitives: create_signal, create_memo, and create_effect, with automatic batching and typed accessors.
  • Async-first data: an async def passed to create_memo is the fetching primitive, and create_deferred is the async memo that never holds the rest of the UI; Loading and Errored boundaries handle the pending and failure states.
  • action with create_optimistic and create_optimistic_store for mutations.
  • Draft-first stores (create_store, reconcile, create_projection).
  • Flow control (Show, For, Repeat, Switch, dynamic), callable Context objects, Portal, lazy, and lazy_module.
  • Typed components: inputs declared as plain annotations on a Props class that pyright and mypy check without a plugin.
  • A client-side router in wybthon.router with Router, Route, and Link.
  • Server rendering: prerender routes at build time or render per request in CPython, stream Loading boundaries, set the status and headers with http_status and http_header, and hydrate the result in the browser.
  • Form state, validators, and accessibility helpers in wybthon.forms.
  • A test renderer, wybthon.testing, that mounts components into an in-memory DOM in plain CPython, and a pytest plugin that compiles templates in test modules.
  • A dev server (wyb dev) with hot reload via Server-Sent Events, production builds (wyb build) with templates compiled ahead of time, dev-mode checks turned off, the asset manifest inlined, and the runtime preloaded, and wyb run for scripts.

docs.title: Try it in 30 seconds
docs.text:
The smallest interactive Wybthon component looks like this:

from wybthon import component, create_signal, html, render


@component
def Counter():
    count, set_count = create_signal(0)

    def increment():
        set_count(lambda n: n + 1)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <p>Count: {count()}</p>
        <button onclick={increment}>Increment</button>
      </div>
    """)


render(Counter(), "#app")

t"..." is a PEP 750 template string, new in Python 3.14. {count()} calls something, so the compiler turns it into a getter: a reactive binding, and only that text node updates when the signal changes. Walk through this example end to end in Getting started, read the Templates guide, or jump straight into the Concepts section.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
1. Install Wybthon (Python 3.14 or newer):

    pip install wybthon

  2. Create a project and run the dev server with auto-reload:

    wyb init my-app
cd my-app
wyb dev --open

  3. Explore the demo apps and the API in the Concepts and API sections.

docs.title: Why Wybthon?
docs.text:
• Run-once components and typed props. A @component declares its inputs on a Props class with plain annotations, and props.title is a tracked read of the parent's value, as in Solid. Use it in the markup to bind it, in a memo or effect to derive from it, or in untrack for a one-time read. Callbacks are fields annotated as callable, passed through untouched.
  • A compiler, as in Solid. The compiler rewrites each template before its module runs: an expression that calls something, reads an attribute, or indexes becomes a getter, and a component call in the markup receives getters for its props. You write {count() * 2}, not a lambda.
  • Markup compiles ahead of time. Each template literal is parsed, validated, and turned into a mount function when its module is compiled; every instance clones its native <template> with one kernel command and fills its slots. Production builds never parse a template or generate code at run time.
  • Holes are the unit of update. Each dynamic expression in the markup becomes its own binding. There are no component re-renders to reason about.
  • Components cost what their markup costs. A constant prop subscribes to nothing, a binding that reads nothing reactive allocates no computation, and Show, For, Repeat, and Switch are native regions rather than wrapper components.
  • Automatic batching. Signal writes are staged and applied once per microtask (and at the end of every event handler). There's no batch(); call flush only when you need the settled state synchronously.
  • Async is part of the graph. Reading an async memo before it resolves raises NotReadyError, which the nearest Loading boundary turns into fallback UI. Content stays mounted while pending, and a later refetch runs as a transition: the UI that depends on the change holds on the previous state until the new value lands, so nothing tears.
  • A virtual DOM where it pays off. Every DOM call crosses the Pyodide bridge, so Wybthon emits DOM operations into a buffer and ships them to a JavaScript kernel in one batch per flush. Only reactive holes that return new markup are diffed, and a template from the same literal is patched slot by slot.
  • Dev-mode diagnostics. Writing a signal inside a tracking scope raises WriteInScopeError; reading a signal or prop at the top level of a component body warns, because that read isn't tracked; an unknown or missing prop raises TypeError; a template that reached html() without the compiler raises TemplateError. Production builds turn these checks off.
  • Runs anywhere Python runs. The reactive core and the VDOM are pure Python, so component tests run in CPython with wybthon.testing.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Wybthon runs client-side Python through Pyodide. Components run once and return HTML written as template strings, and a compiler makes each dynamic expression in that markup update its own part of the page, as Solid's does for JSX. The renderer batches every DOM mutation into one call to a small JavaScript kernel.

docs.title: Create an application
docs.text:
Install Python 3.14 or later and Wybthon:

python -m pip install wybthon
wyb init my-app
cd my-app
wyb dev --open

The generated project has app/main.py, index.html, pyproject.toml, and wybthon.toml. The development server builds the app in dev mode and reloads the browser after source, configuration, or public asset changes. Pyodide requires a network connection on the first load unless you host the runtime locally.

docs.title: Write a component
docs.text:
wyb init generates this app/main.py:

"""A run-once component with a reactive counter."""

from wybthon import component, create_signal, html


@component
def App():
    count, set_count = create_signal(0)

    def increment():
        set_count(lambda n: n + 1)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <h1>My Wybthon app</h1>
        <button onclick={increment}>Count: {count()}</button>
        <p>Doubled: {count() * 2}</p>
      </div>
    """)


def app():
    """Return the root view; the bootstrap renders (or hydrates) it into the mount element."""
    return App()

html takes a t"..." template string (new in Python 3.14) and returns a node. The markup is ordinary HTML, and each {...} is a Python expression placed where it appears.

App runs once. {count()} and {count() * 2} are dynamic expressions: they call something, so Wybthon's compiler turns each one into a getter before the module runs, the way Solid's compiler treats an expression in JSX. When count changes, those two text nodes update and nothing else runs. An expression that's just a name or a constant, such as {title}, is placed once. onclick={increment} binds a delegated click handler; event handlers are never wrapped. The handler takes no arguments because it doesn't need the event, and writes made in a handler batch automatically.

The compiler runs wherever your code does: in wyb dev and wyb build, in modules imported after wybthon, under pytest, and for scripts run with wyb run script.py. You don't call it yourself.

increment is a named function rather than an inline lambda, because Python doesn't allow a bare lambda inside a template interpolation. If you want one inline, wrap it in parentheses: onclick={(lambda: set_count(0))}. See Templates for the full syntax.

app is the entry point named in wybthon.toml. It returns the root view, and the bootstrap mounts it into #app. The generated project prerenders / at build time, so the page shows the counter before Pyodide has loaded and then hydrates it. Outside the production bootstrap, mount a view yourself with render.

docs.title: Add props
docs.text:
A component that takes inputs declares them on a Props class. Fields are plain annotations, and pyright and mypy check every call without a plugin:

from wybthon import Props, component, create_signal, html, untrack


class CounterProps(Props):
    label: str
    initial: int = 0


@component
def Counter(props: CounterProps):
    count, set_count = create_signal(untrack(lambda: props.initial))

    def increment():
        set_count(lambda n: n + 1)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <p>{props.label}: {count()}</p>
        <button onclick={increment}>+1</button>
      </div>
    """)


@component
def App():
    return html(t"""
      <main>
        <h1>My Wybthon app</h1>
        {Counter(label="Clicks", initial=5)}
      </main>
    """)

Reading props.label returns the parent's value, tracked, as in Solid. In the template, {props.label} is dynamic, so it updates if the parent passes an expression that changes. initial only seeds the signal, so it's read once with untrack; reading a prop at the top level of the body without it would warn in dev mode, because that read never updates.

Calling Counter(...) inside an interpolation keeps full type checking of its props. Templates also accept a tag form, <{Counter} label="Clicks" initial={5} />, which reads like the surrounding markup and is checked at run time in dev mode. See Components for children, callbacks, and defaults.

docs.title: Test it
docs.text:
wybthon.testing renders components into an in-memory DOM in plain CPython. Wybthon's pytest plugin compiles the templates in test modules, so they behave exactly as they do in the app:

from wybthon.testing import fire, render


def test_counter():
    screen = render(Counter(label="Clicks"))
    fire.click(screen.get_by_text("+1"))
    assert screen.get_by_text("Clicks: 1")

docs.title: Build and preview
docs.text:
wyb build
wyb preview

The output in dist/ contains prerendered pages, hashed source archives with every template compiled ahead of time, and a browser bootstrap. Each page carries the asset manifest inline and preloads Pyodide and the archives, so the browser starts fetching them while it parses the HTML. Production builds turn dev mode off before your application imports, so dev-only checks and warnings don't ship. Deploy those files to a static host. See Deployment for base paths, pinned dependencies, lazy chunks, and route fallback configuration.

Continue with the mental model, templates, the compiler, stores, and runtime contracts.

docs.title: compiler
docs.text:
The Wybthon compiler: Solid's compile step, done on Python's syntax tree.

Solid's compiler does two things with JSX. It turns static markup into templates, and it turns every dynamic expression in the markup into a getter, so {count() * 2} stays reactive without being wrapped. This module does both for html(t"..."):

@component
def Counter(props: CounterProps):
    count, set_count = create_signal(0)
    return html(t"<p>{count()} doubled is {count() * 2}, step {props.step}</p>")

compiles to (roughly):

return html(
    t"<p>{getter(lambda: count())} doubled is {getter(lambda: count() * 2)}, step {getter(lambda: props.step)}</p>",
    __wybthon_t0__,  # the literal's parse tree and mount function, built at compile time
)

The rule. An interpolation is dynamic when its expression contains a call, an attribute access, or a subscript (not counting the bodies of lambdas inside it). A dynamic interpolation becomes a getter: a hole in a child position, a binding in an attribute, a getter prop on a component tag. Event handlers, refs, spreads, the component in a component tag, and nested html(t"...") markup are never wrapped. Anything that isn't dynamic (a name, a constant, a lambda) is passed as is.

Calls in child position are dispatched when the template is created (see wybthon._compiled.call): a component (Card(title=user().name), Show(...), For(...)) is built with each dynamic argument as a getter, the way a JSX component receives its props; any other callable (badge(user()), str(n())) becomes one reactive expression.

Captured names. A getter runs later, so the names its expression reads from enclosing function scopes are captured by value when the template is created (as keyword-only defaults of the getter's lambda). A template made in a loop sees that iteration's values.

Precompiled templates. Each literal is parsed and validated here, so a malformed template is a SyntaxError with its file and line. Its parse tree and the mount function for each of its elements are written into the module, so html() never parses a template or generates code at run time.

The compiler runs from the import hook that import wybthon installs, from wyb build and wyb dev, from the pytest plugin, and from wyb run.

docs.title: What's in this module
docs.text:
compiler is Wybthon's compile step, the counterpart of Solid's JSX compiler, done on Python's syntax tree. It rewrites every html(t"...") call whose argument is a t-string literal: each dynamic interpolation (one containing a call, an attribute access, or a subscript) becomes a getter, a call in a child position is dispatched to a component or made a reactive hole, and the literal's parse tree and mount functions are emitted as ordinary module code. Nothing else in the module changes. See Concepts: Compiler for the rules and how to inspect the output.

You rarely call it directly. It runs in wyb build and wyb dev, in the import hook that import wybthon installs, in the pytest plugin, and in wyb run script.py.

Name Description install Install the import hook (idempotent); import wybthon calls it. uninstall Remove the import hook. compile_source compile_source(source, filename): a module's code object with its templates compiled, ready for exec. transform transform(tree, filename="<unknown>", source=""): rewrite a module's ast in place and return it; raises SyntaxError for a malformed template. is_dynamic Whether an expression node contains a call, attribute access, or subscript (outside the lambdas inside it). is_candidate Whether a module's source bytes might hold html(t"...") calls: it mentions wybthon and html and contains a t-string. defers Whether the compiler would defer an interpolation's source text in a given position; html() uses it for the dev-mode check of uncompiled templates. COMPILER_TAG The optimization tag of cached compiled bytecode (*.opt-wyb1.pyc); it changes when the compiler's output does. 
from wybthon.compiler import compile_source

source = """
from wybthon import create_signal, html

count, set_count = create_signal(2)
view = html(t"<p>{count() * 2}</p>")
"""

namespace = {}
exec(compile_source(source, "generated.py"), namespace)  # {count() * 2} is a reactive hole
  • html is resolved through the module's imports (from wybthon import html, from wybthon.templates import html, an alias of either, or wybthon.html), so a module that defines its own html is left alone.
  • A malformed template is a SyntaxError with its file and line when the module is compiled, not a TemplateError at run time.
  • The generated names (__wybthon__, __wybthon_t0__, __wybthon_m0__) are dunder names, which Python never mangles inside classes.

docs.title: component
docs.text:
The @component decorator and the Component type it produces.

Wybthon components run once: the body executes a single time when the component mounts and returns a tree. Inputs are declared on a Props class and arrive as one typed parameter, the counterpart of Solid's props object:

class CounterProps(Props):
    label: str = "Count"
    initial: int = 0


@component
def Counter(props: CounterProps):
    count, set_count = create_signal(untrack(lambda: props.initial))

    def increment():
        set_count(lambda n: n + 1)

    return html(t"<div><p>{props.label}: {count()}</p><button onclick={increment}>+</button></div>")


render(Counter(initial=10), "#app")

Reading props.label returns the parent's value, tracked; in markup the compiler turns {props.label} into a getter, so it updates when the parent passes an expression that changes.

Calling a component with keyword props returns a node, and so does a component tag in a template (<{Counter} initial={5} />). Type checkers see the call as constructing the props class, so missing, mistyped, and unknown props are errors without a plugin. A component with no inputs takes no parameters.

Children are the children prop. Pass them as a tag's content, as a keyword, or with item syntax on the call: Card(title="Hi")[html(t"<p>Body</p>")]. Declare them with ParentProps.

component(fn: Callable[..., Any]) -> Any

Declare a function as a run-once Wybthon component.

The function takes no parameters, or one parameter annotated with a Props subclass. Calling the result returns a node for the tree.

Static typing: the decorated object is typed as the props class (or as a no-argument callable), so a type checker validates each call's keywords against the declared fields. At run time it's a Component that returns a VNode.

Example 
class GreetingProps(Props):
    name: str = "world"


@component
def Greeting(props: GreetingProps):
    return html(t"<p>Hello, {props.name}!</p>")


Greeting(name="Ada")                       # a node
html(t"<{Greeting} name={user().name} />")  # updates when user() changes

docs.title: What's in this module
docs.text:
The @component decorator turns a function into a run-once Component. The body executes a single time when the component mounts and returns a tree, usually an html template. Inputs are declared on a Props subclass and arrive as one typed parameter, the counterpart of Solid's props object: reading props.label returns the parent's current value, tracked, so later changes flow into the places that read it without re-running the body. Calling a component with keyword arguments returns a VNode, so trees compose like any other node.

Name Description component Decorator producing a Component from a function with one Props-annotated parameter, or none. Component Callable wrapper; Counter(label="Clicks") returns a VNode. Type checkers see the call as constructing the props class. builtin Internal: marks a built-in that renders markup (Show, For, Loading, ...) so a compiled template builds it with getters for its dynamic arguments, as it does a component.

docs.title: Declaring props
docs.text:
• Fields are plain annotations (title: str). Reading props.title returns the value and tracks it. The parent may pass a value, an accessor, or a getter (what the compiler makes of <{Card} title={user().name}>); getters and accessors are unwrapped on read.
  • Defaults work as in a dataclass: step: int = 1. Use prop(default_factory=...) for a mutable default (the factory runs once per instance); prop(default=...) also works.
  • Callable fields (Callable[...] or Accessor[...], alone or in a union with None) return what the parent passed, never calling it, so callbacks and accessors you mean to keep arrive intact.
  • ParentProps declares children. Pass children as the content of a component tag in a template (<{Card} title="Hi">...</{Card}>), as the children keyword, or with item syntax (Card(title="Hi")[...]).
  • key= is accepted by every component.
  • A component with no inputs takes no parameters.

In dev mode, an unknown prop or a missing required one raises TypeError at the call site. There's no **rest; to forward attributes, spread a merge or omit view onto an element (<div {omit(props, "title")}> in a template).

from collections.abc import Callable

from wybthon import ParentProps, Props, component, create_signal, html, omit, untrack


class CounterProps(Props):
    label: str = "Count"
    initial: int = 0
    on_change: Callable[[int], None] | None = None  # callable field: returned as passed


@component
def Counter(props: CounterProps):
    count, set_count = create_signal(untrack(lambda: props.initial))  # a one-time read

    def increment():
        set_count(lambda n: n + 1)
        if props.on_change is not None:
            props.on_change(count.peek() + 1)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <p>{props.label}: {count()}</p>
        <button onclick={increment}>+</button>
      </div>
    """)


class CardProps(ParentProps):
    title: str
    class_: str = "card"


@component
def Card(props: CardProps):
    return html(t"<div {omit(props, 'title', 'children')}><h2>{props.title}</h2>{props.children}</div>")


heading, set_heading = create_signal("Hello")

Counter(initial=5, label="Clicks", on_change=print)
html(t"<{Card} title={heading()}><p>body text</p></{Card}>")  # title stays live
html(t"{Card(title=heading(), children=html(t'<p>body text</p>'))}")  # the same, type-checked

Reading a reactive prop or signal at the top level of the body reads it once and warns in dev mode; read it inside a template expression, memo, or effect, or make the one-time read explicit with untrack. A prop the parent passed as a constant can't change, so reading one doesn't warn.

docs.title: Using components in templates
docs.text: Call a component inside an interpolation, {Counter(initial=5)}, to keep full type checking of its props; the compiler still passes each dynamic argument as a getter. The tag form, <{Card} title="Hi">...</{Card}> or <{Card} />, passes attributes as keyword props (a hyphen becomes an underscore) and nested markup as children; type checkers can't see inside the template string, so dev mode checks its props at run time. See Templates.

docs.title: What a component costs
docs.text:
A component is only patched with new props when a reactive hole re-renders a tree that contains it, or when render runs again into the same container. Everywhere else (inside a template, another component's output, a list row, or a Show branch) its props object never changes, so:

  • reading a prop that the parent passed as a constant subscribes to nothing;
  • a prop passed as a getter or accessor is read through, so the reader subscribes to that source directly;
  • a binding that reads nothing reactive never allocates a computation.

A component whose props never change costs about what its markup costs. Components that can be patched track one version signal per props instance, created on the first tracked read. Use is_static to ask whether the parent passed a plain value for a key.

A plain, undecorated function used as a tag, as in h(fn, props), receives the props dictionary and runs again when it's patched with changed props. Use @component when you want typed, reactive props.

docs.title: context
docs.text:
Context: pass values down the tree without threading props.

A Context is created with create_context and is its own provider: call it with a value and children to expose that value to every descendant, and read it with use_context.

Values live on the reactive ownership tree, so use_context works anywhere an owner exists: component bodies, effects, memos, and list rows. The value is handed to consumers exactly as provided, so pass a signal (or any accessor) when consumers should react to changes.

Example 
Theme: Context[Accessor[str]] = create_context()

@component
def Button():
    theme = use_context(Theme)
    return html(t'<button class="btn-{theme()}">Hi</button>')

@component
def App():
    theme, set_theme = create_signal("light")
    return Theme(theme, Button())   # value first, then children

The value is handed to consumers exactly as provided, so pass a signal or accessor when consumers should react to changes, and call it where you need the value.

from wybthon import Accessor, Context, component, create_context, create_signal, html, use_context

Theme: Context[Accessor[str]] = create_context(name="Theme")


@component
def ThemedButton():
    theme = use_context(Theme)  # the accessor the provider passed
    return html(t'<button class="btn-{theme()}">Hi</button>')


@component
def App():
    theme, set_theme = create_signal("light")

    def toggle():
        set_theme("dark" if theme.peek() == "light" else "light")

    return Theme(  # value first, then children
        theme,
        html(t"""
          <div>
            {ThemedButton()}
            <button onclick={toggle}>Toggle</button>
          </div>
        """),
    )

Nested providers for the same context shadow outer ones. Outside a component, use_context still works inside any reactive scope (create_root, an effect, a memo).

docs.title: What's in this module
docs.text:
dev is the wyb command. It works on projects: a directory with a wybthon.toml, created by wyb init. wyb dev builds the project in development mode, serves the build, rebuilds when a source file changes, and pushes a reload event over Server-Sent Events at /__sse so open pages refresh. wyb build writes a production build, which turns dev mode off, and wyb preview serves one. Both wyb dev and wyb build run every application module through the compiler, so a malformed template fails the build with its file and line, and they ship the compiled bytecode (when the build's Python matches the Pyodide runtime's; see Deployment), so the page never parses a template at run time. wyb run runs a single script with its templates compiled. Every built page carries its build manifest inline (<script type="application/json" id="wyb-manifest">) and preloads what boot needs: a <link rel="modulepreload"> for Pyodide's pyodide.mjs, and <link rel="preload" as="fetch" crossorigin> for the runtime and application archives, so they download in parallel with Pyodide.

Name Description main CLI entry point (wyb init, wyb dev, wyb build, wyb preview, wyb run). serve serve(directory=".", host="127.0.0.1", port=8000, open_browser=False, open_path=None): the wyb dev server, callable from Python. run_script run_script(path, argv): what wyb run does, callable from Python. 
wyb init my-app
wyb dev --dir my-app --port 8000 --open
wyb build --dir my-app --base /app/
wyb preview --dir my-app/dist
wyb run scripts/seed.py --verbose
Command Flag Default Description wyb dev --dir . Project directory (containing wybthon.toml). wyb dev --host 127.0.0.1 Host interface to bind. wyb dev --port 8000 Starting port (tries the next 20 on conflict). wyb dev --open off Open a browser at the app's base path. wyb dev --open-path none Path to open instead of the base path. wyb build --dir . Project directory. wyb build --out <dir>/dist Output directory. wyb build --base from wybthon.toml Base URL path the app is served from. wyb preview --dir, --host, --port dist, 127.0.0.1, 8000 Serve a production build. wyb run script [args ...] none Run a Python script as __main__ with its templates compiled; the arguments after it are passed to the script.

Live reload: wyb dev watches the app directory, public/, index.html, and wybthon.toml, rebuilds on any change, and broadcasts reload; the snippet it injects into each served page reloads it. The static-directory mode of earlier versions, with its /__manifest endpoint and --mount and --watch flags, is gone; every served directory is a project. See the dev server guide.

wyb run script.py is for code outside a project: a script that renders components with wybthon.testing or wybthon.server, a benchmark, or a quick experiment. python script.py compiles the __main__ module before Wybthon is imported, so its templates aren't compiled, and dev mode raises TemplateError when a dynamic expression in one of them was evaluated once. wyb run compiles the script itself, installs the import hook for the modules it imports, puts the script's directory first on sys.path, and sets sys.argv, so the script behaves as it would inside an application.

wyb run render_page.py --out page.html  # sys.argv[1:] == ["--out", "page.html"]

docs.title: dom
docs.text:
Lightweight DOM wrapper utilities for Pyodide/browser environments.

This module exposes a thin Pythonic facade over the browser's DOM API, designed to feel familiar to JavaScript developers while integrating cleanly with Wybthon's batched renderer:

  • Element wraps a single DOM node and offers ergonomic helpers for attributes, classes, styles, and queries.
  • Ref is a mutable container used by the renderer to hand out a reference to a mounted element.

The renderer itself never touches raw DOM nodes; it refers to nodes by integer ids and batches mutations through wybthon.kernel. Element is the escape hatch for imperative work: it can be backed by either a raw node or a kernel node id, and materializes the underlying node on first access (committing any pending batched ops first, so the node is guaranteed to exist and be up to date).

The wrapper deliberately mirrors familiar DOM property names (e.g. value, checked, files) so that event handlers can read state exactly as they would in JavaScript:

def on_input(e):
    name(e.target.value)
See Also
  • Hello-world tutorial
  • Forms guide

Ref

docs.title: Element
docs.text:
Element(tag: str | None = None, existing: bool = False, node: Any = None, node_id: int | None = None)

Thin wrapper around a DOM node with convenience methods.

Element can be constructed in four ways:

  • With a tag name to create a brand-new node (Element("div")).
  • With a CSS selector and existing=True to wrap an existing node (Element("#root", existing=True)).
  • With an opaque node value to wrap a node returned by another API.
  • With a kernel node_id (used internally by the renderer for refs and event targets); the raw node is materialized lazily on first access.

The wrapper proxies common form-input properties (value, checked, files) so handlers can read state from e.target.value exactly as in React or SolidJS.

docs.title: Ref
docs.text:
Ref()

Mutable container holding a reference to a mounted Element.

Pass a Ref to an element's ref= prop. After mount ref.current is the wrapped element; after unmount it's reset to None. The ref prop also accepts a callback ref(el) or a list mixing both, so a component can forward a parent's ref and keep its own:

class FancyInputProps(Props):
    ref: Ref | Callable[[Element], Any] | None = None


@component
def FancyInput(props: FancyInputProps):
    local = Ref()
    on_settled(lambda: local.current.element.focus())
    return html(t'<input type="text" ref={[local, props.ref]}>')

Refs are assigned during mount, so read them in on_settled or an effect, not at the top of the component body.

docs.title: What's in this module
docs.text:
dom is the imperative escape hatch. The renderer refers to nodes by integer id and batches every mutation through the kernel; Element wraps a real node (or a kernel node id, materialized on first access after committing pending ops) so you can read a value, focus an input, or call a browser API directly. Ref is the container the renderer fills in when an element with ref= mounts.

Name Description Element Thin wrapper over a DOM node: .element (raw node), .node_id, .value, .checked, .files, attribute, class, style, and query helpers. Ref Holds .current (an Element) after mount; reset to None on unmount.

Construct an Element four ways: Element("div") creates a node, Element("#app", existing=True) queries one, Element(node=raw) wraps a node from another API, and Element(node_id=42) wraps a kernel id (what refs and event targets hand you).

from wybthon import Props, Ref, component, html, on_settled


class FancyInputProps(Props):
    ref: Ref | None = None  # a ref is returned as the parent passed it


@component
def FancyInput(props: FancyInputProps):
    local = Ref()

    def focus():
        local.current.element.focus()

    on_settled(focus)
    # Forward the parent's ref (if any) and keep a local one.
    return html(t'<input type="text" ref={[local, props.ref]}>')

Refs are assigned during mount, so read them in on_settled, an effect, or an event handler, not at the top of the component body. The ref attribute (or the ref prop of h()) also accepts a callback that receives the Element, which is closer to Solid 2.0's function refs:

def measure(el):
    print(el.element.offsetWidth)


html(t"<div ref={measure}>Sized</div>")
html(t"<div ref={(lambda el: el.element.focus())}>Inline</div>")  # an inline lambda needs parentheses

Element.query(selector), .find(selector), and .element commit pending batched ops first, so nodes created earlier in the same update are visible to the read.

docs.title: error_boundary
docs.text:
Errored: catch render and effect errors in a subtree.

Errored installs an error handler on its owner scope. When a child render, hole, or effect raises, the boundary swaps in a fallback while leaving sibling trees untouched. It's the recommended way to surface unexpected errors without crashing the whole app.

Boundaries heal automatically: the boundary remembers which reactive inputs the failing computation had read, and when any of them changes it re-renders its children. A fixed user_id, a re-fetched memo, or a corrected form field clears the error without an explicit reset(); reset and reset_on remain for manual retries.

The fallback receives the error as an accessor, as in Solid 2.0: call err() to read it.

Example 
def failed(err, reset):
    return html(t"<div><p>Something went wrong: {str(err())}</p><button onclick={reset}>Retry</button></div>")


html(t"<{Errored} fallback={failed}><{Dashboard} /></{Errored}>")

docs.title: What's in this module
docs.text:
Errored installs an error handler on its owner scope. When a descendant component body, hole, prop binding, effect, or action raises, the boundary swaps in a fallback and leaves sibling trees untouched. It's the recommended way to keep one broken widget from taking down the page.

Name Description Errored Errored(children, *, fallback=None, on_error=None, reset_on=None).
  • children: a node, a zero-arg callable, or a list of either. A node is enough: a component inside it doesn't run until the boundary mounts it, so Errored(Dashboard()) needs no lambda.
  • fallback: a node, a string, or a callable (err, reset) -> VNode (a one-argument (err) or zero-argument form also works). err is an Accessor for the caught exception, as in Solid 2.0, so read it with err(), in a template expression or anywhere else. reset() clears the error and re-renders the children. Without a fallback the boundary renders "Something went wrong."
  • on_error: called with the exception (send it to your monitoring).
  • reset_on: an accessor whose change clears the current error automatically, for example current_path.
from wybthon import Errored, component, html
from wybthon.router import current_path


def fallback(err, reset):
    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <p>Something went wrong: {err()}</p>
        <button onclick={reset}>Try again</button>
      </div>
    """)


@component
def Page():
    return Errored(
        Dashboard(),
        fallback=fallback,
        on_error=report,
        reset_on=current_path,
    )

Async memos store an exception raised by their body and re-raise it on read, so a failed fetch inside a Loading surfaces at the nearest Errored too. To handle an effect's error locally instead, pass error=handler to create_effect.

docs.title: events
docs.text:
Delegated event handling for the batched renderer.

Event delegation lives in the rendering kernel: one native listener per event type is installed on each render root (the container passed to render, plus any Portal target), walks the ancestor chain of the event target natively, and calls into Python once for the bubbling route. Non-bubbling events and explicit native listener options use direct listeners. The call carries a small JSON payload (event type, target value/checked state, key, mouse buttons, modifiers), so the common handler patterns (evt.target.value, evt.key, evt.prevent_default()) never touch a JsProxy at all.

Registering a handler costs no bridge crossing: a template declares its delegated listeners when it's registered, so cloning a row marks them natively, and other handlers ride the same command buffer as the DOM mutations (LISTEN).

A handler may take the DomEvent or no arguments at all: on_click=lambda: set_open(False).

Public surface:

  • DomEvent: the event object passed to handlers, exposing type, target, current_target, key and mouse fields, and helpers like prevent_default and stop_propagation.

The remaining helpers are internal: set_handler and remove_handlers_for are called by the renderer, and dispatch_event is the entry point the kernel invokes when a native event fires.

See Also
  • Forms guide

docs.title: What's in this module
docs.text:
Event handling is delegated at the render root. The JS kernel installs one native listener per event type on each container passed to render (falling back to document when no root is registered), walks the ancestor chain natively when an event fires, and calls into Python once for the matching bubbling route with a small JSON payload. Handlers receive a DomEvent built from that payload, so the common reads (evt.target.value, evt.key) never touch a JsProxy. Registering a handler costs no bridge crossing: handlers on template-mounted nodes are declared by the template itself, so a cloned row marks its listeners natively, and other handlers ride the command buffer as a batched LISTEN op.

Name Description DomEvent The event object: type, target (.value, .checked, .files, .element), current_target, key, code, alt_key, ctrl_key, meta_key, shift_key, button, client_x, client_y, prevent_default(), stop_propagation(), raw. event event(handler, *, capture=False, passive=False, once=False): attach a direct native listener with options instead of delegating. EventHandler What event returns: the callback plus its listener options.

set_handler, remove_handlers_for, and dispatch_event are internal entry points used by the renderer and the kernel.

docs.title: Handler props
docs.text:
• In a template, an attribute named on<type> is a handler: onclick={save}, oninput={edit}. onClick and on:click work too. The DOM event type is the rest of the name, lower-cased.
  • In a spread (<input {bind_text(field)}>) or an h() props dict, a key named on_<type> (or on<Type>) is a handler: on_click, on_input, on_keydown, onChange.
  • A capture suffix listens in the capture phase: onClickCapture in a template, on_click_capture in a spread or h() props.
  • A handler takes the DomEvent or no arguments at all; the arity is checked once, at registration. Signal writes made inside a handler are flushed automatically when it returns, so the DOM updates before the browser paints.
  • The compiler never wraps a handler: onclick={save} passes save itself, and onclick={make_handler(id)} calls make_handler once, when the template is created. Python doesn't allow a bare lambda as a whole interpolation, so name the handler, or wrap an inline one in parentheses: onclick={(lambda: set_open(False))}.
  • evt.raw is the native event and is valid only synchronously during dispatch.
from wybthon import DomEvent, create_signal, event, html

items, set_items = create_signal([])
draft, set_draft = create_signal("")


def submit(evt: DomEvent) -> None:
    evt.prevent_default()
    set_items(lambda xs: [*xs, draft.peek()])
    set_draft("")


def edit(evt: DomEvent) -> None:
    set_draft(evt.target.value)


def keydown(evt: DomEvent) -> None:
    if evt.key == "Escape":
        set_draft("")


def clear() -> None:  # no event needed
    set_items([])


ignore_touch = event(lambda: None, passive=True)  # direct native listener

view = html(t"""
  <form onsubmit={submit} ontouchstart={ignore_touch}>
    <input value={draft()} oninput={edit} onkeydown={keydown}>
    <button type="button" onclick={clear}>Clear</button>
    <ul>{[html(t"<li>{x}</li>") for x in items()]}</ul>
  </form>
""")

docs.title: Delegation notes
docs.text:
• Delegation relies on bubbling, so non-bubbling types (focus, blur, mouseenter, mouseleave, pointerenter, pointerleave, scroll, load, error, invalid, and toggle) get a direct native listener on the element instead. For listener options such as passive or capture, wrap the handler in event, which also attaches a direct listener.
  • stop_propagation() stops both the delegated walk and native propagation; prevent_default() is applied by the kernel after the handler returns.
  • Unmounting a subtree drops its handlers on the Python side, and the kernel's DISPOSE_RANGE or DISPOSE command clears its listener bookkeeping natively. Root.dispose() unregisters the container as a delegation root.
  • In CPython tests, wybthon.testing fires events through the real dispatcher: fire.click(node), fire.input(node, value), fire.key_down(node, key).

docs.title: flow
docs.text:
Control flow: Show, For, Repeat, Switch/Match, dynamic, and client_only.

Show, For, Repeat, and Switch mount as native regions: one reactive computation that selects what to render, and an owned scope per branch or row. There's no wrapper component. A condition or source is an accessor (or a plain value); children and fallback are nodes or callables evaluated inside the region's own scope.

When a reactive hole re-renders and returns the same kind of region at the same place, the new condition or source is pushed into the mounted region; branches and rows that are still selected survive.

Callback shapes follow SolidJS 2.0:

  • Show(when, children): a callable children receives an Accessor for the truthy value (or the value itself with keyed=True).
  • For(each, children, keyed=True): children(item, index) where the shapes depend on keyed (see For).
  • Repeat(count, children): children(index: int).
  • Switch(Match(when, children), ..., fallback=...).
  • dynamic(source): a component whose implementation is chosen reactively.
  • client_only(children, fallback=...): content that only renders in the browser, after hydration.
Example 
Show(is_logged_in, html(t"<p>Welcome!</p>"), fallback=html(t"<p>Please log in</p>"))

For(todos, lambda todo, i: html(t"<li>{todo['title']}</li>"))

Repeat(rating, lambda i: html(t"<span>*</span>"))

Render a list with a stable subtree per row.

The mapping callback runs once per row; when the list changes, existing rows keep their DOM and are only moved, never re-diffed. A row's reactive scope is disposed when it leaves the list.

keyed selects how rows are matched, and with it the callback shape:

  • True (default): match by identity (scalars by value). children(item, index) receives the raw item and an Accessor[int] index.
  • False: match by position. children(item, index) receives an Accessor for the item at that position and an int index.
  • a callable key(item): match by key, updating the row in place when a new object has the same key. children(item, index) receives accessors for both.

The returned callable behaves like any component: call it with children and props to get a VNode. Each instance re-mounts when source resolves to a different component; while source is an async computation with no value yet, the instance keeps its current content and the nearest Loading shows its fallback. Passing None renders nothing.

In a page that wasn't server-rendered, the children render immediately. Use it for widgets that need browser APIs or whose output depends on the browser (a map, a chart measured from the viewport, the user's local time).

Run callback once the browser has finished hydrating the page.

Registered while hydrate mounts, it runs after the hydrated page has committed. Registered anywhere else (a page that wasn't server-rendered, or after hydration), it runs on the next tick. It doesn't say hydration succeeded, only that it's over. During a server render it does nothing. Matches Solid 2.0's onHydrationEnd.

While the browser hydrates, the region's server-rendered DOM is kept as is and nothing inside it is mounted, so it costs no Python work and never updates. In a page that wasn't server-rendered, the children render normally. Use it for content that never changes after the first paint: article bodies, footers, legal text.

Matches Solid 2.0's <NoHydration>.

docs.title: What's in this module
docs.text:
Control-flow primitives that create isolated reactive scopes, so only the relevant subtree updates when a condition or list changes. Conditions and sources are accessors, getters, or plain values, and children and fallback slots are nodes or callables evaluated inside the primitive's own scope. All arguments are positional except the keyword-only options noted below. In a compiled template, a call such as {Show(count() > 5, ...)} or {For(todos(), row)} receives each dynamic argument as a getter, exactly as a component does, so the condition or source stays reactive without a lambda.

Show, For, Repeat, and Switch mount as native regions, not wrapper components: each is one computation that selects what to render, plus an owned scope per branch or row. There's no component context or props object. When a reactive hole re-renders and returns the same kind of region in the same place, the new condition or source is pushed into the mounted region, so branches and rows that are still selected survive.

Name Description Show Show(when, children, fallback=None, *, keyed=False): render one branch by truthiness. For For(each, children, fallback=None, *, keyed=True): one cached row per item; rows move, never re-diff. Repeat Repeat(count, children, fallback=None, *, start=0): children(i) for i in range(start, start + count). Switch / Match Switch(Match(when, children, keyed=False), ..., fallback=None): first truthy branch wins. dynamic dynamic(source): a component whose implementation (a component or tag) is chosen by a reactive source. Call the result with children and props. client_only client_only(children, *, fallback=None): render children only in the browser, after hydration; fallback renders on the server. NoHydration NoHydration(*children): server-rendered HTML the browser keeps as static DOM instead of hydrating. Hydration Hydration(*children, id=None): a passthrough kept for parity with Solid 2.0. is_hydrating True only during the synchronous mount of hydrate. on_hydration_end on_hydration_end(callback): run callback once the page has finished hydrating (on the next tick when nothing is hydrating; never during a server render).

docs.title: For keying shapes
docs.text:
keyed selects how rows are matched between updates, and with it the callback shape:

keyed Rows match by children(item, index) receives True (default) Identity (scalars by value) the raw item, Accessor[int] False Position Accessor[T], int key(item) callable The key; a new object with the same key updates the row in place Accessor[T], Accessor[int]

The row callback runs once per row inside the row's owner scope and untracked; anything reactive inside a row belongs in a template expression, memo, or effect. With the default keying, the index accessor is the row itself, and the signal behind it is only created when something reads i() in a tracking scope. Passing a plain list for each (a name bound to a list, not an accessor or a compiled expression) renders once and warns in dev mode. A store list can be passed as is.

docs.title: Typed callbacks
docs.text:
For and Show have generic overloads, so type checkers infer the callback's parameters from the source (Repeat's callback is typed as taking an int):

Call Inferred parameters For(todos(), lambda todo, i: ...) todo: Todo, i: Accessor[int] For(todos(), lambda todo, i: ..., keyed=False) todo: Accessor[Todo], i: int For(todos(), lambda todo, i: ..., keyed=lambda t: t.id) todo: Accessor[Todo], i: Accessor[int] Show(user, lambda u: ...) u: Accessor[User] Show(user, lambda u: ..., keyed=True) u: User

For accepts the list or an accessor for it, and both infer the same row type. A callback inside a call ({For(todos(), lambda todo, i: ...)}) may be a bare lambda; only a lambda that is the whole interpolation needs parentheses. Pass the accessor to Show (Show(user, ...)) when its callback takes the value.

from wybthon import For, Match, Repeat, Show, Switch, create_signal, html

todos, set_todos = create_signal([{"id": 1, "title": "Ship", "done": False}])
status, set_status = create_signal("ready")
rating, set_rating = create_signal(3)
user, set_user = create_signal(None)


def greeting(u):
    return html(t"<li>Hello, {u()['name']}</li>")


def numbered(todo, i):
    return html(t"<li>{i() + 1}. {todo['title']}</li>")


def live_title(todo, i):
    return html(t"<li>{todo()['title']}</li>")


loading = html(t"<li>Loading...</li>")
ready = html(t"<li>Ready</li>")
unknown = html(t"<li>Unknown</li>")

view = html(t"""
  <ul>
    {Show(user, greeting, fallback=html(t"<li>Sign in</li>"))}
    {For(todos(), numbered)}
    {For(todos(), live_title, keyed=lambda t: t["id"])}
    <li>{Repeat(rating(), lambda i: html(t"<span>*</span>"), start=1)}</li>
    {Switch(Match(status() == "loading", loading), Match(status() == "ready", ready), fallback=unknown)}
  </ul>
""")
  • Show tracks only the truthiness of when; a callable children may take the value accessor (or the raw value with keyed=True, which re-creates the branch on every change). Show and Switch are one branch computation that re-mounts only when the selected branch changes.
  • children and fallback may be nodes, such as templates, or callables. A node branch is mounted afresh each time it's selected.
  • Repeat is driven purely by the count: growing mounts tail slots, shrinking disposes them, and nothing else is touched. count and start may be accessors or ints.
  • dynamic accepts a tag name, a component, None, or an accessor returning one of those; each instance remounts when the resolved component changes.
  • client_only renders its fallback during a server render and while hydrating, then its children; see Server rendering. For one-off work after hydration (starting a widget that measures the DOM, say), register it with on_hydration_end.
  • NoHydration costs no Python work while hydrating: the kernel keeps the region's server DOM as is (CLAIM_STATIC) and nothing inside it mounts or updates. In a page that wasn't server-rendered, its children render normally.

docs.title: forms
docs.text:
Form state, validation helpers, and accessibility attribute utilities.

This module gives you a small but complete toolkit for building controlled form components on top of Wybthon's reactive primitives:

  • form_state creates a map of Field entries (each backed by signals for value, error, and touched flags).
  • bind_text, bind_checkbox, and bind_select return prop dictionaries you can spread onto inputs.
  • on_submit and on_submit_validated wrap submit handlers with the right preventDefault / validation glue.
  • Validator helpers (required, min_length, max_length, email) compose with validate, validate_field, and validate_form.
  • a11y_control_attrs and error_message_attrs generate ARIA attributes (reactively) so error messages are announced correctly.
Example 
form = form_state({"name": "", "email": ""})
rules = {"name": [required()], "email": [required(), email()]}

def save(fields):
    print({k: f.value() for k, f in fields.items()})

html(t'''
  <form onsubmit={on_submit_validated(rules, save, form)}>
    <input {bind_text(form["name"], validators=rules["name"])}>
    <span {error_message_attrs(id="name-error")}>{form["name"].error()}</span>
    <button type="submit">Save</button>
  </form>
''')
See Also
  • Forms guide

docs.text:
A small toolkit for controlled forms on top of signals: per-field state, binding helpers that return prop dicts to spread onto inputs, composable validators, submit wrappers, and reactive ARIA attributes. Import it from wybthon.forms; these names aren't re-exported from wybthon.

Name Description Field Reactive state for one field: value/set_value, error/set_error, touched/set_touched, and .validate(validators). form_state {name: initial} to a FormState. FormState A {name: Field} dict with aggregate dirty, validating, submitting, and submit_error state, plus data(), reset(), and await submit(handler, rules=...). bind_text {"value": accessor, "on_input": handler} for text inputs, validating on every input event. bind_number Numeric input binding that keeps an empty value as None. bind_checkbox {"checked": accessor, "on_change": handler} for a boolean field. bind_select {"value": accessor, "on_change": handler} for <select>. bind_multiselect Binds every selected option of a <select multiple> to a list field. on_submit Submit handler that prevents default and calls handler(form). on_submit_validated Same, but validates the whole form against rules first. Validator, AsyncValidator Type aliases: (value) -> str | None, and the same returning an awaitable. required, min_length, max_length, email Validator factories with optional custom messages. validate, validate_field, validate_form Run validators on a value, a field, or a whole form. rules_from_schema Build a rules map from {"name": {"required": True, "min_length": 2}, ...}. a11y_control_attrs Reactive aria_invalid and aria_describedby for a control. error_message_attrs id, role="alert", and aria_live="polite" for the message container. 
from wybthon import component, html
from wybthon.forms import (
    a11y_control_attrs,
    bind_checkbox,
    bind_text,
    email,
    error_message_attrs,
    form_state,
    on_submit_validated,
    required,
)


@component
def Signup():
    fields = form_state({"name": "", "email": "", "agree": False})
    rules = {"name": [required()], "email": [required(), email()]}
    name = fields["name"]

    def save(f):
        print({k: field.value.peek() for k, field in f.items()})

    return html(t"""
      <form onsubmit={on_submit_validated(rules, save, fields)}>
        <label for="name">Name</label>
        <input
          id="name"
          {bind_text(name, validators=rules["name"])}
          {a11y_control_attrs(name, described_by_id="name-error")}
        >
        <span {error_message_attrs(id="name-error")}>{name.error()}</span>
        <label><input type="checkbox" {bind_checkbox(fields["agree"])}> I agree</label>
        <button type="submit">Save</button>
      </form>
    """)
  • The binding helpers return prop mappings: spread them onto a template tag (<input {bind_text(field)}>) or pass them to h() (h("input", bind_text(field))).
  • A field's error accessor returns None while the field is valid, so {name.error()} renders nothing until there's a message.
  • touched becomes True on the first input, so you can delay showing errors with an expression such as {name.error() if name.touched() else None}.
  • email() accepts empty values; combine it with required().
  • In CPython tests, drive a form with wybthon.testing: fire.input(screen.get_by_label_text("Name"), "Ada"), then fire.submit(form_node).

docs.title: kernel
docs.text:
Batched DOM command buffer and rendering backends.

This module is the single point of contact between Wybthon's renderer and the real DOM. Instead of calling DOM APIs directly (each call crosses the Python-to-JS bridge in Pyodide), the reconciler and prop appliers emit compact operations into a buffer. At well-defined commit points (end of a render, end of an effect flush) the whole buffer is serialized once and handed to a small JavaScript kernel that applies every operation natively. A mount of a 1,000-row table becomes one bridge crossing instead of tens of thousands.

Core concepts:

  • Node handles. DOM nodes are referred to by integer ids allocated on the Python side. The kernel keeps an id -> Node registry, so no JsProxy objects flow through the hot path.
  • Ops. Each operation is a small tuple, (opcode, ...args), serialized as a JSON array. See the OP_* constants.
  • Backends. BrowserBackend drives the real DOM through the embedded JS kernel. PythonBackend is a reference interpreter that applies the same ops to any DOM-like stub document; it backs the unit tests and the stubbed benchmark so both exercise the exact protocol the browser sees.
  • Hydration. CLAIM_* ops adopt server-rendered nodes in document order instead of creating them. Claims are tolerant: a node that doesn't match is created in place, and HYDRATE_END removes server nodes nobody claimed.
  • Events. Event delegation lives in the kernel: one native listener per event type walks the ancestor chain natively and calls into Python once for the matching bubbling route with a JSON payload. See wybthon.events for the Python half.

Application code never imports this module directly; it's plumbing for the reconciler, wybthon._dom_props, and wybthon.events.

docs.title: What's in this module
docs.text:
kernel is the single point of contact between the renderer and the real DOM. The reconciler, the compiled template mounts, the prop appliers, and the event system emit compact ops (JSON-serializable tuples against integer node ids) into a buffer; commit() hands the whole buffer to the active backend in one Python-to-JS bridge crossing. The browser half lives in _kernel.js, shipped with the package. Application code never imports this module; it matters when you're writing low-level tests against the stub backend or debugging the wire protocol. For component tests, use wybthon.testing.

Name Description commit Flush every queued op to the backend in one crossing (no-op when empty). BrowserBackend Drives the real DOM through the JS kernel; created automatically in Pyodide. PythonBackend Reference interpreter applying the same ops to a DOM-like stub document (used by wybthon.testing, the unit tests, and the stubbed benchmark). set_backend Install a backend (tests pass a PythonBackend). reset Test helper: clear the op buffer, id counters, and template registry, optionally installing a backend.

Two more module-level hooks matter to tests. register_template(shape) registers the static skeleton of a compiled html template in the same batch as its first clone. html_templates (True, False, or None for "ask the backend") gates template mounting; set it to False to force per-node commands.

docs.title: Wire protocol
docs.text:
Each op is a JSON array whose first element is the opcode. Node ids are allocated on the Python side, so no JsProxy objects flow through the hot path; None anchors mean "append".

Op Payload Effect CREATE_ELEMENT id, tag document.createElement CREATE_ELEMENT_NS id, namespace, tag document.createElementNS (SVG, MathML) CREATE_TEXT id, text document.createTextNode CREATE_COMMENT id[, data] Comment marker (fragment and hole anchors); Loading boundaries carry a key in data during server rendering and hydration REGISTER_TPL tpl_id, html, count, [text offsets], [[offset, event_type], ...] Parse a template's or shape's skeleton once via <template>, and record its text slots and delegated listeners CLONE first_id, tpl_id, parent_id, anchor_id, *texts Clone the prototype, register a dense id block in pre-order, fill the text slots, mark the delegated listeners, and insert before the anchor INSERT parent_id, id, anchor_id insertBefore (None anchor appends) REMOVE id Detach from the parent; the node stays registered MOVE_RANGE parent_id, first_id, last_id, anchor_id Move a contiguous mounted range DISPOSE_RANGE first_id, last_id Remove a contiguous range of siblings and release every registered node inside it, walking the removed nodes natively DISPOSE id Remove one node and release every registered node inside it HOLE_TEXT id, text Reuse a hole's placeholder as a visible text node RELEASE_TPL tpl_id Evict a native template prototype SET_TEXT id, text nodeValue assignment SET_ATTR id, name, value setAttribute, or removeAttribute when value is None SET_PROP id, name, value DOM property assignment (value, checked, selectedValues, innerHTML) SET_STYLE id, decls style.setProperty / removeProperty per kebab-case declaration LISTEN / UNLISTEN id, event_type[, options] Delegated bookkeeping for nodes outside a template, or a direct native listener with options; unlisten omits options RELEASE [ids] Drop registry entries and listener sets (used for a disposed root's container) ROOT / UNROOT id Start or stop delegating events from this container instead of document HYDRATE root_id Start claiming server-rendered nodes under root_id CLAIM_ELEMENT id, parent_id, tag, namespace Adopt the parent's next element, or create one in place on a mismatch CLAIM_TEXT id, parent_id, text Adopt the next text node, splitting text the HTML parser merged; empty text is created CLAIM_COMMENT id, parent_id, data Adopt the next comment; a keyed end marker (/...) resynchronizes by searching forward CLAIM_STATIC parent_id, end_marker Keep the server nodes before the marker as static DOM (a NoHydration region) HYDRATE_END none Remove server nodes nobody claimed and stop claiming

A row of the js-framework-benchmark table costs one command, a CLONE that carries the row's text and its label's first value, when it's written as an html template. Clearing a list is one DISPOSE_RANGE. Unmounting never sends lists of every node id: the kernel releases the removed nodes itself. See Virtual DOM for how compiled templates, precompiled mount functions, and lazy node ids fit together.

hydrate emits the claim ops; see Server rendering. stats() reports node, template, listener, and root counts plus hydration_mismatches, and take_state() and replay_events() read the server state and replay input recorded before hydration.

Events travel the other way: the JS kernel installs one native listener per event type on each render root, walks the ancestor chain natively, and calls the Python dispatcher once for the matching bubbling route with a small JSON payload (see events).

from wybthon import kernel

# In a CPython test, install the stub backend over any DOM-like document
# (wybthon.testing and the test suite's conftest do this for you).
kernel.reset(kernel.PythonBackend(stub_document))
kernel.html_templates = False  # optional: force per-node commands

docs.title: lazy
docs.text:
Lazy-loaded components integrated with Loading boundaries.

lazy wraps a loader callback (sync or async) that produces a component. The component loads on first mount, backed by an async create_memo: while the load is in flight, the nearest Loading boundary shows its fallback, and a load failure raises into the nearest Errored boundary. This matches SolidJS's lazy(() => import(...)) semantics, adapted to Python's import system.

The loader may return:

  • a component callable directly,
  • an imported module (an export is picked by convention: Page, then default, then the first callable), or
  • a module path string, or a (module_path, attr) tuple, imported via importlib.

Async loaders can await arbitrary work first (for example micropip.install(...) in Pyodide) before returning any of the above.

Example 
About = lazy(lambda: ("app.about.page", "Page"))

async def load_chart():
    import micropip
    await micropip.install("app-charts")
    import app_charts
    return app_charts.Chart

Chart = lazy(load_chart)
Chart.preload()  # warm the cache on hover/intent

html(t"<main>{Loading(About(), fallback=html(t'<p>Loading...</p>'))}</main>")
See Also
  • Async and loading guide

docs.title: What's in this module
docs.text:
lazy defers loading a component until it first mounts, and lazy_module defers any other import until it's first needed. A lazy component's load is backed by an async create_memo, so it suspends into the nearest Loading while in flight and raises into the nearest Errored on failure, matching SolidJS's lazy(() => import(...)) adapted to Python's import system.

Name Description lazy lazy(loader, *, chunk=None); the loader is a zero-arg callable, sync or async, returning a component, a module, a module-path string, or a (module_path, attr) tuple. chunk names a build chunk to fetch first. LazyComponent What lazy returns: a Component with .preload() to start the load early and .retry() to retry a failed load. lazy_module lazy_module(loader, *, chunk=None): a cached, on-demand import of a module that isn't a component, the counterpart of Solid 2.0's lazyModule. LazyModule What lazy_module returns: call it (or .preload()) for an awaitable of the module; .peek() returns the module once it has loaded, else None. 
from wybthon import Loading, component, html, lazy
from wybthon.router import Link, Route, Router

About = lazy(lambda: ("app.about.page", "Page"))  # importlib, attribute "Page"


async def load_chart():
    import micropip

    await micropip.install("app-charts")
    import app_charts

    return app_charts.Chart


Chart = lazy(load_chart)


@component
def App():
    return Loading(
        Router([Route("/about", About), Route("/chart", Chart)]),
        fallback=html(t"<p>Loading...</p>"),
    )


nav_link = Link("Chart", href="/chart", on_mouseover=Chart.preload)
  • When the loader returns a module, the export is picked by convention: Page, then default, then the first callable.
  • The loader runs at most once; the resolved component is cached across unmounts.
  • Props and children passed to the lazy component are forwarded to the loaded component unchanged.

lazy_module loads code that isn't a component: a route table, a parser, a charting library's helpers. The loader runs once, on the first call or .preload(), and every caller awaits the same import.

from wybthon import lazy_module

admin = lazy_module(lambda: "app.admin.routes", chunk="admin")


async def open_admin():
    routes = await admin()  # imports on first use, then cached
    routes.register()


admin.peek()  # the module, or None until it has loaded

docs.title: loading
docs.text:
Loading and Reveal: fallback UI for async computations.

Loading is the async boundary (SolidJS 2.0's Loading, the successor to Suspense). It covers initial readiness: any read of an async computation under the boundary that raises NotReadyError registers the computation with the boundary, and the boundary shows its fallback until every registered computation has produced its first value.

Once content is on screen the boundary gets out of the way. A recompute of an async memo that already has a value is a transition: the parts of the UI that depend on the changed input hold their previous state until the new value lands, and the boundary never shows its fallback again. Use is_pending to render inline refresh hints. Pass on= to opt back into the fallback for specific changes (swapping the record being shown rather than refreshing it).

Reveal coordinates multiple Loading boundaries beneath it, controlling the order their contents reveal (order) and whether every pending boundary shows its own fallback (collapsed).

Example 
async def load_user():
    return await fetch_json(f"/api/users/{user_id()}")

user = create_memo(load_user)

html(t'''
  <{Loading} fallback={html(t"<p>Loading...</p>")} on={user_id}>
    <div>{user()["name"]}</div>
  </{Loading}>
''')
See Also
  • Async and loading guide

The boundary waits for them initially even if the children never read them, and when one of them changes while data under the boundary is pending, the fallback shows again instead of the old content being held. docs.title: Reveal
docs.text:
Reveal(children: Any = None, *, order: RevealOrder = 'sequential', collapsed: bool = False) -> VNode

Coordinate the reveal order of multiple Loading boundaries.

Each Loading boundary mounted underneath (that isn't nested inside another boundary) registers with the Reveal in mount order, and the Reveal decides when each may show its content and whether it shows its fallback. A Reveal nested inside another is one composite slot in the parent's order: its boundaries stay on their fallbacks until the parent releases the slot, then follow the inner order.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default children Any

Content containing one or more Loading boundaries.

None order RevealOrder

"sequential" (default; contents reveal in DOM order, each waiting for the ones before it), "together" (the whole group reveals at once when every boundary has loaded), or "natural" (each boundary reveals on its own data; useful for a nested group that should count as one slot in the parent without coordinating internally).

'sequential' collapsed bool

Only consulted with order="sequential". When True, boundaries past the current frontier render nothing instead of their own fallback, so only one fallback shows.

False

Returns:

Type Description VNode

A component VNode.

Example 
html(t'''
  <{Reveal} collapsed>
    {Loading(PanelA(), fallback=html(t"<p>Loading A...</p>"))}
    {Loading(PanelB(), fallback=html(t"<p>Loading B...</p>"))}
  </{Reveal}>
''')
Note

Every boundary's content mounts immediately (parked off-document while pending), so all of them load in parallel; order only controls when each is revealed.

docs.title: What's in this module
docs.text:
Loading is the async boundary. Any read of an async computation under it that raises NotReadyError registers that computation with the boundary, and the boundary shows its fallback until every registered computation has a first value. Content stays mounted the whole time, parked off-document, so async memos created inside it keep running and nothing is torn down. Revalidations never re-trigger the boundary: a recompute of a memo that has a value is a transition, which holds the affected UI on the old state until the new value lands, and is_pending is the tool for inline refresh hints. on= names inputs whose change should show the fallback again instead (a new record, not a refresh).

Reveal coordinates several Loading boundaries beneath it: the order their contents appear and how many fallbacks show at once.

Name Description Loading Loading(children, *, fallback=None, on=None); children is a node, callable, or list; on is an accessor or list of accessors the boundary waits for, and whose change shows the fallback again. Reveal Reveal(children, *, order="sequential", collapsed=False); order is "sequential", "together", or "natural"; collapsed=True shows only the next fallback in a sequential group. 
from typing import Any

from wybthon import Loading, Props, Reveal, component, create_memo, html, is_pending


class UserCardProps(Props):
    user_id: int


@component
def UserCard(props: UserCardProps):
    async def load_user():
        uid = props.user_id  # tracked: refetches when it changes
        return await fetch_json(f"/api/users/{uid}")

    user = create_memo(load_user)

    return Loading(
        html(t"""
          <div>
            <p>{user()["name"]}</p>
            <span>{"Refreshing..." if is_pending(user) else ""}</span>
          </div>
        """),
        fallback=html(t"<p>Loading...</p>"),
    )


class DashboardProps(Props):
    settings: dict[str, Any]


@component
def Dashboard(props: DashboardProps):
    return Reveal(
        [
            Loading(UserCard(user_id=1), fallback=html(t"<p>Loading user...</p>")),
            Loading(Activity(), fallback=html(t"<p>Loading activity...</p>"), on=lambda: props.settings),
        ],
        collapsed=True,
    )
  • on= takes accessors, so wrap a prop in a function (on=lambda: props.settings) to watch it.
  • on= makes the boundary wait for specific accessors even if the children never read them, and when one of them changes while data under the boundary is pending, the fallback shows again instead of the old content being held.
  • With order="sequential" contents reveal in DOM order, each waiting for the ones before it; "together" reveals all at once; "natural" lets each boundary reveal on its own data. With collapsed=True only the next pending fallback shows.
  • Every boundary's content mounts immediately, so all of them load in parallel; order only controls when each is revealed. A Reveal nested inside another is one slot in the parent's order; boundaries nested inside another boundary coordinate with that boundary.

docs.text:
Portal component for rendering children into a different DOM container.

Use Portal to render content outside of the current component's DOM ancestor while keeping it part of the same reactive ownership tree (so signals, effects, and context still work). Common use cases include modals, tooltips, and toast notifications.

docs.text:
Portal(children: Any = None, *, mount: Any = 'body') -> VNode

Render children into a different DOM container.

Matches SolidJS's <Portal mount={...}>. The children mount into mount (by default document.body) while remaining linked to the surrounding component's reactive scope, so signals, context, and lifecycle hooks still apply, and they're removed when the portal unmounts.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default children Any

A VNode, a list of VNodes, or a zero-arg callable (rendered as a reactive hole).

None mount Any

The target container: an Element instance, a CSS selector string, or a kernel node id. Defaults to "body".

'body'

Returns:

Type Description VNode

A component VNode whose children render inside mount.

Note

A portal renders nothing during a server render. Its children mount in the browser once the page has hydrated.

Example 
modal = html(t'<div class="modal"><p>Modal content</p></div>')
html(t"<main>{Show(show_modal(), Portal(modal, mount='#modal-root'))}</main>")

docs.title: What's in this module
docs.text:
Portal renders its children into a different DOM container while keeping them inside the current reactive ownership tree, so signals, context, cleanups, and error boundaries behave exactly as they would for in-place children. It's the tool for modals, tooltips, popovers, and toasts that must escape their parent's layout.

Name Description Portal Portal(children, *, mount="body"); children is a node, a list, or a zero-arg callable (rendered as a hole); mount is an Element, a CSS selector, or a kernel node id. 
from wybthon import Portal, Show, component, create_signal, html


@component
def Modal():
    is_open, set_open = create_signal(False)

    def toggle():
        set_open(lambda v: not v)

    dialog = Portal(
        html(t"""
          <div class="modal">
            <p>I'm in #modal-root</p>
            <button onclick={toggle}>Close</button>
          </div>
        """),
        mount="#modal-root",
    )

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <button onclick={toggle}>Open</button>
        {Show(is_open(), dialog)}
      </div>
    """)
  • Content is removed when the portal's owner is disposed (here, when Show flips back to falsy).
  • The mount target becomes an event delegation root for as long as the portal is mounted, so event handlers inside it fire even when the target sits outside the container passed to render (a <body>-level modal layer, for example).
  • Context flows through the reactive tree, not the DOM tree, so use_context inside the portal sees the surrounding providers.

docs.title: Accessor
docs.text:
A zero-argument callable that returns a reactive value.

Calling an accessor inside a tracking scope (a memo, an effect's compute stage, or a reactive hole) subscribes that scope to the value. peek reads without subscribing.

Every reactive read in Wybthon goes through an Accessor: create_signal getters are Signals, create_memo returns a Memo. Embedding an accessor in a template or VNode tree creates a reactive hole. Type it as Accessor[T] in signatures when you accept any of them.

docs.title: Computation
docs.text:
Computation(fn: Callable[..., Any], *, kind: int, value: Any = None, equals: Any = _DEFAULT_EQUALS, apply: Callable[..., Any] | None = None, defer: bool = False, error: Callable[[BaseException], Any] | None = None, lazy: bool = False, unobserved: Callable[[], Any] | None = None, pass_prev: bool | None = None, name: str | None = None, eager: bool = False, apply_scope: bool = True, data: bool = False, keep: bool = False)

Bases: Owner

A tracked function: the node type behind memos and effects.

A computation re-runs when a source it read changes. It's also an owner: children created during a run are disposed before the next run, so conditionally created effects never leak.

Kinds:

  • memo: carries a value that other computations can read.
  • render effect: runs in the render phase of a flush (holes and prop bindings) before the DOM commit.
  • effect: runs after the DOM commit and may have a split compute/apply shape.

Effects take part in transitions: when a re-run's compute stage read data a transition holds, the apply stage is postponed until the transition reveals. Eager effects (eager=True, used for projections and selectors whose apply stage produces more graph data) always apply immediately and hold what they write instead.

A Memo is both a Computation (it tracks sources and recomputes lazily) and an Accessor (call it to read). Recomputation happens on read after a source changed, and observers are notified only when the recomputed value differs under the memo's equals policy.

Async bodies (async def, or an async generator) make the memo an async computation; see create_memo.

docs.title: NotReadyError
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

Raised when reading an async computation that has no value yet.

Propagates "not ready" through the graph: a memo whose body reads a pending async memo becomes pending itself, and a reactive hole that hits NotReadyError keeps its previous content while the nearest Loading boundary shows its fallback.

Application code rarely raises or catches this directly; use is_pending and latest to observe pending state without suspending.

Owners form a tree. Disposing an owner disposes its children first (depth-first), then runs its own cleanup callbacks LIFO. Every computation is an owner, as is each component instance, each For row, and each create_root.

Owners also carry context values (see create_context) and an optional error handler installed by Errored.

Tear down this owner and every descendant.
