docs.title: The compiler
docs.text: Wybthon's compiler is the step that makes {count() * 2} reactive without a lambda around it. It rewrites every html(t"...") call in a module before the module runs, the way Solid's compiler rewrites JSX. This page explains what it changes, where it runs, how to see what it did, and where its rule stops. You don't need any of it to write components, but it's what to read when a template doesn't behave as you expect.

docs.title: What Solid's compiler does, and what Wybthon's does
docs.text:
Solid's compiler does two jobs with JSX:

  1. It turns the static markup into a <template> that the browser clones per instance.
  2. It turns every dynamic expression in the markup into a getter, so {count() * 2} re-runs when count changes, and a component receives its props as getters it reads later.

Wybthon does both for html templates. A PEP 750 t-string keeps each interpolation as a separate node in the module's syntax tree, so a small transform over Python's ast can make the same decisions before the module runs. There's no new syntax and no change to the language: the source you write is ordinary Python 3.14.

@component
def Counter(props: CounterProps):
    count, set_count = create_signal(0)
    return html(t"<p>{count()} doubled is {count() * 2}, step {props.step}</p>")

compiles to, roughly:

@component
def Counter(props: CounterProps):
    count, set_count = create_signal(0)
    return html(
        t"<p>{lambda: count()} doubled is {lambda: count() * 2}, step {lambda: props.step}</p>",
        __wybthon_t0__,  # the literal's parse tree and mount function, built at compile time
    )

Each deferred expression is a slot's binding: the renderer runs it as its own computation and updates only that text node when what it read changes. The component body still runs once.

docs.title: The rule: dynamic or static
docs.text:
An interpolation is dynamic when its expression contains a call, an attribute access, or a subscript, not counting the bodies of lambdas inside it. Everything else (a name, a constant, a lambda, an f-string of names) is static. This is Solid's rule: a name can't change by itself, but a call or a member access can read a signal, a store, or a prop.

What a dynamic expression becomes depends on where it sits:

Position Example A dynamic expression becomes Child <p>{count() * 2}</p> A getter: a reactive hole. Call in a child position {Show(count() > 5, ...)} A component built with getters, or a reactive hole; see Calls in a child position. Attribute <li class={row_class(id)}> A getter: a reactive binding. Part of an attribute <div class="card {kind()}"> A getter for that part; the parts render as one string. Component tag attribute <{Card} title={user().name}> A getter, which the component reads through props.title. Event handler onclick={make_handler(id)} Nothing: it's evaluated once. Handlers are values. ref <input ref={refs[i]}> Nothing: it's evaluated once. Spread <input {omit(props, "label")}> Nothing: it's evaluated once, when the template is created. The component in a tag <{views["card"]}> Nothing: it's evaluated once. Nested template {html(t"<b>{name()}</b>")} Nothing: it's markup, compiled in place with its own getters.

On a component tag, an attribute named like a handler (on_close, onClose) or ref is passed as is too.

A static expression keeps its run-time meaning. A signal or memo placed directly ({count}) is an accessor, so it's bound reactively; a lambda ({(lambda: count() * 2)}) is a reactive expression; any other value is applied once. Both {count} and {count()} update when count changes.

The rule is syntactic, so it errs on the side of deferring. {item.name} on a plain object becomes a getter that reads nothing reactive. That costs almost nothing: before allocating a computation, the renderer runs such an expression once under a lightweight probe, and when it reads nothing reactive the value is applied and no computation exists. A getter whose value is itself an accessor ({row["label"]} returning a signal) binds to that accessor directly.

docs.title: Calls in a child position
docs.text:
{Show(...)}, {Card(title=user().name)}, and {badge(user())} are all calls, but they mean different things. In JSX the difference is syntactic (<Card> against badge()); in Python it isn't, and a naming convention can't tell Card(...) from Decimal(...). So a call in a child position whose callee is a name (Card), or a dotted name ending in a capitalized attribute (ui.Card), is dispatched when the template is created:

{Card(title=user().name)}
# compiles to
__wybthon__.call(Card, lambda: Card(title=user().name), lambda: Card(title=__wybthon__.getter(lambda: user().name)))
  • When the callee is a component, it's called with the prepared arguments: each dynamic argument is a getter, exactly what <{Card} title={user().name}> passes. Components are @component functions, lazy and dynamic components, contexts, and the built-ins that render markup (Show, For, Repeat, Switch, Loading, Errored, Portal, Link, and the rest). Arguments are prepared recursively, so Errored(Loading(...)) builds its inner component the same way, and handler-named keywords (on_close=...) and ref are passed as they are.
  • Any other callee (badge, str, Decimal) gets the deferred call: the whole call becomes one reactive hole, which is what Solid does with a function call in JSX.

A built-in that takes a callback (For's row function, Show's children, a keyed function) unwraps a getter it receives once, untracked, so {For(rows(), make_row(kind))} behaves as it reads.

A method call ({item.upper()}) isn't a component, and a call with no arguments ({Header()}) has no props to prepare, so both are ordinary dynamic expressions: a hole that makes the call.

docs.title: Captured names
docs.text:
A getter runs later, possibly after a loop variable has moved on. So the compiler captures, by value, every name the expression reads from an enclosing function scope whose binding can change: loop and comprehension variables, names assigned more than once or with += or :=, and nonlocal names. They become keyword-only defaults of the getter's lambda:

def rows(items):
    out = []
    for item in items:
        out.append(html(t"<li>{item.name}</li>"))  # the getter is `lambda *, item=item: item.name`
    return out

Each row reads its own item, so Python's late binding never shows through a template. A name bound once is read through its closure as usual, and templates in class bodies can read class-level names.

docs.title: Conversions and format specs
docs.text: {price():.2f} and {name()!r} fold into the getter, so the hole renders the formatted text and re-formats it when the value changes. A static value with a format spec is formatted once.

docs.title: Precompiled templates
docs.text:
The compiler parses and validates each literal with the same code html() uses at run time, so a malformed template is an error when the module is compiled, with the file and line:

  File "app/views.py", line 5
    return html(t"<i>{count()} <input {attrs}>")
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
SyntaxError: Unclosed tag <i>
  in template: t'<i>{...} <input {...}>'

It then writes three things at the top of the module:

  • the literal's normalized parse tree, as a tuple of constants;
  • one mount function per element (__wybthon_m0__, ...), as an ordinary def;
  • an entry (__wybthon_t0__ = __wybthon__.template(...)) holding both, which does its work on first use.

The call becomes html(t"...", __wybthon_t0__). On first use, the entry rebuilds the template's slot plan from the tree and installs the mount functions. A precompiled template therefore skips everything html does for an uncompiled literal: tokenizing the markup, validating it against the HTML parser's rules, and generating each mount function with compile and exec. When the build's Python version matches the Pyodide runtime's, wyb build also ships every compiled module as bytecode, so the browser doesn't compile the Python source either; see Deployment. With bytecode = false, the import hook compiles each module once, as the page imports it. The engine v4 evaluation measures the difference.

The generated names (__wybthon__, __wybthon_t0__, __wybthon_m0__) are dunder names, which Python never mangles inside classes and applications don't define.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text:
You don't call the compiler yourself. It runs in each place Python code enters a Wybthon application:

  • wyb build and wyb dev run every application module through the compiler, which also checks every template, and write the compiled bytecode into the archives when the build's Python version matches the runtime's. The import hook uses that bytecode as is, so such a page never compiles anything.
  • The import hook. import wybthon installs it, and it compiles candidate modules imported after that: source files outside the standard library that mention wybthon and html and contain a t-string. Everything else loads exactly as it would without the hook. Compiled code is cached next to the normal bytecode under its own tag (views.cpython-314.opt-wyb1.pyc), so a plain compile cached earlier is never mistaken for a compiled one. wybthon.compiler.install() and uninstall() add and remove it explicitly.
  • The pytest plugin. Installing Wybthon registers a pytest11 plugin that compiles test modules and conftest.py files alongside pytest's assertion rewriting, so templates in tests behave exactly as they do in the application. Disable it with -p no:wybthon.
  • wyb run script.py runs a script with its own templates compiled and the hook installed, for scripts and quick experiments. Arguments after the script are passed to it.
  • Prerendering imports the application after Wybthon, so the hook compiles it.

For code you build at run time, wybthon.compiler.compile_source(source, filename) returns a code object with the templates compiled, ready for exec.

docs.title: Templates that weren't compiled
docs.text:
html() still works on a template that reaches it uncompiled: it compiles the literal itself on its first call. But by then Python has already evaluated each interpolation once, so {count() * 2} arrived as a number and would never update. In dev mode, html() checks each interpolation's source text and raises TemplateError when an expression the compiler would have deferred arrived as a plain value:

wybthon.templates.TemplateError: {count() * 2} was evaluated once instead of becoming
reactive, because this template wasn't compiled. Templates compile automatically in
modules imported after wybthon, in wyb build and wyb dev, and under pytest; run a
script with `wyb run script.py`, or wrap the expression in a lambda.
  in template: t'<p>{...}</p>'

The usual causes, and their fixes:

  • A script run with python script.py. The __main__ module is compiled by Python before Wybthon is imported. Run it with wyb run script.py, or move its components into a module the script imports.
  • A module that was already loading when Wybthon was first imported. The hook only sees modules imported after import wybthon has run, so the module whose own from wybthon import ... line is the first import of Wybthon isn't compiled. Import wybthon first, for example in your package's entry point.
  • The REPL, exec, and eval. Compile the source with compile_source before executing it, or write {(lambda: count() * 2)}, which is reactive with or without the compiler.
  • A t-string that isn't written in the html() call. The compiler only rewrites html(t"...") where the argument is the literal itself. tpl = t"..."; html(tpl) isn't compiled; write the literal in the call.

Production builds turn dev mode off, but they compile every module, so the check has nothing to catch there.

docs.title: Inspecting what it did
docs.text:
wybthon.compiler.transform is the compiler's entry point: it takes a module's syntax tree and rewrites it in place. Print the result to see the generated header and the rewritten calls. ast.unparse prints each interpolation as you wrote it, so print the interpolations' new expressions separately:

import ast

from wybthon.compiler import transform

source = """
from wybthon import Show, html

def view(count, kind, price, items):
    rows = [html(t"<li>{item.name}</li>") for item in items]
    return html(t"<p class={kind()}>{count()} {count} {price():.2f} {Show(count() > 5, rows)}</p>")
"""

tree = transform(ast.parse(source))
print(ast.unparse(tree))
for node in ast.walk(tree):
    if isinstance(node, ast.Interpolation):
        print(f"{{{node.str}}}  ->  {ast.unparse(node.value)}")

The module now starts with import wybthon._compiled as __wybthon__, followed by each template's mount functions and its entry:

__wybthon_t0__ = __wybthon__.template(("<li>", "</li>"), ((0, "li", (), ((2, 0),)),), (__wybthon_m0__,), (0,))

The entry's arguments are the literal's static strings, its parse tree, its mount functions, and the slots whose expressions make no calls (the ones the renderer probes before allocating a computation). The interpolations print as:

{kind()}  ->  lambda: kind()
{count()}  ->  lambda: count()
{count}  ->  count
{price()}  ->  lambda: __wybthon__.fmt(price(), None, f'.2f')
{Show(count() > 5, rows)}  ->  __wybthon__.call(Show, lambda: Show(count() > 5, rows), lambda: Show(__wybthon__.getter(lambda: count() > 5), rows))
{item.name}  ->  lambda *, item=item: item.name

{price():.2f} prints as {price()} because the format spec is part of the getter now.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• A call's callee is evaluated when the template is created. {Card(...)} looks up Card once, and the choice between building a component and making a hole is made then. To choose a component reactively, use dynamic.
  • await, yield, and assignment expressions stay eager. Moving {await load()} or {(n := count())} into a lambda would change what it means, so the compiler leaves it alone and it's evaluated once.
  • Type checkers don't see inside the markup. The HTML around the interpolations is a string, so a tag's attributes (<{Card} title={...}>) aren't checked statically; dev mode checks them at run time. The interpolated expressions are ordinary Python and are checked: {Card(title=user().name)} is checked against Card's props, and the checker sees title as a str even though the compiler passes a getter. Use the call form when you want the checker's help.
  • Tracebacks point into getters you didn't write. Each getter keeps its interpolation's source position, so the traceback names the right file and line.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read Templates for the markup syntax.
  • Read Components for how props read the getters the compiler passes.
  • Read Testing for templates under pytest.
  • Browse the wybthon.compiler API reference.
  • Read RFC 0004 for the design and the alternatives considered.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Wybthon uses function components exclusively, following the SolidJS model.

Mental model

A component body runs once when it mounts and returns its markup, usually a template. Inputs are declared on a typed Props class, and reading props.title returns the parent's value, tracked, as reading a property of Solid's props object does. In the returned template, {props.title} is a dynamic expression, so the compiler makes it a binding and only that node updates when the value changes. See Primitives for the full story.

docs.title: Declaring a component with @component
docs.text:
The component decorator turns a function into a Component. Declare inputs on a subclass of Props as plain annotations, give defaults the way a dataclass does, and take one parameter annotated with that class:

from wybthon import Props, component, html, prop


class HelloProps(Props):
    name: str = "world"
    tags: list[str] = prop(default_factory=list)


@component
def Hello(props: HelloProps):
    return html(t"<p>Hello, {props.name}!</p>")

Reading a field returns its value, tracked:

  • In the template, {props.name} is dynamic, so the compiler turns it into a getter: a binding that updates when the parent's value changes.
  • In a memo or effect, props.name subscribes to the parent's value like any other tracked read.
  • untrack(lambda: props.name) reads it once without subscribing, for example to seed local state.

An ordinary default (name: str = "world") needs nothing more. Use prop(default_factory=...) for a mutable default; the factory runs once per component instance. Type checkers only recognize a field specifier's default when it's passed by keyword. Props is a PEP 681 dataclass_transform base, so pyright and mypy check every call site with no plugin: a missing required prop, a wrong type, or an unknown name is a type error.

A component with no inputs takes no parameters:

@component
def App():
    return html(t"<main>{Hello(name='Wybthon')}</main>")

docs.title: Bodies run once
docs.text:
There's no re-render. The only things that update later are the bindings and holes in the returned markup and the effects created in the body.

from wybthon import Props, component, create_signal, html, untrack


class CounterProps(Props):
    initial: int = 0


@component
def Counter(props: CounterProps):
    count, set_count = create_signal(untrack(lambda: props.initial))

    def increment():
        set_count(lambda n: n + 1)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <p>Count: {count()}</p>
        <button onclick={increment}>+1</button>
      </div>
    """)

The compiler turns {count()} into a getter, so the renderer gives that slot one render effect and only that text node updates. The surrounding body never runs again. Event handlers may take the event or no arguments at all; prefer the zero-argument form when you don't use the event.

docs.title: Values, expressions, and accessors
docs.text:
A child never has to care how the parent produced a prop. The parent may pass a value, a template expression, or an accessor, and props.count returns the current value in every case:

from wybthon import Props, component, create_signal, html


class BadgeProps(Props):
    count: int


@component
def Badge(props: BadgeProps):
    return html(t"<span>count: {props.count}</span>")


n, set_n = create_signal(7)

Badge(count=7)  # a value
html(t"{Badge(count=n() * 2)}")  # an expression: the compiler passes a getter
html(t"<{Badge} count={n()} />")  # the same, in tag form

A dynamic expression in a component call or tag reaches the child as a getter, the counterpart of the property getters Solid's compiler puts on a props object, so the child's bindings follow n without the parent re-running. Passing an accessor directly (Badge(count=n)) works the same way at run time, but a type checker flags it against count: int, so prefer writing the call in a template.

docs.title: Top-level reads warn
docs.text:
Reading a reactive prop or signal at the top level of the body isn't tracked, so later updates never reach it. In dev mode Wybthon warns once per component and value. A constant can't change, so reading one doesn't warn:

class NameProps(Props):
    name: str


@component
def Bad(props: NameProps):
    greeting = f"Hello, {props.name}"  # warns when name is reactive: frozen at mount
    return html(t"<p>{greeting}</p>")


@component
def Good(props: NameProps):
    return html(t"<p>Hello, {props.name}</p>")  # one reactive binding


@component
def AlsoFine(props: NameProps):
    initial = untrack(lambda: props.name)  # explicit one-time read, no warning
    return html(t"<p>{initial}</p>")

docs.title: Using a component
docs.text:
There are two ways to use a component in a template.

The call form. Calling a Component returns a VNode. Keyword arguments become props, and every component also accepts key=. Call it inside an interpolation and the type checker sees every prop, while the compiler still passes each dynamic argument as a getter:

html(t"""
  <main>
    {Counter(initial=5)}
    {Card(title=project().name, children=[html(t"<p>one</p>"), html(t"<p>two</p>")])}
    {Card(title="My card")[html(t"<p>one</p>"), html(t"<p>two</p>")]}
  </main>
""")

The last line uses item syntax for children, which reads well when the props are long.

The tag form. <{Card} ...> reads like the rest of the markup and passes the nested markup as the children prop. Close it with </{Card}>, or self-close it with <{Card} />:

html(t"""
  <{Card} title="Settings">
    <p>Changes apply immediately.</p>
    <{Counter} initial={5} />
  </{Card}>
""")

Attributes become keyword props, and a hyphen becomes an underscore (user-id is user_id). A quoted value is a string; pass anything else, including numbers, expressions, and callbacks, with {...}. A dynamic value (title={project().name}) is passed as a getter. Type checkers can't see inside the template string, so the tag form's props are checked at run time in dev mode, like any component call. Use the call form when you want the checker's help.

In dev mode (the default), calling a component with an undeclared prop or without a required one raises TypeError at the call: Counter(bogus=1) fails immediately instead of silently rendering. Statically, a type checker sees the call as constructing the props class, so the same mistakes show up in your editor.

The low-level h form still works (h(Counter, {"initial": 5})).

docs.title: Plain functions as tags
docs.text:
A function without @component whose only parameter is the props can be used as a tag too, with the tag form or h(fn, props). It receives the props dictionary as it was passed, with no Props class, unwrapping, or validation: a dynamic attribute arrives as a getter. It can't observe later changes, so when a re-rendering hole patches it with changed props, it's remounted and its body runs again. Use @component when you want typed, reactive props.

def Note(props):
    return html(t'<p class="note">{props["text"]}</p>')


html(t'<{Note} text="Saved" />')

docs.title: Passing callbacks
docs.text:
Annotate a callback field as callable. A field whose annotation is Callable[...] or Accessor[...], alone or in a union with None, returns exactly what the parent passed, and the read never calls it:

from collections.abc import Callable

from wybthon import Props, component, html


class PickerProps(Props):
    on_pick: Callable[[str], None]
    on_close: Callable[[], None] | None = None


@component
def Picker(props: PickerProps):
    def pick():
        props.on_pick("apple")
        if props.on_close is not None:
            props.on_close()

    return html(t"<button onclick={pick}>Pick</button>")


Picker(on_pick=print, on_close=lambda: print("closed"))

The declared type, not the callback's argument count, decides what's unwrapped, so a zero-argument callback such as on_close is passed through untouched. Every other field unwraps an accessor or getter on read. Annotate a field as Accessor[T] when the child wants the accessor itself rather than its value.

docs.title: What props cost
docs.text:
A component costs about what its markup costs. Whether a prop read allocates anything depends on whether the component can ever receive new props, which the renderer knows when it mounts the component:

  • Most components can't be patched. A component mounted in another component's output, in a list row, in a Show branch, or anywhere else that's mounted once never receives new props. For these, reading a prop that the parent passed as a constant tracks nothing: there's no signal, no subscription, and nothing to dispose. A prop passed as an expression or an accessor is read through it, so the reader subscribes to that source directly.
  • A patchable component is part of the tree a reactive hole returns, or of the tree passed to render, and not inside another component's output. When the hole re-runs (or you render into the same container again), the reconciler patches the component with the new props instead of remounting it. Its prop reads track one version signal per props instance, created on the first tracked read, and a patch that changes a prop bumps it.

The difference is only in what's allocated. Both kinds behave the same for every prop passed as an expression or changed through a patch, so you never need to think about which one you have.

Bindings get the same treatment. A binding whose expression makes no calls, such as {props.title}, first runs under a lightweight probe: when it reads nothing reactive, because the parent passed a constant, the value is applied and no computation is ever allocated. Any other binding or hole that reads nothing reactive on its first run is dropped after that run, keeping only the DOM it produced.

docs.title: Checking for a static prop
docs.text:
is_static(props, "name") reports whether the parent passed a plain value rather than an expression, as Solid 2.0's isStatic does. Nothing is read or tracked. A component library can use it to take a cheaper path for a prop that can't change:

@component
def Icon(props: IconProps):
    if is_static(props, "name"):
        return html(t"<i class={untrack(lambda: props.name)}></i>")
    return html(t"<i class={props.name}></i>")

docs.title: Forwarding with merge and omit
docs.text:
Every prop a component accepts is declared, and undeclared props can't be read. To forward props onto an element, combine sources with merge and drop the ones you handle yourself with omit. Both return views that read like props (view.title is the tracked value), and spreading a view onto an element with <tag {attrs}> binds each key reactively:

from wybthon import ParentProps, component, html, merge, omit


class ButtonProps(ParentProps):
    variant: str = "solid"
    disabled: bool = False


@component
def Button(props: ButtonProps):
    attrs = merge({"type": "button"}, omit(props, "variant", "children"))
    return html(t'<button {attrs} class="btn btn-{props.variant}">{props.children}</button>')

If the parent passes disabled={is_busy()}, the attribute follows the signal. omit also accepts a predicate, such as omit(props, lambda key: key.startswith("on_")).

docs.title: Children
docs.text:
Subclass ParentProps to accept children; it declares children: Any = None. Most layouts interpolate props.children where the content belongs:

from wybthon import ParentProps, component, html


class CardProps(ParentProps):
    title: str


@component
def Card(props: CardProps):
    return html(t'<section class="card"><h3>{props.title}</h3>{props.children}</section>')


html(t'<{Card} title="Hi"><p>a</p><p>b</p></{Card}>')  # tag form
Card(title="Hi")[html(t"<p>a</p>"), html(t"<p>b</p>")]  # item syntax
Card(title="Hi", children=[html(t"<p>a</p>")])  # children as a keyword

When you need to inspect or iterate children, resolve them with children. It takes a getter for the children and returns a ChildrenAccessor that resolves nested accessors, flattens lists, and drops None and booleans. Calling it returns the single child or a list; to_array() always returns a list. flatten is the unmemoized form, for a one-off resolution:

from wybthon import ParentProps, children as resolve_children, component, html


@component
def List(props: ParentProps):
    kids = resolve_children(lambda: props.children)

    def items():
        return [html(t"<li>{kid}</li>") for kid in kids.to_array()]

    return html(t"<ul>{items()}</ul>")


List()["Apples", "Pears"]

docs.title: What a component may return
docs.text:
The body may return a template or any other VNode, a string, a list (mounted as a fragment), None (renders nothing), or a reactive expression (mounted as a single hole):

class LabelProps(Props):
    text: str


@component
def Label(props: LabelProps):
    return create_memo(lambda: props.text.upper())  # a hole that tracks text

docs.title: Keys force a remount
docs.text:
The reconciler patches a component in place when a hole re-renders it with the same tag and key: new props flow into the existing props instance and the body doesn't run again. Give it a different key to force a fresh instance with fresh local state:

class EditorProps(Props):
    user_id: int


@component
def Editor(props: EditorProps):
    draft, set_draft = create_signal("")  # reset when the key changes

    def update(event):
        set_draft(event.target.value)

    return html(t"<textarea value={draft()} oninput={update}></textarea>")


def editor():
    return Editor(user_id=current_id(), key=current_id())


html(t"<div>{editor()}</div>")

{editor()} is a call with no arguments, so it's a reactive hole that re-runs when current_id changes.

docs.title: Refs through components
docs.text:
There's no forward_ref. Declare ref as a plain field and pass it on; an element's ref takes a Ref, a callback, or a list of either, so a component can forward the parent's ref and keep its own:

from wybthon import Props, Ref, component, html, on_settled


class FancyInputProps(Props):
    ref: Ref | None = None


@component
def FancyInput(props: FancyInputProps):
    local = Ref()
    on_settled(lambda: local.current.element.focus())
    return html(t'<input type="text" class="fancy" ref={[local, props.ref]}>')

docs.title: Fragments
docs.text:
A template with several top-level nodes returns a fragment, so you rarely need a wrapper element. The reconciler mounts a fragment's children directly in the parent between two empty comment markers, so fragments never disturb CSS selectors or layout.

from wybthon import component, html


@component
def PageContent():
    return html(t"<h1>Title</h1><p>Body text here.</p>")

When you build the children in code, group them with Fragment: Fragment(*sections).

docs.title: Portal
docs.text:
Portal mounts children into another DOM container (an Element, a CSS selector, or a kernel node id; the default is "body") while keeping them in the current ownership tree, so context, signals, and cleanup work as usual:

from wybthon import Portal, Props, Show, component, html


class ModalProps(Props):
    open: bool


@component
def Modal(props: ModalProps):
    return html(t"""
      {Show(props.open, Portal(html(t'<div class="modal"><p>Modal content</p></div>'), mount="#modal-root"))}
    """)

Writing the Show call in the template matters: there, props.open is passed as a getter, while Show(props.open, ...) in the body would read the prop once.

docs.title: Flow control
docs.text:
Show, For, Repeat, and Switch aren't components: they're native regions the renderer mounts directly, with no component context or props object of their own. Each one owns a scope, so only the relevant subtree updates when a condition or list changes. Called in a template, each dynamic argument arrives as a getter; children and fallback slots are nodes or callables evaluated inside the region's scope.

from wybthon import For, Match, Repeat, Show, Switch, html


def welcome(u):
    return html(t"<p>Welcome, {u().name}</p>")  # u is an accessor for the truthy value


def todo_row(todo, i):
    return html(t"<li>{todo.title}</li>")  # matched by identity: the raw item


def name_row(name, i):
    return html(t"<li>{name()}</li>")  # keyed=False: matched by position, name is an accessor


def keyed_row(todo, i):
    return html(t"<li>{todo().title}</li>")  # a key function: both are accessors


def star(i):
    return html(t"<span>*</span>")


loading = html(t"<p>Loading...</p>")
ready = html(t"<p>Ready</p>")
unknown = html(t"<p>Unknown</p>")

html(t"""
  {Show(user(), welcome, fallback=html(t"<p>Please log in</p>"))}
  <ul>{For(todos(), todo_row)}</ul>
  <ul>{For(names(), name_row, keyed=False)}</ul>
  <ul>{For(todos(), keyed_row, keyed=lambda t: t.id)}</ul>
  {Repeat(rating(), star)}
  {Switch(Match(status() == "loading", loading), Match(status() == "ready", ready), fallback=unknown)}
""")

The callbacks are typed. With a todos: Accessor[list[Todo]], the default For infers todo: Todo and i: Accessor[int]; keyed=False gives (Accessor[Todo], int), and a key function gives (Accessor[Todo], Accessor[int]). Show(user, lambda u: ...) infers u: Accessor[User], or u: User with keyed=True.

dynamic picks a component or tag at run time: View = dynamic(lambda: views[mode()]), then {View(title="Hello")} in a template.

When a reactive hole re-renders a region of the same kind, the new condition or source is pushed into the mounted region instead of remounting it, so rows and branch state survive.

Outside a template, For needs an accessor for each (For(todos, todo_row)); a plain list renders once and triggers a dev warning. The full callback shapes are on the For API page and in Primitives.

docs.title: Dev-mode diagnostics
docs.text:
With dev mode on (the default; check it with is_dev_mode), Wybthon reports the common footguns:

  • Unknown or missing props: calling a component with an undeclared prop, or without a required one, raises TypeError. This covers the tag form too.
  • Top-level reactive read in a component body (warned once per component and value).
  • Write in a tracking scope: writing a signal or store from a memo, a tracked effect, or a hole raises WriteInScopeError.
  • Plain list in For: the list renders once.
  • Uncompiled template: a template that reached html() without the compiler, with a dynamic expression that was evaluated once, raises TemplateError. See Templates that weren't compiled.

Template markup errors aren't dev-only: markup the HTML parser would rewrite is an error in every mode, reported when the module is compiled. See Templates.

Production builds made with wyb build turn dev mode off before your application imports. Call set_dev_mode to change it yourself, for example in tests.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read Templates, The compiler, Mental model, and Lifecycle and ownership.
  • Browse the component and Props API references.
  • See Authoring patterns for recipes.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Context passes values down the tree without threading props through every level. A Context created with create_context is its own provider: call it with a value and children to expose that value to every descendant, and read it with use_context.

from wybthon import component, create_context, html, use_context

Theme = create_context("light")


@component
def Label():
    theme = use_context(Theme)
    return html(t"<p>Theme: {theme}</p>")


@component
def App():
    return html(t"<div>{Theme('dark', Label())}</div>")  # value first, then children

docs.title: Providing a value
docs.text:
The context object is callable: Theme(value, *children) returns a provider VNode. Children may be templates, component calls, VNodes, or lists. Place the provider in a template with an interpolation, as above; the compiler treats a context like any other component, so the children it builds there (Label()) don't run until the provider mounts them. Item syntax works too, as it does on components:

Theme("dark", Header(), Main())
Theme("dark", [Header(), Main()])
Theme("dark")[Header(), Main()]

There's no separate Provider component and no Theme.Provider(...) form.

docs.title: Reading a value
docs.text:
use_context(Theme) walks up the ownership tree from the active scope and returns the nearest provided value. Because values live on the ownership tree rather than a render-time stack, it works anywhere an owner exists: component bodies, effects, memos, holes, and For rows.

@component
def Button():
    theme = use_context(Theme)  # read once, in the body
    return html(t'<button class="btn-{theme}">Hi</button>')

docs.title: Defaults and ContextNotFoundError
docs.text:
create_context(default) declares a value to return when no provider is above the reader. Without a default, reading outside a provider raises ContextNotFoundError:

from wybthon import ContextNotFoundError, create_context, use_context

Session = create_context(name="Session")  # no default

try:
    use_context(Session)
except ContextNotFoundError:
    ...

Pass name= for readable diagnostics; it appears in the error message and the context's repr.

docs.title: Live values: pass an accessor
docs.text:
use_context returns the value exactly as provided. A static string stays a string; a signal or any accessor stays an accessor, so consumers call it where they need the value and stay reactive without the provider or the subtree re-mounting:

from wybthon import Accessor, Context, component, create_context, create_signal, html, use_context

Theme: Context[Accessor[str]] = create_context()


@component
def ThemedButton():
    theme = use_context(Theme)
    return html(t'<button class="btn btn-{theme()}">Hi</button>')


@component
def App():
    theme, set_theme = create_signal("light")

    def toggle():
        set_theme(lambda t: "dark" if t == "light" else "light")

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        {Theme(theme, ThemedButton())}
        <button onclick={toggle}>Toggle</button>
      </div>
    """)

Provide a setter alongside the accessor when descendants need to write:

Theme((theme, set_theme), App())

theme, set_theme = use_context(Theme)

Passing a plain value is fine when it never changes. The class="btn btn-{theme()}" attribute above joins its parts into one reactive binding, so the class follows the signal.

Pass the accessor, not its value

In a template, {Theme(theme(), ThemedButton())} looks reactive, but the provider evaluates its value once, untracked, when it mounts: consumers get the string "light" and never see a change. The value is what the provider stores, not a binding. Pass the accessor itself, Theme(theme, ...), and let consumers call it. A lambda: theme() works too, but an accessor already is one.

docs.title: How it works: the ownership tree
docs.text:
The provider is a tiny component that stores value on its own Owner. use_context walks parent pointers until it finds a scope that carries the context:

Root owner
└── Component (App)
    └── Provider owner        <- context map: {Theme: value}
        └── Component (Label)
            └── hole scope
                └── render effect   <- use_context(Theme) walks up from here

The lookup is a parent-pointer walk with no copying, so cost is proportional to the depth between reader and provider. Nested providers for the same context shadow outer ones because the walk finds the nearest first:

Theme(
    "light",
    Theme("dark", Label()),  # sees "dark"
    Label(),  # sees "light"
)

docs.title: Where to call use_context
docs.text: Call it in the component body (or at the top of an effect or memo) and close over the result. Calling it inside a hole works too, since holes are owners under the component, but reading once in the body is clearer and avoids repeating the walk on every re-evaluation. Context values are also visible inside Show, For, Loading, and Portal subtrees, because those primitives mount their content under the surrounding owner.

docs.text:
• See the context API for Context, create_context, and use_context.
  • Read Lifecycle and ownership for how the ownership tree works.
  • Explore Stores when you need a richer reactive container to share.

docs.title: DOM interop
docs.text:
Element is Wybthon's thin wrapper around browser DOM nodes. It provides helpers for attributes, classes, styles, and queries while still giving you the raw element for any escape hatch you need. For events, use the delegated on* attributes (see Events); for non-bubbling event types, attach a native listener via ref.current.element.addEventListener with a Pyodide proxy.

from wybthon import Element

root = Element("#app", existing=True)
box = Element("div")
box.set_text("Hello")
box.append_to(root)

You rarely instantiate Element yourself when authoring components; the renderer creates and manages nodes for you. Reach for it when you need to bridge to imperative DOM APIs (focus management, scrolling, measuring, third-party widgets) or when you receive a node back from a ref or an event.

docs.title: Refs: holding onto an element
docs.text:
A Ref is a small mutable container that the renderer fills with the mounted Element. Pass it as the ref attribute of any host element (a ref prop in h) and read ref.current after mount:

from wybthon import Ref, component, html, on_settled


@component
def AutoFocusInput():
    ref = Ref()

    def focus():
        if ref.current is not None:
            ref.current.element.focus()

    on_settled(focus)
    return html(t'<div><input type="text" placeholder="Focus me" ref={ref}></div>')

Refs are assigned while the element mounts and reset to None when it unmounts. Read them in on_settled (which runs after the first commit), in an effect, or in an event handler, never at the top of the component body during initial render.

docs.title: Ref shapes
docs.text:
The ref prop accepts three shapes:

  • A Ref object: ref.current is set on mount and cleared on unmount.
  • A callable: ref(element) is called once on mount. It isn't called again on unmount, so pair it with on_cleanup if you need teardown. A callback ref is the closest match to Solid 2.0's function refs. Name it, or wrap an inline lambda in parentheses: ref={(lambda el: el.element.focus())}.
  • A list or tuple mixing both: every entry is assigned. This is how a component forwards a parent's ref while keeping one of its own:
from collections.abc import Callable

from wybthon import Element, Props, Ref, component, html, on_settled


class FancyInputProps(Props):
    ref: Ref | Callable[[Element], None] | None = None


@component
def FancyInput(props: FancyInputProps):
    local = Ref()
    on_settled(lambda: local.current.element.focus())
    return html(t'<input type="text" ref={[local, props.ref]}>')

Refs pass through components like any other prop; there's no special forwarding API. Because the field's annotation includes a Callable, props.ref returns the Ref or callback the parent passed, untouched, instead of calling it. The compiler never wraps a ref attribute, so ref={[local, props.ref]} is evaluated once, when the element is created. A None entry in the list is ignored.

docs.title: Ownership and disposal order
docs.text:
Refs follow the ownership tree. A component's ref.current is set from the first commit until the component unmounts. Unmounting queues one kernel command that removes the component's nodes and releases them natively, then runs the component's own cleanups, then clears its host nodes' refs. So an on_cleanup registered in the component body can still reach ref.current to tear down a native listener or a third-party widget.

The raw node is another matter. Materializing ref.current.element for the first time inside a cleanup commits the queued removal, and the kernel has already released the node by then, so element is None. If teardown needs the raw node, read ref.current.element while the component is mounted (in on_settled, say); the Element caches it, and the cleanup gets the detached node. Use it for teardown, not for measurements. Cleanups that run later (for example ones registered by an ancestor) see ref.current is None, so guard for it. See Lifecycle and ownership.

docs.title: How the renderer relates to Element
docs.text:
The renderer itself never touches raw DOM nodes or Element wrappers. Every host node is identified by an integer node id, and all mutations (clone, insert, set-attr, dispose) are emitted as compact operations into a command buffer that a small JavaScript kernel applies in one bridge crossing per commit. See Virtual DOM.

Element sits on top of that system as the escape hatch for imperative work:

  • An Element can be backed by a raw DOM node (when you construct one yourself, or wrap one with Element(node=...)) or by a kernel node id (what the renderer hands out through ref= and evt.current_target).
  • Id-backed elements materialize the raw node lazily: the first element access commits any pending batched ops, then fetches the node from the kernel's registry, so what you see always reflects every queued mutation.
  • node_id goes the other way: it registers a raw-node-backed element with the kernel so the renderer can target it. render uses this when you pass an Element container.
  • Query helpers (Element.query, Element.query_all, find, find_all) also commit pending ops first, so nodes created earlier in the same update are visible.

Because commits happen automatically at these boundaries, imperative work through a ref stays in sync with the framework's bookkeeping.

Don't fight the renderer

Attributes, classes, and children that the renderer owns should be driven by reactive bindings, not by Element calls. A binding only writes when its own value changes, so it won't notice manual edits and may leave them in place, or overwrite them unexpectedly. Use Element for things the renderer doesn't manage: focus, selection, scroll position, measurements, and third-party widgets that own their subtree.

docs.title: Element methods
docs.text:
The wrapper mirrors familiar DOM names:

Helper Purpose element The raw JS node (materialized lazily). value, checked, files Form-control state, readable and (for value, checked) writable. set_text, set_html, load_html Replace content. set_html bypasses diffing and doesn't sanitize. set_attr, get_attr, remove_attr Attribute access. set_style(dict_or_kwargs) Calls style.setProperty per entry. add_class, remove_class, toggle_class, has_class classList shortcuts. append, append_to, remove Tree manipulation for nodes you own. Element.query, Element.query_all, find, find_all Selector queries (commit pending ops first). attach_ref(ref) Store this element on ref.current.

docs.title: Styles, classes, and dataset through bindings
docs.text:
You usually don't need Element for styling. Templates and h share one set of prop appliers, so these work the same in both:

  • style takes a dict with camelCase or snake_case keys (background_color, fontSize); the renderer converts to kebab-case and emits a single style op. Keys missing on update are removed, and passing None clears earlier styles. Values may be accessors, and a raw style string is accepted too.
  • dataset takes a dict; entries render as data-* attributes and missing keys on update are removed. A plain data-testid="x" attribute (data_testid in h() props) also works.
  • class (class_ in h() props) accepts a string, a list of strings, a {name: truthy_or_accessor} dict, or an accessor returning any of those.
styles = {"background_color": "white", "fontSize": "14px"}
classes = {"card": True, "active": is_active}  # is_active is an accessor

html(t'<div class={classes} style={styles} data-testid="card">...</div>')

classes is a name, so the compiler passes the dict as is, and each accessor inside it becomes its own binding. An expression that reads signals, such as class={"card active" if is_active() else "card"}, becomes one binding for the whole attribute.

docs.title: Rendering into an existing node
docs.text:
render(vnode, container) accepts an Element container and returns a Root. Call root.dispose() to unmount, run every cleanup, and clear the container's kernel bookkeeping:

from wybthon import Element, html, render

root = render(html(t"<h1>Hello</h1>"), Element("#app", existing=True))
root.dispose()

docs.text:

  • See Forms for accessible patterns built on top of Element.
  • Browse the dom API reference.

docs.title: Error boundaries
docs.text:
Errored catches errors raised while rendering its subtree and shows a fallback in its place, leaving sibling trees untouched. It's the recommended way to surface unexpected errors without crashing the whole app.

from wybthon import Errored, component, html


@component
def Failing():
    raise RuntimeError("boom")


def fallback(err, reset):
    return html(t"""
      <div class="error">
        <p>Oops: {err()}</p>
        <button onclick={reset}>Try again</button>
      </div>
    """)


view = Errored(Failing(), fallback=fallback)

children may be a node (a template, a component call, or any other VNode), a zero-arg callable, or a list of either. Pass nodes directly: component bodies and a template's dynamic expressions don't run until the boundary mounts them, so their errors are caught. A callable is only needed when building the node can raise, for example when Python code outside a template computes a prop eagerly: Errored(lambda: Chart(points=parse(raw)), fallback=...).

The fallback receives the error as an accessor, as in Solid 2.0: call err() to read the exception. In a template, {err()} shows its message. reset takes no arguments, so it can be passed straight to onclick.

docs.title: What gets caught
docs.text:
The boundary installs an error handler on its owner scope. Errors from any of these route to the nearest enclosing boundary:

  • A component body raising during mount.
  • A hole's expression or a reactive prop binding raising when it (re-)evaluates.
  • An effect's compute stage raising, unless the effect has its own error= handler.
  • An async memo rejecting: the error is stored and re-raised when the memo is read, so it surfaces in the hole that reads it.
  • An action raising: routed to the boundary that was active when the action was called, and re-raised to the awaiter.

The nearest boundary wins. An inner Errored handles errors from its own subtree; only errors outside it reach the outer one:

Errored(
    html(t"""
      <div>
        {Sidebar()}
        {Errored(RiskyPanel(), fallback=html(t"<p>Panel failed</p>"))}
      </div>
    """),
    fallback=html(t"<p>Page failed</p>"),
)

docs.title: Fallback shapes
docs.text:
fallback may be:

  • a VNode or a string, shown as is;
  • a callable () -> VNode;
  • a callable (err) -> VNode, where err is an accessor for the caught exception;
  • a callable (err, reset) -> VNode, where reset() clears the error and re-renders the children;
  • omitted, in which case the boundary renders the text "Something went wrong."

A callable fallback runs each time an error is caught, so it can inspect the exception by calling err():

from wybthon import html


def describe(err, reset):
    if isinstance(err(), PermissionError):
        return html(t"<p>You don't have access to this.</p>")
    return html(t"<div><p>{err()}</p><button onclick={reset}>Retry</button></div>")

docs.title: Resetting
docs.text:
Call the reset argument from the fallback, or pass reset_on=: an accessor (or plain value) whose change clears the current error automatically. Coupling a boundary to the current route is the usual pattern, so navigating away from a broken page recovers on its own:

from wybthon import Errored, html
from wybthon.router import Outlet, current_path

Errored(Outlet(), fallback=html(t"<p>This page failed</p>"), reset_on=current_path)

Resetting re-renders the children. If the cause hasn't been fixed, the error is caught again and the fallback returns.

docs.title: Automatic healing
docs.text: A boundary also resets on its own when any input the failing computation read changes. The boundary records the signals behind the memo or hole that raised (the user_id a fetch read, the store path a hole formatted) and watches them; a change to one of them is a new situation, so the boundary re-renders the children without you wiring reset_on=. A fetch that failed for user 3 heals when the user picks user 4, and an async memo that errored heals when its inputs change and the retry succeeds. Explicit reset() and reset_on= still work for causes the graph can't see, such as a network that came back.

docs.title: Observing errors with on_error
docs.text:
Pass on_error= to be notified when the boundary catches something, for logging or monitoring. It receives the exception itself (not an accessor) and runs in addition to showing the fallback:

Errored(Dashboard(), fallback="Dashboard unavailable", on_error=report_to_monitoring)

docs.title: Effects with their own handler
docs.text:
create_effect accepts error=. Exceptions raised by the compute stage (sync or async) go to that handler instead of the nearest boundary, so a failing background effect doesn't take down the UI around it:

from wybthon import create_effect

create_effect(
    lambda: save_draft(draft()),
    lambda result: set_status("saved"),
    error=lambda exc: set_status(f"save failed: {exc}"),
)

docs.title: Event handlers are not routed
docs.text: Like SolidJS, Wybthon runs event handlers outside rendering. An exception in an onclick handler is logged to the console (with a traceback in dev mode); the boundary isn't involved and the UI stays intact. Handle expected failures inside the handler, or move the work into an action, whose errors are routed to the boundary captured at call time.

docs.title: Pairing with Loading
docs.text:
Errored handles errors; Loading handles not-ready state. Wrap async regions with both, Errored on the outside so a rejected fetch inside the loading content still has a fallback:

from wybthon import Errored, Loading, html


def load_failed(err, reset):
    return html(t"<div><p>Could not load: {err()}</p><button onclick={reset}>Retry</button></div>")


html(t"""
  <main>
    <{Errored} fallback={load_failed}>
      <{Loading} fallback={html(t"<p>Loading...</p>")}>
        <{UserCard} user_id={user_id()} />
      </{Loading}>
    </{Errored}>
  </main>
""")

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• See the error_boundary API reference.
  • Read Async and loading for async error handling.
  • Walk through the Error boundary example.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Event handlers are on* attributes on host elements. They're delegated: one native listener per event type per render root, with a single Python call per handler that matches.

from wybthon import component, html


@component
def Button():
    def clicked():
        print("clicked")

    return html(t"<button onclick={clicked}>Click</button>")

In a template, onclick, onClick, and on:click all bind a click handler; use whichever reads best to you. The compiler never wraps an event handler, so onclick={clicked} passes the function itself. When markup is built by code with h, the same prop takes a Python name, on_click:

h("button", {"on_click": clicked}, "Click")

Both go through the same prop applier, so a handler behaves identically in either. Non-callable values are ignored, and passing None on an update removes the handler.

A handler may take the event or no arguments at all. Wybthon checks the handler's signature once, when it's registered, so a zero-argument handler costs nothing extra. Prefer one whenever you don't read the event:

count, set_count = create_signal(0)


def increment():
    set_count(lambda n: n + 1)


html(t"<button onclick={increment}>+</button>")

Name your handlers, as above. Python doesn't allow a bare lambda inside a t-string interpolation, so an inline handler needs parentheses: onclick={(lambda: set_count(0))}. See Templates.

docs.title: DomEvent
docs.text:
Handlers that take an argument receive a DomEvent built from a small payload the kernel assembles natively, so reading the common fields never crosses the Python-to-JS bridge:

  • type: the event type string ("click", "input").
  • target: a payload-backed view of the original event target. value, checked, and files mirror the DOM properties handlers actually read; the raw JS node is available as target.element when you need more.
  • current_target: an Element for the node whose handler is running during delegated bubbling.
  • key, code, alt_key, ctrl_key, meta_key, shift_key: keyboard fields (key and code are None for non-keyboard events).
  • button, client_x, client_y: mouse and pointer fields.
  • prevent_default(): asks the dispatcher to call preventDefault() on the native event once your handler returns. Safe to call in non-browser tests.
  • stop_propagation(): stops the delegated walk for this event and native propagation above the handled node.
  • raw: the native browser event object for anything not in the payload. Only valid synchronously during dispatch.

Read input values as you would in JavaScript or SolidJS:

name, set_name = create_signal("")


def update_name(e: DomEvent):
    set_name(e.target.value)


html(t"<input value={name()} oninput={update_name}>")

A submit handler:

from wybthon import DomEvent, component, html


@component
def Search():
    def typed(evt: DomEvent):
        print("typed", evt.target.value)

    def submit(evt: DomEvent):
        evt.prevent_default()
        print("submitted from", evt.current_target)

    return html(t"""
      <form onsubmit={submit}>
        <input name="q" oninput={typed}>
        <button type="submit">Go</button>
      </form>
    """)

docs.title: Delegation model
docs.text:
Delegation lives in the rendering kernel, the JavaScript side of the batched renderer. On first use of an event type, the kernel installs one native listener on each delegation root (the container you passed to render and the mount target of any mounted Portal; document is used until a root exists). When an event fires, the kernel walks up from the original target natively and calls into Python once for the bubbling route, running each handler registered for that type along the way. The payload crosses the bridge as one JSON string, so a click on a row in a 10,000-row table costs a single Python call.

Registering a handler costs no bridge crossing of its own. A compiled template declares its delegated listener types when it's registered, so cloning a row marks its handlers natively and sends no LISTEN op. Other handlers register with a batched LISTEN op riding the same command buffer as DOM mutations. Either way, mounting a list with thousands of handlers adds nothing to the bridge-crossing count.

Handlers flush when they return

After a delegated handler returns, the dispatcher flushes: every effect the handler dirtied runs, and the resulting DOM ops commit in one bridge crossing before the browser paints. Signal writes inside a handler update the UI without any manual step, no matter how many writes the handler made. See Staged writes and flush timing.

Handler errors are logged through the dev-mode error channel; they aren't routed to an Errored boundary. See Error boundaries.

Cleanup guarantees:

  • When a node is unmounted, its handlers are dropped on the Python side. The kernel's native DISPOSE_RANGE or DISPOSE op removes the nodes and clears their listener bookkeeping in the same walk, so Python sends no per-node release list.
  • When the last handler for an event type is removed across the whole app (by unmount, or by diffing a handler to None), the native listener for that type is removed from every root.

docs.title: Naming and normalization
docs.text:
Every spelling normalizes to a lowercase DOM event name:

Where Spellings Event Template onclick, onClick, on:click "click" Template ondblclick, onDblClick, on:dblclick "dblclick" h() props and spreads on_click, onClick "click" h() props and spreads on_input, onInput "input"
  • A Capture suffix listens in the capture phase: onClickCapture in a template, on_click_capture in h() props.
  • Any attribute or prop starting with on (on_ or on: included) is treated as an event handler.

docs.title: Event types that work best with delegation
docs.text:
Prefer events that bubble:

  • Mouse: click, dblclick, mousedown, mouseup, mousemove, mouseover, mouseout, contextmenu, wheel
  • Keyboard: keydown, keyup (avoid the deprecated keypress)
  • Input and form: input, change, submit, reset
  • Pointer: pointerdown, pointerup, pointermove, pointerover, pointerout, pointercancel

Non-bubbling events still work as attributes and props. focus, blur, mouseenter, mouseleave, pointerenter, pointerleave, scroll, load, error, invalid, and toggle get a direct native listener on their node instead of the delegated one. Use focusin and focusout when an ancestor should hear focus changes from its descendants.

docs.title: Native listeners through a ref
docs.text:
For anything the on* attributes don't cover, such as a third-party library that wants the element itself, attach a native listener directly through Pyodide using a Ref. Refs are assigned during mount, so do the wiring in on_settled, which runs after the first commit. Wrap the handler in create_proxy so it survives garbage collection, and remove it on cleanup:

from pyodide.ffi import create_proxy

from wybthon import Ref, component, html, on_cleanup, on_settled


@component
def DropZone():
    ref = Ref()
    proxy = create_proxy(lambda e: print("files dropped"))

    def setup():
        if ref.current is not None:
            ref.current.element.addEventListener("drop", proxy)

    def teardown():
        if ref.current is not None:
            ref.current.element.removeEventListener("drop", proxy)
        proxy.destroy()

    on_settled(setup)
    on_cleanup(teardown)

    return html(t'<div class="drop-zone" ref={ref}>Drop files here</div>')

Reading ref.current.element commits any pending batched ops first, so the node exists and reflects every queued mutation. See DOM interop.

docs.title: Pyodide cross-browser notes
docs.text:
• Delegation depends on bubbling to the render root. Non-bubbling types use direct listeners automatically, as described above.
  • Chrome and Edge may treat touchstart and touchmove listeners as passive, so prevent_default() may be ignored for them. Use event(handler, passive=False) or a direct listener with {"passive": False} options if you need to prevent scrolling.
  • keypress is deprecated; prefer keydown and keyup.

docs.title: Testing handlers
docs.text:
wybthon.testing renders into an in-memory DOM in plain CPython and dispatches events through the same delegated handlers. Each fire helper flushes when the handlers return, just as in the browser:

from wybthon import component, create_signal, html
from wybthon.testing import fire, render


@component
def Counter():
    count, set_count = create_signal(0)

    def increment():
        set_count(lambda n: n + 1)

    return html(t"<div><p>Count: {count()}</p><button onclick={increment}>+</button></div>")


def test_counter():
    with render(Counter()) as screen:
        fire.click(screen.get_by_text("+"))
        assert screen.get_by_text("Count: 1")

fire.input(node, value), fire.change(node, checked=True), fire.submit(form), and fire.key_down(node, "Enter") set the matching payload fields. fire(node, "dblclick", shift_key=True) dispatches any other type.

docs.title: Async handlers and native options
docs.text:
An ordinary async def handler is scheduled automatically. It runs in an owned asyncio task and is canceled on handler replacement or unmount. Payload fields and current_target remain usable after an await; event.raw is valid only during synchronous dispatch. Call prevent_default before the first await when you need to prevent native behavior.

from wybthon import event, html

html(t"<button onclick={event(save, once=True)}>Once</button>")

event(callback, capture=False, passive=False, once=False) configures native listener options. It works the same in any spelling: {"on_click": event(save, once=True)} in h() props. Focus, blur, and other non-bubbling events work through direct listeners. Ordinary bubbling uses composedPath, sends one route across the bridge, and flushes after its handlers. Custom event detail, composition state, selected option values, and scroll position are included in the payload. A passive handler can't prevent the default action.

docs.title: Forms
docs.text:
Form state helpers, validators, aggregated validation, and accessibility patterns. Everything here is a thin layer over signals and delegated events, so you can drop down to plain create_signal and an oninput handler whenever the helpers don't fit. Import the helpers from wybthon.forms; they aren't exported from the top-level wybthon package.

from wybthon import component, html
from wybthon.forms import (
    a11y_control_attrs,
    bind_checkbox,
    bind_select,
    bind_text,
    email,
    error_message_attrs,
    form_state,
    min_length,
    on_submit_validated,
    required,
)

fields = form_state({"name": "", "email": "", "agree": False, "choice": ""})

rules = {
    "name": [required(), min_length(2)],
    "email": [email()],
}


@component
def SignupForm():
    name = fields["name"]
    email_field = fields["email"]

    def save(f):
        print({k: field.value.peek() for k, field in f.items()})

    return html(t"""
      <form onsubmit={on_submit_validated(rules, save, fields)}>
        <label for="name">Name</label>
        <input
          id="name"
          {bind_text(name, validators=rules["name"])}
          {a11y_control_attrs(name, described_by_id="name-err")}
        >
        <span {error_message_attrs(id="name-err")}>{name.error()}</span>

        <label for="email">Email</label>
        <input
          id="email"
          type="email"
          {bind_text(email_field, validators=rules["email"])}
          {a11y_control_attrs(email_field, described_by_id="email-err")}
        >
        <span {error_message_attrs(id="email-err")}>{email_field.error()}</span>

        <label><input type="checkbox" {bind_checkbox(fields["agree"])}> Agree</label>

        <label for="choice">Choice</label>
        <select id="choice" {bind_select(fields["choice"])}>
          <option value="">--</option>
          <option value="a">A</option>
          <option value="b">B</option>
        </select>

        <button type="submit">Submit</button>
      </form>
    """)

The helpers return prop dicts, which a template applies with a spread (<input {attrs}>). A spread is evaluated once, when the template is created, and each entry that's an accessor (the field's value, the ARIA state) becomes its own reactive binding. The keys use Python names (on_input, aria_invalid), the same names h props take, so the dicts also work as h("input", {"id": "name", **bind_text(name)}).

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
form_state turns a dict of initial values into a FormState mapping of Field objects. Each field exposes reactive values:

Attribute Type Meaning value / set_value Accessor[T] / method The current input value. error / set_error Accessor[str \| None] The latest validation message, or None. touched / set_touched Accessor[bool] True once the user has interacted with the field.

Because these are ordinary accessors, you can read them anywhere in a template. <span>{name.error()}</span> shows the message reactively and renders nothing while it's None; field.set_value("...") from code updates the bound input too.

Use touched to hold error display until the user has typed:

html(t"<span {error_message_attrs(id='name-err')}>{name.error() if name.touched() else None}</span>")

Field.validate(validators) runs the rules against the current value, marks the field touched, and stores the error. It's what the aggregate helpers call under the hood.

docs.title: Bindings
docs.text:
The bind_* helpers return prop dicts to spread onto a control (<input {bind_text(field)}>):

  • bind_text(field, validators=[...]) gives value, on_input, and on_compositionend. Composition input waits until composition ends. The value entry is the field's accessor, so the DOM follows the signal. Each keystroke stores the value, marks the field touched, and runs the validators.
  • bind_checkbox(field) gives checked and on_change for a boolean field.
  • bind_select(field) gives value and on_change for a <select>.
  • bind_number(field) and bind_multiselect(field) cover numeric inputs and multiple selections; see Dirty state, reset, and async workflows.

Checkbox and select bindings clear the error on change; text bindings revalidate on every input event. Add more attributes alongside the spread as usual: <input {bind_text(field)} placeholder="Name" autocomplete="name">.

docs.title: Validators
docs.text:
A Validator is a function from a value to an error string or None. The built-ins are factories so messages are customizable:

from wybthon.forms import email, max_length, min_length, required

rules = {
    "name": [required("Please enter a name"), min_length(2), max_length(40)],
    "email": [required(), email()],
}
  • required rejects None and blank strings.
  • min_length and max_length compare len(str(value)).
  • email checks a lightweight pattern and treats empty values as valid, so pair it with required when the field is mandatory.

Write your own by returning a message or None:

def matches(other):
    def _v(value):
        return None if value == other.value.peek() else "Passwords don't match"

    return _v

validate(value, validators) returns the first failing message. rules_from_schema builds a rules map from a small declarative dict when you'd rather configure than compose.

docs.title: Submitting
docs.text:
• on_submit(handler, form) prevents the default navigation and calls handler(form).
  • on_submit_validated(rules, handler, form) first runs validate_form, which validates every field in rules, marks them touched, stores their errors, and returns (is_valid, errors). The handler runs only when everything passes.

Both return an event handler for the form's onsubmit attribute (on_submit in h() props). Signal writes inside the handler flush when it returns, so error messages and aria-invalid states update in one commit.

To validate a single field on blur or on demand, call validate_field(field, validators).

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
• Set for on a <label> to match the control's id. In h() props, pass html_for (or for_); the prop applier writes it as the for attribute.
  • a11y_control_attrs(field, described_by_id=...) returns reactive aria_invalid and aria_describedby props: aria-invalid is "true" while the field has an error, and aria-describedby points at the message container only while a message exists, so screen readers don't announce an empty region.
  • error_message_attrs(id=...) returns id, role="alert", and aria-live="polite" for the message container.

Because the ARIA props are accessors, they update through fine-grained bindings without re-rendering the form.

docs.title: Controlled inputs without the helpers
docs.text:
The helpers are optional. A controlled input is a signal, a value binding, and an oninput handler:

from wybthon import DomEvent, component, create_signal, html


@component
def Search():
    query, set_query = create_signal("")

    def update(e: DomEvent):
        set_query(e.target.value)

    return html(t"<input value={query()} oninput={update}>")

e.target.value is read from the dispatch payload, not from the DOM, so it's cheap even in large lists. See Events.

docs.title: Dirty state, reset, and async workflows
docs.text:
Each field has dirty and validating accessors. field.reset() restores its initial value and clears touched and error state; field.reset(value) establishes a new baseline. FormState's dirty and validating accessors aggregate its fields, .data() returns current values, and .reset(values=None) resets the form.

await field.validate_async(validators) accepts synchronous or async validators (AsyncValidator). Editing the value cancels stale validation, and a response for an old revision can't overwrite the current error. Owning scope disposal cancels validation too.

async def save(values):
    return await post_profile(values)


async def submit(event):
    event.prevent_default()
    await fields.submit(save, rules=rules)


html(t"""
  <form onsubmit={submit}>
    <input {bind_text(fields["name"])}>
    <button type="submit">Save</button>
  </form>
""")

FormState.submit validates the fields, snapshots their values, and awaits the handler. .submitting and .submit_error expose the result. If values change during validation, that submission doesn't send stale values. The simpler on_submit helpers also propagate async handler results to the event task.

bind_text(field, parse=..., format=...) separates display text from stored values and reports conversion errors. bind_number(field) handles numeric values and stores an empty input as None. bind_multiselect(field) binds a list of selected values through selected_values, with no per-option Python-to-JS reads. Controlled selections are applied after options are inserted or replaced.

docs.title: Lifecycle and ownership
docs.text:
Wybthon has no lifecycle methods in the React sense. Every component creates an owner, and effects, memos, cleanups, and context lookups attach to that owner. Disposing the owner cleans them all up.

This page explains what an owner is, when it's created, when effects and settled callbacks run, and the order in which things are torn down.

docs.title: The ownership tree
docs.text:
When a component mounts, the reconciler creates a fresh Owner for it and runs the body under that owner. Anything created during the body (effects, memos, child components, holes and bindings in the returned template) attaches to it. When the component unmounts, the owner is disposed and the whole subtree goes with it.

flowchart TD
    Root[Root owner from render] --> App[App]
    App --> Header[Header]
    App --> Main[Main]
    Main --> Counter[Counter]
    Counter --> CountEffect((effect))
    Counter --> Hole((hole scope))
    Hole --> RenderEffect((render effect))
  • Owners form a tree mirroring the component tree, with extra nodes for holes, Show and Switch branches, For and Repeat rows, and create_root roots.
  • Cleanups registered with on_cleanup run when their owner is disposed.
  • Disposing a parent disposes every descendant, so nothing is orphaned.

docs.title: Lifecycle hooks
Effects own their cleanups
docs.text:
A cleanup registered inside an effect belongs to that run of the effect, not to the component. Each re-run fires the previous cleanup first:

from wybthon import create_effect, create_tracked_effect, on_cleanup


def track_resize():
    handler = make_handler(size())
    window.addEventListener("resize", handler)
    on_cleanup(lambda: window.removeEventListener("resize", handler))


create_tracked_effect(track_resize)

The split form expresses the same thing without on_cleanup: return the cleanup from apply, and it runs before the next apply and on disposal:

def attach(current_size):
    handler = make_handler(current_size)
    window.addEventListener("resize", handler)
    return lambda: window.removeEventListener("resize", handler)


create_effect(size, attach)

docs.title: on_settled and refs
docs.text:
Refs are assigned during mount, so ref.current is None while the body runs. Read refs in on_settled or in an effect:

from wybthon import Ref, component, html, on_settled


@component
def AutoFocus():
    ref = Ref()
    on_settled(lambda: ref.current.element.focus())
    return html(t'<div><input type="text" ref={ref}></div>')

on_settled may return a cleanup, which runs when the component unmounts. That makes it the natural home for one-shot integrations that need teardown:

def start():
    chart = ChartLib(ref.current.element)
    return chart.destroy


on_settled(start)

docs.title: Disposal order
docs.text:
Disposal is depth-first:

  1. Children are disposed before their parent.
  2. Within one owner, cleanups run in LIFO order (the last registered runs first).
  3. A component's DOM nodes are removed in the same batch. The kernel releases every node id inside the removed range natively, so Python doesn't walk the subtree to free them.

When a computation re-runs, it disposes its children and runs its cleanups before re-executing, so effects created conditionally in a previous run never leak into the next.

A hole is a scope of its own. Components mounted inside a hole survive the hole's re-evaluations as long as the reconciler can patch them in place (same tag, same key); they're disposed when the hole drops them or when the hole itself unmounts. A hole that returns a template from the same literal again patches it slot by slot, so components in its slots survive the same way.

docs.title: Roots
docs.text: render returns a Root. Calling root.dispose() unmounts the tree, disposes every scope beneath it, and unregisters the container as an event delegation root. For reactive work that outlives any component, use create_root, which hands you a dispose callable of its own.

docs.title: Reading the current owner
docs.text:
You rarely need this, but get_owner returns the active owner so you can capture it before an await and restore it with run_with_owner:

from wybthon import create_effect, get_owner, run_with_owner


async def later():
    owner = get_owner()
    await wait_for_something()
    run_with_owner(owner, lambda: create_effect(count, lambda n: print(n)))

Async memos and async effects do this for you: every resume after an await runs as the same computation, under the same owner.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Forgetting cleanups. If you attach a listener or start an interval, return a cleanup from apply or register one with on_cleanup, so re-runs and unmounts don't leak.
  • Touching the DOM in the body. The body runs before the DOM exists. Use on_settled or an effect.
  • Reading props at the top level. The read is frozen at mount, and dev mode warns when the parent passed an expression. Read props in the returned markup, a memo, or an effect, or use untrack(lambda: props.initial) deliberately.
  • Expecting effects to run at creation. The first run is deferred to the next flush. In tests, call flush after render before asserting on effect output.

docs.text:
