A t-string's static strings are a constant of the code that contains it, so Wybthon can treat each literal as a fixed piece of markup. The compiler parses and validates each literal when its module is compiled and writes the result into the module:

  • The static markup becomes a native <template> that the JavaScript kernel clones with a single command per instance.
  • Each interpolation becomes a slot at a known node offset, and each dynamic expression becomes a getter for that slot.
  • Each element gets a mount function, written as ordinary Python, so mounting an instance builds no VNode tree for its static parts and checks nothing node by node: the literal guarantees its own structure.

That's the job Solid's compiler does for JSX. A production build never parses a template or generates code at run time. A template that reaches html() uncompiled, in a REPL for example, is compiled on its first call and cached; see Templates that weren't compiled.

docs.title: Interpolations
docs.text:
Position Example What happens Child <p>{value}</p> Text, a node, a list, or None. A dynamic expression or an accessor becomes a hole. Attribute <a href={url()}> Applied once, or bound when dynamic or an accessor. Part of an attribute <div class="card card-{kind()}"> The parts form one string; dynamic parts make it one binding. Event <button onclick={save}> A delegated handler. onClick and on:click work too. Ref <input ref={field}> A Ref or a callback that receives the element. Spread <input {attrs}> A mapping of props applied to the element. Component tag <{Card} title="Hi">...</{Card}> Calls the component; see Components in templates.

An expression is dynamic when it contains a call, an attribute access, or a subscript: {count()}, {count() * 2}, {props.title}, {row["label"]}, class={"on" if active() else ""}. The compiler turns it into a getter, so only that text node or attribute updates when what it reads changes. A name or a constant is a value, and an Accessor or a lambda is still a reactive expression, so {count} and {count()} both update. Event handlers, refs, and spreads are never wrapped. The compiler page has the full rule.

count, set_count = create_signal(0)
kind, set_kind = create_signal("primary")
is_saving, set_saving = create_signal(False)

html(t'<button class="btn btn-{kind()}" disabled={is_saving()}>Saved {count()} times</button>')

docs.title: Lambdas need parentheses
docs.text:
With the compiler you rarely write a lambda in a template, but you still need one for an inline event handler. Python's grammar doesn't allow a bare lambda inside {...}, because the : would start a format spec. Wrap it in parentheses, or, usually more readable, give it a name:

html(t"<button onclick={(lambda: set_open(False))}>Close</button>")


def close():
    set_open(False)


html(t"<button onclick={close}>Close</button>")

Named handlers read better than inline lambdas, and they're the idiomatic form in these docs. A lambda in a child or attribute position ({(lambda: count() * 2)}) is a reactive expression, exactly like the plain {count() * 2}.

docs.title: Conversions and format specs
docs.text:
They work as in any t-string. The compiler folds them into the getter, so they're re-applied when the value changes:

html(t"<td>{price():.2f}</td><td>{name()!r}</td>")

docs.title: Markup rules
docs.text:
Templates are HTML, with a few conveniences borrowed from JSX:

  • Attribute names are HTML names: class, for, aria-label, data-id, tabindex. Static values are written into the compiled markup.
  • Any element may self-close (<div />). Void elements (<br>, <input>, <img>) may be written either way.
  • Text follows JSX's whitespace rules. Text that spans lines is trimmed line by line and joined with single spaces, and whitespace-only text containing a newline is dropped, so you can indent markup freely. <pre> keeps its text verbatim.
  • Character references such as & and   are decoded.
  • <!-- comments --> are dropped.
  • <script>, <style>, and <textarea> take static content only. Give a <textarea> its value with value={...}.
  • <svg> and <math> work like any other element, and their children get the right namespace.

A template with several top-level nodes returns a fragment, and a template with no elements is text:

html(t"<dt>{term}</dt><dd>{definition}</dd>")
html(t"Hello, {name}!")

docs.title: Markup the parser would rewrite is an error
docs.text:
Wybthon hands each template's markup to the browser's HTML parser and relies on getting back exactly the nodes it wrote. Markup the parser would silently rearrange is rejected with the template's source and the fix. The compiler reports it as a SyntaxError with the file and line when the module is compiled; a template compiled at run time raises TemplateError the first time it's used:

Markup Why it's rejected <table><tr>...</tr></table> The parser inserts a <tbody>; write it yourself. <p><span><div>...</div></span></p> A block element closes an open <p>, however deeply it's nested (a <button> or table cell in between stops this). <a><span><a>...</a></span></a> Links, buttons, and forms can't nest. <li><div><li>...</li></div></li> A <li> closes an open one unless a list wraps it; <dd> and <dt> work the same way inside a <dl>. <tbody>text</tbody> Table sections can't hold text. <div><span></div> Mismatched or unclosed tags.

docs.title: Components in templates
docs.text:
There are two ways to use a component in a template. Calling it inside an interpolation keeps full type checking of its props:

html(t"""
  <main>
    {Header(title="Dashboard", user=user())}
    {For(panels(), panel_row)}
  </main>
""")

A call in a child position is dispatched when the template is created: a component, or a built-in such as Show or For, is built with a getter for each dynamic argument, so Header reads props.user and sees each new value of user(). Any other call, such as {format_date(created())}, becomes one reactive hole. See Calls in a child position.

The tag form reads like the rest of the markup and passes nested markup as children:

html(t"""
  <{Card} title={project().name}>
    <p>Changes apply immediately.</p>
    <button onclick={reset}>Reset</button>
  </{Card}>
""")

Attributes become keyword props (a hyphen becomes an underscore, and class and for become class_ and html_for), and the content becomes the children prop, one child per top-level node. A dynamic attribute value, such as title={project().name}, is passed as a getter, the way Solid passes JSX props. Close the tag with </{Card}>, or self-close it with <{Card} />. The built-ins work the same way, called the way their signatures take children:

html(t"""
  <{Show} when={user()} fallback={sign_in}>
    <p>Welcome back.</p>
  </{Show}>
  <{Theme} value="dark"><{Toolbar} /></{Theme}>
  <{Link} href="/settings" class="nav">Settings</{Link}>
""")

Type checkers can't see inside the template string, so the tag form's props are checked at run time in dev mode, like any component call. Use the call form when you want the checker's help.

docs.title: Templates and reactivity
docs.text:
A component runs once, so the template it returns is mounted once; only its slots' bindings ever update. Each dynamic expression is its own binding, so <b title={user().role}>{user().name}</b> updates the attribute and the text separately, with no re-run of anything else.

When a reactive hole returns a template, the hole re-runs when its inputs change. If it returns an instance of the same literal as before, Wybthon patches the mounted instance slot by slot instead of replacing it, the way lit-html does:

def summary():
    if user().is_admin:
        return html(t"<b>{user().name} (admin)</b>")
    return html(t"<span>{user().name}</span>")


html(t"<div>{summary()}</div>")

Here {summary()} is a hole, and it re-runs when user changes. While the user stays an admin, it returns the same literal again and the mounted <b> is patched in place; when that changes, a template from the other literal replaces it.

docs.title: Templates and h()
docs.text:
h(tag, props, *children) is the programmatic layer, the counterpart of Solid's h. Use it when markup is built by code: generated forms, recursive trees, or components that compute their tag. The two mix freely, and they share one set of prop appliers, so a prop means the same thing in both:

from wybthon import h, html


def heading(level, text):
    return h(f"h{level}", {"class": "title"}, text)


html(t"<section>{heading(2, title())}{body}</section>")
h("div", {"class_": "page"}, html(t"<h1>Title</h1>"))

h() props accept Python names (class_, html_for, aria_label, on_click) as well as HTML names. The compiler only rewrites templates, so the arguments of an h() call are evaluated when it runs: pass an accessor or a lambda where a value should stay reactive (h("p", None, count)). A t-string isn't markup outside html(); pass it to html() first.

docs.title: Server rendering, hydration, and SVG
docs.text: A server render, a hydrating client, and SVG or MathML content expand a template into the same VNodes h() would build and mount those, so output and hydration keys are identical whichever style you use. Everything else, which is every browser update after hydration, uses the compiled path.

docs.title: Editor support
docs.text: Python expressions inside {...} are highlighted and type-checked as code. The surrounding HTML is a string, so editors don't highlight or format it unless you add an extension for HTML in t-strings, and type checkers don't check a component tag's attributes.

docs.text:
• The compiler: what it rewrites, where it runs, and how to inspect it.
  • Components: props, children, and the run-once model.
  • Virtual DOM: how compiled templates mount and update.
  • html API reference.

docs.title: Virtual DOM
docs.text: Wybthon keeps a small virtual DOM as a rendering implementation detail. This page explains why it exists, how compiled templates and h() trees mount through it, how reactive holes, bindings, and native regions update, and how DOM operations reach the browser.

docs.title: Why a VDOM in a fine-grained framework?
docs.text:
SolidJS compiles JSX ahead of time, splitting each template into a static skeleton and the expressions that change. Wybthon's compiler makes the same split for t-string templates before a module runs: each literal becomes a skeleton and a mount function, and each dynamic expression becomes a getter, so every instance only supplies its values.

What the VDOM adds is batching. In Pyodide every DOM call crosses the Python-to-JavaScript bridge, which dominates rendering cost. So nothing in the renderer touches the DOM directly:

  • A component returns its markup once, usually a template instance.
  • Reactive expressions inside it become holes and bindings, each updating its own node.
  • When a hole re-evaluates, the reconciler patches only the hole's region and emits compact operations against integer node ids.
  • All operations from one flush are handed to a small JavaScript kernel in one bridge crossing.

The reactive model is Solid's. The VDOM never diffs whole components, only the region under a hole, and static markup never becomes VNodes at all when it's written as a template. Removing the batch in favor of direct DOM calls would put a bridge crossing behind every node. See RFC 0004 for the design of the current engine and RFC 0003 for compiled templates.

docs.title: Two ways to write markup
docs.text:
Templates are the primary path: html(t"<div class={cls()}>{count()}</div>") is compiled ahead of time and mounts with one clone command. h(tag, props, *children) is the programmatic path, the counterpart of Solid's h, for markup built by code: generated forms, recursive trees, or components that compute their tag. The two mix freely, and they share one set of prop appliers, so a prop means the same thing in both.

from wybthon import Fragment, h, html

view = html(t'<div class="app"><h1>Hello</h1><p>Welcome</p></div>')
built = h("div", {"class": "app"}, h("h1", {}, "Hello"), h("p", {}, "Welcome"))
grouped = Fragment(h("h1", {}, "Title"), html(t"<p>Body</p>"))

For h:

  • tag is an HTML tag, an SVG tag, or a component.
  • Props are attributes, DOM properties, event handlers, ref, key, or reactive bindings.
  • Children are strings, numbers, VNodes (templates included), lists (flattened), None (dropped), or reactive expressions (holes). A t-string isn't a child; pass it to html() first.

Template attributes use HTML names (class, for, aria-label). h() props accept those and Python names, and the prop applier maps them when it writes the attribute: class_ becomes class, html_for becomes for, and other underscores become hyphens (aria_label, data_testid). In both styles, True sets a boolean attribute and False or None removes it; value and checked are written as DOM properties; class accepts a string, a list, or a {name: bool} dict; and style accepts a string or a dict with snake- or kebab-case keys.

The compiler only rewrites templates, so an h() call's arguments are evaluated when it runs. An h() element mounts node by node: one create command per node, all in the same batch as everything else.

docs.title: Compiled templates
docs.text: The compiler parses and validates each template literal when its module is compiled, and writes the result into the module: the literal's normalized parse tree as constants, and a mount function for each of its elements. The first html() call of a literal rebuilds its slot plan from that tree and installs the mount functions, with no parsing and no code generation. A template that reaches html() uncompiled is compiled there instead, once, and cached by the identity of the t-string's strings tuple (holding a reference, so the identity can't be reused). Literals are code, so that cache is bounded by the size of the program; a template built by hand, whose strings aren't a literal's constant, falls back to a bounded structural cache.

docs.title: What a compiled template holds
docs.text:
For each top-level element, a compiled template has:

  • the static skeleton, serialized to HTML with every static attribute and all static text written in, and with a placeholder wherever a child slot sits;
  • the slot plan: the pre-order node offset and kind of every interpolation (attribute, part of an attribute, event, ref, spread, child, or component tag);
  • the delegated event types per offset, so cloning marks listeners natively;
  • the tree it was parsed from, used for expansion (see When templates expand).

Validation rejects markup the browser's HTML parser would rewrite, such as <tr> directly inside <table> or a <div> inside a <p>, with the template's source and the fix: a SyntaxError with the file and line when the compiler finds it, or a TemplateError for a template compiled at run time. That's what lets Python and the kernel agree on every node's offset without reading anything back.

html() itself does almost nothing per call: it wraps the compiled template with the call's values. A template with one top-level element is one instance; several top-level nodes make a fragment of instances, text, and values.

docs.title: One mount function per template
docs.text:
Each compiled element has a mount function that mounts an instance in straight-line code, with its offsets and prop names as constants. The compiler writes it into the module as an ordinary def, so a production build turns it into bytecode with the rest of the application. It:

  1. allocates a dense block of node ids, one per node in the skeleton;
  2. appends one CLONE command, registering the skeleton with the kernel (REGISTER_TPL, in the same batch) the first time it's needed;
  3. walks the slot plan with the instance's values, applying each attribute, event, ref, and spread through the same appliers h() uses;
  4. fills each child slot and mounts each component tag at its placeholder;
  5. records each slot's state on the instance, for patching and teardown.

There are no structural guards and no VNodes for the static parts: the literal guarantees its own structure.

docs.title: The clone command and placeholders
docs.text:
CLONE clones the registered <template>, registers its nodes in pre-order, fills its text slots, marks its delegated listeners, and inserts the clone before an anchor, all in one command: [CLONE, first_id, tpl_id, parent_id, anchor_id, *texts].

A child slot keeps its placeholder as a permanent anchor:

  • When the slot's neighbors aren't text or another child slot, the placeholder is a one-space text node. A text value (a string or number) is written straight into the clone command, so a row's label costs no extra command. A reactive hole whose first result is text fills that slot of the command too, and later text results are a single nodeValue write (HOLE_TEXT).
  • Otherwise the placeholder is an empty comment.
  • A node, list, or component is mounted in front of the placeholder, and the placeholder stays. Nothing is created and then thrown away.

A component tag (<{Card}>) always gets a comment placeholder, and the component mounts in front of it.

docs.title: Patching slot by slot
docs.text:
When a reactive hole re-runs and returns a template from the same literal as before, the reconciler doesn't diff a tree. It walks the slot plan and compares each value with the previous one by identity, as lit-html does:

  • An unchanged slot costs one comparison.
  • A changed text value is one SET_TEXT write.
  • A changed attribute, event handler, ref, or spread is re-applied.
  • A child slot's new value is patched into its region, and a component tag's component is patched with its new props, so its state survives.

A template from a different literal replaces the instance.

docs.title: Reactive holes and bindings
docs.text:
A getter, an accessor, or a zero-argument function in a child position becomes a hole; in an attribute position (other than events and ref), it becomes a binding. In a template, the compiler makes every dynamic expression a getter, so {count() * 2} and class={status()} are a hole and a binding. Each binding updates on its own, so unrelated attributes on the same element update independently. Use hole to create a hole explicitly in an h() tree when you need a key.

from wybthon import create_signal, html

count, set_count = create_signal(0)

view = html(t"<p class={'odd' if count() % 2 else 'even'}>Count: {count()} (x2={count() * 2})</p>")

A hole's expression may return a string, a template or other VNode, a list (mounted as a fragment), None, or another accessor. Holes are ownership scopes: components mounted inside one survive its re-evaluations while the reconciler can patch them in place, and on_cleanup inside the expression runs before each re-run.

Bindings keep their state in slots. Each hole and attribute binding is a small computation that holds its node, name, and last value directly, and applies its result as a method, not through a closure and its cells. A mounted template row therefore keeps about half as many objects for the cyclic garbage collector to track as it did in the previous engine; see the engine v4 evaluation.

A static probe before a computation. A binding whose expression makes no calls ({props.title}, {row["label"]}) first runs under a lightweight observer. If it reads nothing reactive, creates nothing, and returns synchronously, the value is applied and no computation is ever allocated. The probe stops at the first reactive read, and the binding then runs as a computation. A probe that returns an accessor without reading anything ({row["label"]} returning a signal) binds directly to that accessor.

Inert bindings are dropped. Any other hole or binding that finishes its first run without reading a reactive source, and without creating children, cleanups, or async work, can never run again. The renderer disposes it immediately and keeps only the DOM it produced. Together with constant props that subscribe to nothing (see What props cost), a component whose props never change costs about what its markup costs.

docs.title: Native regions
docs.text:
Show, Switch, For, and Repeat aren't components. They return region nodes that the reconciler mounts directly, with no component context, props object, or wrapper memo:

  • Show and Switch are one branch computation. It selects a branch from the condition and re-mounts the content only when the selected branch changes, between two comment markers.
  • For and Repeat are list regions. Each row is its own owner, rows are moved rather than re-diffed, and a store list's edit records apply directly. A row's index is a plain integer until something reads index() in a tracking scope, which is when the signal behind it is created.

Matching a keyed list against its mounted rows skips the common prefix and suffix by identity without calling into each row, detects swapped ends the way Solid's reconcileArrays does, and only then falls back to a key table for what's left. Swapping two rows is two native moves.

When a reactive hole re-renders a region of the same kind, the new condition or source is pushed into the mounted region instead of remounting it. That's the only part that was ever reactive, so rows and branch state survive.

docs.title: The reconciler
docs.text:
When a hole re-evaluates, patch compares the old result with the new one:

  • Same VNode instance (for example a cached For row): skipped.
  • Template instances from the same literal: patched slot by slot.
  • Regions of the same kind: the new condition or source is pushed in.
  • Same component and key: patched in place. New props flow into the existing props instance, and the body doesn't run again.
  • Same element tag and key: props are diffed, text is updated, and children are reconciled.
  • Anything else: the old subtree is unmounted and the new one mounted at the same position.

Children are matched in three passes: by identity, by key, then by type in document order. DOM moves are minimized with a longest-increasing-subsequence pass, so a reorder emits only the inserts that are strictly necessary.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
Give siblings a stable key when their order can change and they carry state (form inputs, components with local signals). Every component accepts key=. A component re-rendered with a different key remounts with fresh state:

def editor():
    return Editor(user_id=current_id(), key=current_id())


html(t"<div>{editor()}</div>")

Prefer For for lists: it caches each row's node and scope, so rows are moved rather than re-diffed at all.

docs.title: When templates expand
docs.text: Some renderers need ordinary VNodes. Server rendering, hydration, SVG and MathML (a template containing <svg> or <math>, or one mounted inside an SVG parent), and backends that can't parse HTML expand a template into the same VNode tree h() would build, and mount that. Output and hydration keys are identical whichever style you use. A hydrated instance keeps its expanded tree, so a hole that later patches it diffs the expanded trees; everything mounted after hydration uses the clone path.

docs.title: The batched rendering kernel
docs.text:
The reconciler, templates, and prop appliers emit operations such as clone, insert, set-text, and set-attr against integer node ids into a command buffer. At each commit point (the end of render, the DOM phase of every flush) the buffer is serialized once and handed to the JS kernel, which applies every operation natively and keeps an id -> Node registry. A mount of a thousand-row table is one bridge crossing instead of tens of thousands. The kernel page documents the wire protocol.

The same protocol drives a pure-Python backend (kernel.PythonBackend) that applies the ops to an in-memory stub document. Unit tests, wybthon.testing, and the stubbed benchmark run against it, so all of them exercise exactly what the browser sees. See the Testing guide.

docs.title: Template-declared listeners
docs.text: Template registration lists the delegated event types at each offset. Cloning an instance marks those listeners natively, so mounting a row with two handlers sends no LISTEN commands. Python stores the handlers in one table keyed by node id; a node with a single handler stores it directly, without a dictionary of its own.

docs.title: Teardown
docs.text:
Unmounting doesn't visit every node in Python. DISPOSE_RANGE removes a contiguous range of siblings and releases every registered node inside it, and DISPOSE does the same for one node's subtree; the kernel walks the removed nodes natively. Python-side registrations (handlers, reactive bindings, refs) are found through the template's slot plan.

Lists benefit most:

  • Clearing a For list emits one DISPOSE_RANGE, plus the disposal of each row's owner.
  • When a keyed list reuses no rows (every row replaced), the new rows mount as one splice and the old ones go in one DISPOSE_RANGE, instead of reconciling a thousand unrelated pairs.

docs.title: Event delegation
docs.text: Handlers such as onclick={save} (or on_click=save in an h() call) don't attach native listeners per element. The kernel installs one native listener per event type on each render root (the container passed to render). Template nodes declare their listener types at registration, and handlers on other nodes ride the same buffer as a LISTEN command. When an event fires, the kernel walks the ancestor chain natively and calls into Python once for the matching route, with a small JSON payload. Handlers may take the event or no arguments at all. See Events.

docs.title: render and Root
docs.text:
render(vnode, container) mounts a tree into an Element, a CSS selector, or a kernel node id, commits the buffer, registers the container as an event root, and returns a Root. Rendering into the same container again patches the existing tree in place.

from wybthon import html, render

root = render(html(t"<h1>Hello, world!</h1>"), "#app")
root.container  # the container Element
root.vnode  # the mounted root VNode
root.dispose()  # unmount, dispose every scope, unregister the event root

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• compiler: the AST transform that defers dynamic expressions and precompiles template literals, and the import hook that runs it.
  • templates: html and TemplateError: parsing, validation, the runtime fallback and its cache, mount function generation, slot-wise patching, and expansion.
  • vnode: VNode, h, Fragment, hole, and child normalization (no browser dependency).
  • _compiled (private): the run-time helpers compiled modules call (getters, call dispatch, format specs, precompiled entries).
  • _dom_props (private): attribute, property, class, style, dataset, ref, and reactive-binding application, shared by templates and h(), all op-based.
  • _html_rules (private): the HTML parser's content rules, used by template validation.
  • _regions (private): the native Show, Switch, For, and Repeat regions.
  • reconciler: mount, patch, unmount, render, hydrate, and Root.
  • kernel: the command buffer, the JS kernel (_kernel.js), and the Python reference backend.
  • events: the Python half of delegation and DomEvent.

The common names are re-exported from the top-level wybthon package.

docs.title: Error reporting
docs.text: In dev mode, render errors are logged with the component name and a full traceback. An Errored boundary above the failing subtree catches the error and shows a fallback instead. Production builds (wyb build) turn dev mode off before the application imports; call set_dev_mode(False) yourself when you mount outside the production bootstrap. A malformed template isn't a render error: the compiler rejects it when the module is compiled, and html() raises TemplateError the first time an uncompiled one runs, in every mode.

  • See Primitives for the hole mental model.
  • Read Lifecycle and ownership for mount and unmount semantics.
  • Browse the reconciler and kernel API pages.
  • Read RFC 0004 for the compiler, leaner bindings, and keyed matching, and RFC 0003 for compiled templates and zero-cost components.

docs.title: Authoring patterns example
docs.text:
A single page that exercises the idioms from the Authoring patterns guide:

  • Markup written as html templates, with components used as tags.
  • Composition through children (a Card component built on ParentProps that forwards an id with omit).
  • State with create_signal and derived values with create_memo.
  • Reactive list rendering with For over a draft-first store.
  • A mutation wrapped in action with a pending indicator.
  • Cleanup with on_settled and on_cleanup (a ticking Timer).

docs.title: Full listing
docs.text:
import asyncio

from wybthon import (
    For,
    ParentProps,
    Show,
    action,
    component,
    create_memo,
    create_signal,
    create_store,
    html,
    omit,
    on_cleanup,
    on_settled,
    render,
)


class CardProps(ParentProps):
    title: str = ""
    id: str | None = None


@component
def Card(props: CardProps):
    return html(t"""
      <section class="card" {omit(props, "title", "children")}>
        <h3>{props.title}</h3>
        {props.children}
      </section>
    """)


@component
def NamesList():
    store, set_store = create_store({"names": []})
    draft, set_draft = create_signal("")

    total = create_memo(lambda: len(store.names))
    starts_with_a = create_memo(lambda: sum(1 for n in store.names if n["text"].lower().startswith("a")))

    @action
    async def add(text: str):
        # Simulate a slow save; the button is disabled while ``add.pending()``.
        await asyncio.sleep(0.3)
        set_store(lambda s: s.names.append({"id": len(s.names) + 1, "text": text}))
        set_draft("")

    def save():
        add(draft())

    def clear():
        set_store(lambda s: s.names.clear())

    def edit(e):
        set_draft(e.target.value)

    def row(item, index):
        return html(t"<li>{index() + 1}. {item()['text']}</li>")

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <p>Total: {total()} | Starts with A: {starts_with_a()}</p>
        <div>
          <input value={draft()} oninput={edit} placeholder="Name">
          <button onclick={save} disabled={add.pending()}>Add</button>
          <button onclick={clear}>Clear</button>
        </div>
        {Show(add.pending(), html(t"<p>Saving...</p>"))}
        <ul>
          {For(store.names, row, fallback=html(t"<li>No names yet.</li>"), keyed=lambda n: n["id"])}
        </ul>
      </div>
    """)


@component
def Timer():
    seconds, set_seconds = create_signal(0)

    def start():
        from js import clearInterval, setInterval
        from pyodide.ffi import create_proxy

        proxy = create_proxy(lambda: set_seconds(lambda s: s + 1))
        handle = setInterval(proxy, 1000)

        def stop():
            clearInterval(handle)
            proxy.destroy()

        return stop  # cleanup runs on unmount

    on_settled(start)
    on_cleanup(lambda: print("Timer unmounted"))

    return html(t'<div class="timer"><span>Seconds: {seconds()}</span></div>')


@component
def Page():
    show_timer, set_show_timer = create_signal(True)

    def toggle_timer():
        set_show_timer(lambda v: not v)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <{Card} title="State and derived values" id="names">
          <{NamesList} />
        </{Card}>
        <{Card} title="Cleanup">
          <button onclick={toggle_timer}>Toggle timer</button>
          {Show(show_timer(), Timer())}
        </{Card}>
      </div>
    """)


render(Page(), "#app")

docs.title: What to notice
docs.text:
• Card subclasses ParentProps, so it accepts children, and declares the props it handles as plain annotations with defaults. {props.title} is a tracked read the compiler turns into a getter. It forwards id by spreading omit(props, "title", "children") onto the <section> (<section {...}> is a spread), so the parent's id="names" lands there, and each forwarded key stays reactive. A None value removes the attribute.
  • Page uses the component tag form: <{Card} title="...">...</{Card}> passes the attributes as props and the nested markup as children, and <{NamesList} /> takes none. The call form, {Card(title="Cleanup", children=[...])} or Card(title=...)[...], does the same and is fully type-checked; dev mode checks the tag form's props at run time.
  • NamesList keeps its list in a store. set_store(lambda s: s.names.append(...)) mutates a draft; only the leaf signals that changed notify, and For matches rows by id so existing <li> elements are kept.
  • The store list goes to For as is: For(store.names, ...) tracks it without a wrapping lambda.
  • With a key function, For hands the row callback accessors for both the item and the index, so row reads item() and index() right in its template; the expression is one hole.
  • The summary line reads two memos, total() and starts_with_a(); each is its own text binding.
  • add is an action. While it's in flight, add.pending() is True, which disables the button (disabled={add.pending()}) and shows the "Saving..." line.
  • save reads draft() in an event handler, which isn't a tracking scope, so the read doesn't subscribe anything.
  • Handlers that don't need the event take no arguments (onclick={clear}); edit takes the event to read e.target.value. The compiler never wraps a handler. Every handler is a named function, since Python doesn't allow a bare lambda inside a t-string interpolation (an inline one needs parentheses: onclick={(lambda: set_draft(""))}).
  • Show and For mount as native regions, not wrapper components: each is one computation that selects what to render, with no component scope or props of its own.
  • Timer starts its interval in on_settled and returns a cleanup from it, so the interval stops when Show unmounts the timer. on_cleanup in the body runs at the same time. Showing it again mounts a fresh Timer with its own state.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read Components and Lifecycle and Ownership.
  • Browse the Counter example for a smaller starting point.
  • See Stores for reconcile, snapshot, and derived stores.

docs.title: Counter
docs.text:
Signals, derived values, a template, and typed props with defaults in one small component.

from wybthon import Props, component, create_memo, create_signal, html, render, untrack


class CounterProps(Props):
    initial: int = 0
    step: int = 1


@component
def Counter(props: CounterProps):
    # ``untrack`` reads ``initial`` once without subscribing, which is
    # exactly what a signal seed needs.
    count, set_count = create_signal(untrack(lambda: props.initial))

    # Memos are cached and glitch-free; ``parity`` recomputes only when
    # ``count`` changes.
    parity = create_memo(lambda: "even" if count() % 2 == 0 else "odd")

    def increment():
        # Writes are staged until the next flush, so use the functional form
        # when the new value depends on the current one.
        set_count(lambda n: n + props.step)

    def reset():
        set_count(props.initial)

    return html(t"""
      <div class="counter">
        <p>Count: {count()}, doubled: {count() * 2}</p>
        <p>{parity()}</p>
        <p>Next: {count()} + {props.step}</p>
        <button onclick={increment}>Increment</button>
        <button onclick={reset}>Reset</button>
      </div>
    """)


render(Counter(initial=5, step=2), "#app")

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• CounterProps declares two optional inputs as plain annotations with ordinary defaults. Use prop only when a default needs a factory: tags: list[str] = prop(default_factory=list).
  • html takes the t"..." template string and returns a node. Wybthon's compiler prepares each literal when the module is compiled, and the static markup becomes a native <template> that's cloned for every instance. See Templates.
  • {count()}, {count() * 2}, {parity()}, and {props.step} contain a call or an attribute access, so the compiler turns each into a getter. Each one becomes a reactive hole: only that text node changes when what it reads changes. Everything else in the markup is static.
  • count() * 2 needs no memo: it's cheap, and the hole recomputes it only when count changes. parity is a memo to show the other option; a memo is worth it when a derived value is expensive or read in several places.
  • props.step is a tracked read of the current value. If the parent passes a reactive value, the hole updates.
  • onclick={increment} registers a delegated click handler. The compiler never wraps an event handler. Attribute names in templates are the HTML names (class, onclick).
  • The component body runs once. There's no re-render to worry about, so closures like increment never go stale.
  • The handlers take no arguments; a handler may also accept the event. props.step and props.initial inside a handler are plain reads: event handlers aren't tracking scopes, so they neither subscribe nor warn.

docs.title: Calling the component
docs.text:
@component returns a Component. Calling it with keyword arguments returns a node:

Counter()  # every prop has a default
Counter(initial=5)
Counter(initial=5, step=10)

An unknown or misspelled prop (Counter(stpe=2)) is a type error in pyright and mypy, and a TypeError at run time in dev mode.

Inside another template, call it in an interpolation to keep that type checking, or use the tag form, which dev mode checks at run time:

html(t"<main>{Counter(initial=5)}</main>")
html(t"<main><{Counter} initial={5} /></main>")

Pass a dynamic expression to react to parent state. In a template, the compiler passes the counter a getter, so props.initial reads the parent's current value:

from wybthon import create_signal

seed, set_seed = create_signal(0)
html(t"<main>{Counter(initial=seed())}</main>")  # props.initial reflects seed()

Because the counter reads initial once, untracked, to seed its own signal, later changes to seed don't reset the count; "Reset" reads the current seed. That's the intended semantics of a seed. If you want a prop to drive the display directly, place it in the template instead of copying it into a signal. A prop passed as a constant, like step=2 above, costs nothing to read: it never changes, so nothing subscribes to it.

docs.title: Testing it
docs.text:
wybthon.testing renders the counter in plain CPython:

from wybthon.testing import fire, render

with render(Counter(initial=5, step=2)) as screen:
    fire.click(screen.get_by_role("button", name="Increment"))
    assert screen.get_by_text("Count: 7, doubled: 14")

  • Browse the reactivity API for signal helpers.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Catch errors raised while rendering with Errored, show a fallback, and recover with a reset callback or automatically when a route changes.

from wybthon import Errored, Props, component, create_signal, html, render
from wybthon.router import current_path


class RiskyPanelProps(Props):
    should_fail: bool = False


@component
def RiskyPanel(props: RiskyPanelProps):
    # A hole that raises routes the error to the nearest Errored boundary.
    def body():
        if props.should_fail:
            raise RuntimeError("the panel exploded")
        return "Everything is fine."

    return html(t"<p>{body()}</p>")


def fallback(err, reset):
    return html(t"""
      <div style="color: crimson">
        <p>Caught: {err()}</p>
        <button onclick={reset}>Retry</button>
      </div>
    """)


def log_error(err):
    print("logged:", err)


@component
def App():
    fail, set_fail = create_signal(False)

    def toggle():
        set_fail(lambda v: not v)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <button onclick={toggle}>Toggle failure</button>
        {Errored(RiskyPanel(should_fail=fail()), fallback=fallback, on_error=log_error, reset_on=current_path)}
      </div>
    """)


render(App(), "#app")

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Errored installs an error handler on its owner scope. Errors raised in a descendant hole, component body, effect, or async memo route to the nearest boundary; sibling trees are untouched.
  • Its children can be a node, as here: RiskyPanel(...) doesn't run until the boundary mounts it, so there's no need to wrap it in a lambda. Because the call sits in a template, the compiler passes should_fail as a getter, so the panel reads the current value of fail() each time body() runs.
  • body() is a plain function call in the template, so the whole call is one reactive hole: it reruns when props.should_fail changes, and when it raises, the error goes to the boundary.
  • fallback may be a node, a string, or a callable. A callable receives (err, reset) (or just (err)). err is an accessor for the caught exception, as in Solid 2.0, so {err()} in the fallback's template shows the message. Calling reset() clears the error and re-renders the children; it takes no arguments, so it works directly as a click handler.
  • on_error is a plain callback for logging or reporting. It receives the exception itself.
  • reset_on is an accessor whose change clears the error automatically. Passing current_path from wybthon.router resets the boundary on every navigation, which is the usual behavior for a page-level boundary.
  • Boundaries also heal on their own: the boundary remembers which reactive inputs the failing computation read, so toggling the failure off re-renders RiskyPanel without a click on "Retry."

docs.title: Errors in async data
docs.text:
An async memo that rejects raises into the boundary as well. Nest Errored outside Loading so the fallback replaces the pending UI:

from wybthon import Errored, Loading, component, create_memo, html


async def load_profile():
    response = await fetch_json("/api/profile")
    if response is None:
        raise LookupError("profile not found")
    return response


def profile_failed(err, reset):
    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <p>{err()}</p>
        <button onclick={reset}>Try again</button>
      </div>
    """)


@component
def Profile():
    profile = create_memo(load_profile)

    return Errored(
        Loading(html(t"<p>{profile()['name']}</p>"), fallback=html(t"<p>Loading...</p>")),
        fallback=profile_failed,
    )

The memo keeps its error until it runs again, so to retry the request itself, call refresh on it before reset(), as the Async fetch example does.

docs.title: Errors in effects
docs.text:
create_effect accepts an error= handler that receives exceptions from its compute stage instead of routing them to the boundary:

from wybthon import create_effect

create_effect(
    lambda: parse(raw_input()),
    lambda parsed: show(parsed),
    error=lambda exc: print("parse failed:", exc),
)

Event handlers run outside rendering, so an exception in an onclick handler is logged to the console and doesn't involve any boundary; the UI stays intact.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read the Error Boundaries concept page.
  • See the error_boundary API reference.
  • Combine with Loading for async failure handling.

docs.title: Async fetch
docs.text:
Fetch data with an async create_memo and show a loading state with Loading. There's no separate resource primitive: a memo whose body is async def is the async computation.

from js import fetch

from wybthon import Errored, Loading, component, create_memo, create_signal, html, is_pending, refresh, render


@component
def TodoViewer():
    todo_id, set_todo_id = create_signal(1)

    async def load_todo():
        # Reads are tracked before and after ``await``: changing ``todo_id``
        # refetches automatically.
        response = await fetch(f"https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/{todo_id()}")
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {response.status}")
        return (await response.json()).to_py()

    todo = create_memo(load_todo)

    def previous():
        set_todo_id(lambda i: max(1, i - 1))

    def next_todo():
        set_todo_id(lambda i: i + 1)

    def failed(err, reset):
        def retry():
            refresh(todo)  # fetch again
            reset()  # and re-render the boundary's children

        return html(t"""
          <div>
            <p>Failed: {err()}</p>
            <button onclick={retry}>Retry</button>
          </div>
        """)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <button onclick={previous}>Previous</button>
        <button onclick={next_todo}>Next</button>
        <{Errored} fallback={failed}>
          <{Loading} fallback={html(t"<p>Loading...</p>")}>
            <p>
              Todo #{todo()["id"]}: {todo()["title"]}
              <span>{" (refreshing...)" if is_pending(todo) else ""}</span>
            </p>
          </{Loading}>
        </{Errored}>
      </div>
    """)


render(TodoViewer(), "#app")

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Reading todo() inside the boundary is what wires it to Loading. Each expression that calls todo() or is_pending(...) is dynamic, so the compiler turns it into a getter, and each becomes its own reactive hole. Until the coroutine resolves for the first time, the read raises NotReadyError; the hole keeps its previous content and the nearest boundary shows its fallback. The content stays mounted the whole time (parked off-document), so any state created inside it survives.

Once the memo has a value, the fallback never returns. When todo_id changes, the memo recomputes inside a transition: it keeps serving the previous todo, and the UI that read todo_id holds with it, until the new one arrives, so the id and the todo never disagree on screen. is_pending is True during that window, which drives the inline hint.

If load_todo raises, the error routes to the nearest Errored boundary. Its fallback reads the error through the err accessor. The memo keeps the error until something makes it run again, so retry calls refresh to fetch again and reset to re-render the children. Changing todo_id with "Previous" or "Next" also clears the error, because the boundary heals when an input of the failed computation changes.

The boundaries take nodes directly: Errored(Loading(...)) needs no wrapping lambdas, because nothing in a node runs until it mounts inside the boundary. Written inside the template, the boundary calls are built the way component tags are, with getters for their dynamic arguments; the nested template's holes don't run until Loading mounts them. An interpolation can span several lines, as this one does.

docs.title: Refetching
docs.text:
Signal reads inside the async body are dependencies, so any signal works as a refetch trigger. A "version" counter is the simplest:

from wybthon import create_memo, create_signal, html

version, set_version = create_signal(0)


async def load_report():
    version()  # tracked: bumping it refetches
    return await fetch_report()


report = create_memo(load_report)


def refetch():
    set_version(lambda v: v + 1)


html(t"<button onclick={refetch}>Refetch</button>")

To refetch quietly after a mutation, without showing a pending state, use refresh. It returns an awaitable for the next settled value:

from wybthon import action, refresh


@action
async def save_report(data):
    await post_report(data)
    await refresh(report)

docs.title: Reading outside a boundary
docs.text:
latest evaluates an expression without ever raising NotReadyError; unresolved computations yield None:

from wybthon import html, latest


html(t"<span>{latest(lambda: todo()['title']) or 'nothing yet'}</span>")

resolve awaits the next settled value, which is handy in actions and scripts:

from wybthon import resolve


async def main():
    data = await resolve(todo)
    print(data["title"])

docs.title: Waiting on data the children don't read
docs.text:
Pass on= to make a boundary wait for specific accessors even if nothing inside reads them, for example to keep a layout from partially rendering:

from wybthon import Loading, html

Loading(html(t"<p>Ready</p>"), fallback=html(t"<p>Loading...</p>"), on=[user, settings])

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read Async and Loading for the full model, including Reveal for coordinating several boundaries.
  • See create_memo for async memo semantics, including async generators.
  • Browse the Error handling example for failure-state UI.

docs.title: Forms
docs.text:
Bindings, validation, an aggregated submit handler, and accessible error messages. The form helpers live in wybthon.forms.

from wybthon import Show, component, html, render
from wybthon.forms import (
    a11y_control_attrs,
    bind_checkbox,
    bind_select,
    bind_text,
    email,
    error_message_attrs,
    form_state,
    min_length,
    on_submit_validated,
    required,
)


@component
def SignupForm():
    fields = form_state({"name": "", "email": "", "plan": "free", "subscribe": False})
    rules = {
        "name": [required(), min_length(2)],
        "email": [required(), email()],
    }

    def save(f):
        print({k: field.value.peek() for k, field in f.items()})

    name = fields["name"]
    mail = fields["email"]
    plan = fields["plan"]
    subscribe = fields["subscribe"]

    return html(t"""
      <form onsubmit={on_submit_validated(rules, save, fields)}>
        <p>
          <label for="name">Name</label>
          <input
            id="name"
            {bind_text(name, validators=rules["name"])}
            {a11y_control_attrs(name, described_by_id="name-err")}
          >
          <span {error_message_attrs(id="name-err")}>{name.error()}</span>
        </p>
        <p>
          <label for="email">Email</label>
          <input
            id="email"
            type="email"
            {bind_text(mail, validators=rules["email"])}
            {a11y_control_attrs(mail, described_by_id="email-err")}
          >
          <span {error_message_attrs(id="email-err")}>{mail.error()}</span>
        </p>
        <p>
          <label for="plan">Plan</label>
          <select id="plan" {bind_select(plan)}>
            <option value="free">Free</option>
            <option value="pro">Pro</option>
          </select>
        </p>
        <p>
          <label><input type="checkbox" {bind_checkbox(subscribe)}> Subscribe to the newsletter</label>
        </p>
        {Show(plan.value() == "pro", html(t"<p>Pro plans are billed monthly.</p>"))}
        <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
      </form>
    """)


render(SignupForm(), "#app")

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• form_state returns a dict of Field objects. Each field carries value, error, and touched accessors with matching setters, so every piece of form state is a signal.
  • bind_text returns {"value": field.value, "on_input": handler}. The value entry is the accessor itself, so programmatic writes through field.set_value(...) update the input too. Validators run on every input event.
  • {bind_text(...)} in the <input> tag is a spread: the mapping's entries are applied as props. A spread is evaluated once, when the template is created; the accessors inside it (the value, the ARIA state) are what keep the input in sync. A tag can take several spreads alongside ordinary attributes. Spread keys use Python names (on_input, aria_invalid), the same names h props take.
  • <span ...>{name.error()}</span> reads the error in the template, so the message appears and disappears as validation runs.
  • a11y_control_attrs produces reactive aria-invalid and aria-describedby props; error_message_attrs marks the message container as a polite live region.
  • on_submit_validated calls prevent_default(), validates every field in rules (marking them touched), and only invokes save when all pass. Use on_submit when you want to handle validation yourself.
  • A Field is a container of accessors, not an accessor itself, so the condition reads plan.value(). The compiler passes Show a getter for plan.value() == "pro", and Show mounts the note only while it's true.
  • Static attributes such as for="name" and type="email" are written into the compiled template, so they cost nothing per instance.

docs.title: Schema-driven rules
docs.text:
rules_from_schema builds the validators map from a small declarative schema:

from wybthon.forms import rules_from_schema

rules = rules_from_schema(
    {
        "name": {"required": True, "min_length": 2},
        "email": {"required": "Email is required", "email": True},
    }
)

docs.title: Validating on demand
docs.text:
Call validate_form to validate everything and get an (is_valid, errors) tuple, or validate_field for one field:

from wybthon.forms import validate_field, validate_form

ok, errors = validate_form(fields, rules)
validate_field(fields["name"], rules["name"])
