  • Browse the forms API reference.
  • See Events for delegated handler details.

docs.title: Router
docs.text:
Client-side routing with Router, Route, and Link from wybthon.router, including path parameters, query strings, nested routes, and lazy-loaded pages.

from wybthon import Errored, Loading, component, html, lazy, render
from wybthon.router import Link, Outlet, Route, RouteProps, Router, current_path


@component
def Home():
    return html(t"<div><h1>Home</h1><p>Welcome.</p></div>")


@component
def About():
    # Child routes (here, /about/team) render at the Outlet.
    return html(t"<div><h1>About</h1><p>A small routed app.</p>{Outlet()}</div>")


@component
def User(props: RouteProps):
    # Navigating from /users/1 to /users/2 updates ``params`` in place;
    # the component isn't remounted, and only these two text nodes change.
    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <h1>User {props.params["user_id"]}</h1>
        <p>Tab: {props.query.get("tab", "info")}</p>
      </div>
    """)


@component
def NotFound():
    return html(t"<div><h1>Not found</h1><p>No page at {current_path()}</p></div>")


# Loaded on first visit; the import runs inside an async memo.
Team = lazy(lambda: ("app.about.team", "Page"))

routes = [
    Route("/", Home),
    Route("/about", About, children=[Route("team", Team)]),
    Route("/users/:user_id", User),
]


def page_failed(err, reset):
    return html(t"<p>Page failed to load: {err()}</p>")


@component
def App():
    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <nav>
          <ul>
            <li>{Link("Home", href="/", end=True)}</li>
            <li>{Link("About", href="/about")}</li>
            <li>{Link("Team", href="/about/team", on_mouseenter=Team.preload)}</li>
            <li>{Link("User 1", href="/users/1?tab=posts")}</li>
          </ul>
        </nav>
        <main>
          <{Errored} fallback={page_failed} reset_on={current_path}>
            <{Loading} fallback={html(t"<p>Loading page...</p>")}>
              {Router(routes, not_found=NotFound)}
            </{Loading}>
          </{Errored}>
        </main>
      </div>
    """)


render(App(), "#app")

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Router reads current_path and renders the component of the first matching Route. Only a change in which route matches re-mounts the outlet; param and query changes flow into the mounted component as prop updates.
  • The matched component receives params and query as props. Declare them by annotating the component's parameter with RouteProps, or subclass it to add fields of your own. Both are plain props holding dicts: props.params["user_id"] is a tracked read, and in the template the compiler turns each expression into a getter, so each is its own hole. Outside the route component, use_params and use_query return accessors for the same values: params = use_params(), then params()["user_id"].
  • Link renders an <a> that navigates with the History API. It adds active_class (default "active") while its path matches; end=True requires an exact match, which keeps "Home" from being active everywhere. Modifier-key clicks and middle clicks pass through to the browser. Link works as a call in an interpolation or as a <{Link} href="/">...</{Link}> tag.
  • Nested Route.children paths are joined with the parent path, so Route("team", Team) under /about matches /about/team. The parent renders the matched child wherever it places Outlet().
  • Wrapping the router in Loading and Errored with reset_on=current_path gives every page a loading state and an error state that clears on navigation. The error fallback reads the error through the err accessor. An interpolation can span several lines, as the Errored(...) call does here.

docs.title: Programmatic navigation
docs.text:
from wybthon.router import navigate

navigate("/about")
navigate("/users/2?tab=info", replace=True)

Outside a browser (for example in unit tests), navigate only updates the current_path signal; call flush afterward to apply it.

docs.title: Lazy routes
docs.text:
lazy takes a loader that returns a component, a module, a module path string, or a (module_path, attr) tuple. The loader may be async def, so it can await micropip.install(...) first. Call .preload() on user intent (hover, focus) to warm the import before the click:

from wybthon import lazy


async def load_docs():
    import micropip

    await micropip.install("my-docs-package")
    from my_docs import DocsPage

    return DocsPage


Docs = lazy(load_docs)

docs.title: Base paths
docs.text:
Serve the app under a prefix by passing base_path; Link prepends it and the router strips it before matching:

from wybthon.router import Router

Router(routes, base_path="/app")

Inside the tree, use_base_path returns the active base path.

docs.title: Wildcards
docs.text:
A trailing /* matches any remainder:

from wybthon.router import Route

Route("/docs/*", Docs)

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read the Router concept page.
  • See Async and Loading for code-splitting routes.
  • Browse the router API, including resolve for matching paths without a browser.

docs.title: Authoring patterns
docs.text:
This guide shows how to author components in Wybthon's run-once model, with recipes for the situations that come up in every app.

Mental model in one line

Components run once. Inputs are declared on a Props class with plain annotations, and reading props.title returns the value, tracked. Anything that should update over time is an expression in the markup, a memo, or an effect: the compiler turns each dynamic expression in a template ({count() * 2}, {props.title}) into a getter, so only the text node or attribute that reads it updates.

The examples write markup with html templates; see Templates for the syntax. Where markup is built by code, h(tag, props, *children) is the programmatic layer, the counterpart of Solid's h.

docs.title: Run-once bodies
docs.text:
The body of a @component function executes exactly once per mount. Its return value is mounted, and from then on updates flow through the reactive graph, never by calling the body again.

from wybthon import Props, component, create_signal, html


class CounterProps(Props):
    step: int = 1


@component
def Counter(props: CounterProps):
    print("body runs once")
    count, set_count = create_signal(0)

    def increment():
        set_count(lambda n: n + props.step)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <p>Count: {count()}</p>
        <button onclick={increment}>+</button>
      </div>
    """)

Consequences:

  • Local variables are stable. There's no need to memoize callbacks or worry about stale closures.
  • if statements in the body run once. Use Show or Switch for conditions that should track a signal.
  • Reading a signal or a reactive prop at the top level of the body isn't tracked, and dev mode warns about it. When a one-time read is what you want, say so with untrack (untrack(lambda: props.initial)), or .peek() on a signal. Reading inside a handler, like props.step in increment, is fine: handlers run untracked.

docs.title: Declaring props
docs.text:
A component takes no parameters, or one parameter annotated with a subclass of Props. Each annotated field is an input:

from collections.abc import Callable

from wybthon import Props, component, html, prop, untrack


class ToggleProps(Props):
    label: str  # required
    initial: bool = False  # optional
    tags: list[str] = prop(default_factory=list)
    on_toggle: Callable[[bool], None] | None = None  # a callback


@component
def Toggle(props: ToggleProps):
    on = untrack(lambda: props.initial)

    def flip():
        if props.on_toggle is not None:
            props.on_toggle(not on)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <p>{props.label}</p>
        <button onclick={flip}>Toggle</button>
      </div>
    """)


def report(value: bool) -> None:
    print("now", value)


@component
def App():
    return Toggle(label="Dark mode", on_toggle=report)
  • Fields are plain annotations. Reading props.label returns the parent's current value and tracks it, as reading a property of Solid's props object does. In a template, {props.label} is dynamic, so the compiler makes it a getter and the text follows the parent.
  • The parent may pass a value, an accessor, or (in a compiled template) a getter: <{Toggle} label={user().name}>. Getters and accessors are unwrapped on read, so the child sees a str either way.
  • Callable annotations are returned as passed. A field annotated Callable[...] (or Accessor[...], alone or in a union with None) returns exactly what the parent passed, and the read never calls it. Declare callbacks this way.
  • Defaults are ordinary (= False, = None). Use prop(default_factory=...) for mutable values; the factory runs once per instance. Pass the keyword: type checkers only recognize a field specifier's default by keyword.
  • Every component also accepts key=, declared on the Props base.
  • A component with no inputs takes no parameters: def App():.

In dev mode, calling a component with an unknown prop or without a required one raises TypeError at the call site. Pyright and mypy report the same mistakes statically for calls like Toggle(label=...), including calls inside a template's interpolations; see the Typing guide.

A prop that the parent passes as a constant costs nothing to read: a binding that reads nothing reactive allocates no computation. is_static(props, "label") tells a component whether the parent passed a plain value, when a cheaper path is worth taking.

docs.title: Reactive expressions
docs.text:
Any interpolation in a template whose expression contains a call, an attribute access, or a subscript is dynamic: the compiler turns it into a getter. In a child position the getter becomes a hole that runs inside its own render effect and re-renders only its subtree when a dependency changes. A hole may produce a node, a string, a list, None, or an accessor. None, True, and False render nothing, so {ready() and Panel()} works the way {ready() && <Panel />} does in JSX.

from wybthon import component, create_memo, create_signal, html


@component
def Greeting():
    name, set_name = create_signal("Ada")
    letters = create_memo(lambda: len(name()))

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <p>Hello, {name()}</p>
        <p>{name()} has {letters()} letters</p>
        {html(t"<p>That's a long name.</p>") if letters() > 5 else None}
      </div>
    """)

{name()} and {letters()} each update one text node; the text around them is static markup. The conditional mounts or removes a subtree. Names, constants, and lambdas aren't wrapped: an accessor placed directly ({name}) still binds reactively, and anything else that isn't callable is applied once. Conversions and format specs fold into the getter ({price():.2f}).

A function call in a child position is dispatched when the template is created: a component or built-in ({Card(title=user().name)}, {Show(...)}, {For(...)}) is built with a getter for each dynamic argument, and any other call ({badge(user())}, {str(n())}) becomes one reactive hole. See The compiler for the full rule.

Keep holes small. A hole that produces a subtree runs again on every change: if it returns a template from the same literal, Wybthon patches the mounted instance slot by slot, but anything else is rebuilt. A hole around a single text node patches one node. Use hole when you need an explicit key for a hole inside a fragment.

Attributes work the same way. A dynamic expression as an attribute value creates a per-attribute binding, and an attribute that mixes text with interpolations becomes one binding:

from wybthon import create_signal, html

selected, set_selected = create_signal(False)
saving, set_saving = create_signal(False)
user_id, set_user_id = create_signal(1)

html(t"""
  <div class={"active" if selected() else ""} hidden={not selected()}>
    <button disabled={saving()}>Save</button>
    <a href="/users/{user_id()}">Profile</a>
  </div>
""")

class also accepts a list or a dict of {name: bool}, and style accepts a dict. Write a literal dict with spaces inside the braces (class={ {"card": True, "active": active()} }), because {{ in a t-string is an escaped brace, or give it a name.

docs.title: Event handlers
docs.text:
In a template, a handler is an on attribute: onclick, onClick, and on:click all bind a delegated click handler. With h(), use on_* keys ({"on_click": save}). A handler may take the DomEvent or no arguments at all; Wybthon checks the arity once when it registers the handler:

from wybthon import create_signal, html

text, set_text = create_signal("")


def clear():
    set_text("")


def update(e):
    set_text(e.target.value)


html(t"""
  <input value={text()} oninput={update}>
  <button onclick={clear}>Clear</button>
""")

The compiler never wraps handlers or refs, so onclick={props.on_close} passes the callback itself. A named handler reads better than an inline one; when you do write a lambda inline, Python requires parentheses: onclick={(lambda: set_open(False))}.

docs.title: Reading props
Children
docs.text:
Declare children by subclassing ParentProps, which adds children: Any = None. Place props.children in the markup to render it:

from wybthon import ParentProps, component, html


class CardProps(ParentProps):
    title: str = ""


@component
def Card(props: CardProps):
    return html(t'<section class="card"><h3>{props.title}</h3>{props.children}</section>')


html(t"""
  <{Card} title="Composition">
    <p>Body text</p>
    <p>More text</p>
  </{Card}>
""")  # tag form: nested markup is the children
Card(title="Composition")[html(t"<p>Body text</p><p>More text</p>")]  # item syntax
Card(title="Composition", children=html(t"<p>Body text</p>"))  # keyword

The tag form reads like the rest of the markup, but type checkers can't see its props; dev mode checks them at run time. The call forms are fully type-checked, and the keyword form works inside a template too: {Card(title=user().name, children=html(t"<p>Body</p>"))}. Positional children (Card(html(t"<p>Body</p>"), title="Composition")) still work at run time, but type checkers don't validate them, so prefer the keyword or item syntax.

When a component needs to inspect or reorder its children, resolve them with the children helper. It takes a getter, flattens nested lists, calls nested accessors, and drops None and booleans. Calling the result returns the single child or a list; .to_array() always returns a list:

from wybthon import ParentProps, component, html
from wybthon import children as resolve_children


@component
def Bullets(props: ParentProps):
    kids = resolve_children(lambda: props.children)
    return html(t"<ul>{[html(t'<li>{child}</li>') for child in kids.to_array()]}</ul>")

docs.title: Forwarding attributes with merge and omit
docs.text:
There's no **rest: a component reads only the props it declares. To forward attributes to an element, declare them and spread the remainder with omit, which returns a reactive view without the named keys (or without the keys a predicate selects). In a template, a bare {attrs} inside a tag spreads a mapping, binding each key reactively:

from wybthon import ParentProps, component, html, omit


class PanelProps(ParentProps):
    title: str = ""
    id: str | None = None
    hidden: bool = False


@component
def Panel(props: PanelProps):
    attrs = omit(props, "title", "children")
    return html(t"<section {attrs}><h3>{props.title}</h3>{props.children}</section>")

merge combines prop sources (props instances, dicts, or other views) into one reactive view; later sources win:

from collections.abc import Callable

from wybthon import Props, component, html, merge, omit


class ButtonProps(Props):
    label: str
    variant: str = "solid"
    disabled: bool = False
    on_click: Callable[[], None] | None = None


@component
def Button(props: ButtonProps):
    attrs = merge({"type": "button"}, omit(props, "label", "variant"))
    return html(t'<button class="btn btn-{props.variant}" {attrs}>{props.label}</button>')

A view reads like props: attrs.disabled is the tracked value. Spreading binds attributes reactively and passes event handlers and refs through as the callables themselves, so on_click above reaches the button as a click handler. With h(), pass the view as the props: h("section", omit(props, "title", "children"), ...).

docs.title: Keyed remounts
docs.text:
A component stays mounted as long as its hole keeps returning a node with the same tag and key. To force a fresh mount when an identity changes (a different user, a different document), give the node a key:

from wybthon import Props, component, create_signal, html


class DocumentViewProps(Props):
    doc_id: str


@component
def DocumentView(props: DocumentViewProps):
    return html(t"<p>Editing {props.doc_id}</p>")


@component
def Editor():
    doc_id, set_doc_id = create_signal("a")

    def view():
        return DocumentView(doc_id=doc_id(), key=doc_id())

    return html(t"<div>{view()}</div>")

{view()} is a call without arguments, so it's one reactive hole. When doc_id changes, the hole returns a node with a new key: the old instance is disposed (cleanups run) and a new one mounts. Without the key, the hole would patch the mounted DocumentView with the new doc_id, and it would keep its local state. Writing {DocumentView(doc_id=doc_id())} directly in the markup needs no hole at all: the component is built once and reads doc_id through a getter.

The same idea applies to Show(when, children, keyed=True) and Match(when, children, keyed=True), which re-create the branch on every value change and hand the callback the raw value instead of an accessor.

docs.title: dynamic
docs.text:
dynamic turns an accessor for a component (or a tag name) into a component you call like any other. Each instance re-mounts when the resolved component changes; props and children are forwarded.

from wybthon import component, create_signal, dynamic, html


@component
def ListView():
    return html(t"<ul><li>one</li><li>two</li></ul>")


@component
def GridView():
    return html(t'<div class="grid">one two</div>')


VIEWS = {"list": ListView, "grid": GridView}


@component
def Gallery():
    mode, set_mode = create_signal("list")
    View = dynamic(lambda: VIEWS[mode()])
    return html(t"<div>{View()}</div>")


big, set_big = create_signal(True)
dynamic("h2")("Heading text")  # a tag name
dynamic(lambda: "h1" if big() else "h3")(children="Title")

docs.title: Refs
docs.text:
Pass a Ref to an element's ref attribute. After mount, ref.current is an Element with .element for the raw node; it resets to None on unmount. Refs are assigned during mount, so read them in on_settled or an effect.

from wybthon import Props, Ref, component, html, on_settled


class AutoFocusInputProps(Props):
    ref: Ref | None = None


@component
def AutoFocusInput(props: AutoFocusInputProps):
    local = Ref()
    on_settled(lambda: local.current.element.focus())
    # Forward the parent's ref (if any) alongside the local one.
    return html(t'<input type="text" ref={[local, props.ref]}>')

ref also accepts a callback that receives the Element (ref={remember}), and lists mixing refs and callbacks. There's no forward_ref; a ref is an ordinary field.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
• on_settled runs once after the flush that mounted the component. The DOM is live and refs are assigned. Return a callable to register a cleanup.
  • on_cleanup runs when the owning scope is disposed: on unmount for a component body, before each re-run inside an effect, and when a row leaves a For.
  • create_effect runs after the DOM commit; its first run is deferred to the next flush. Prefer the split form create_effect(compute, apply) so incidental reads in the side effect don't over-subscribe.
from wybthon import component, create_effect, create_signal, html, on_cleanup, on_settled


@component
def Ticker():
    seconds, set_seconds = create_signal(0)

    def start():
        from js import clearInterval, setInterval
        from pyodide.ffi import create_proxy

        proxy = create_proxy(lambda: set_seconds(lambda s: s + 1))
        handle = setInterval(proxy, 1000)
        return lambda: (clearInterval(handle), proxy.destroy())

    on_settled(start)
    create_effect(seconds, lambda value, prev: print("tick", prev, "->", value))
    on_cleanup(lambda: print("ticker unmounted"))
    return html(t"<div>Seconds: {seconds()}</div>")

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
A Context is callable: Theme(value, *children) provides, use_context reads. The value is handed to consumers exactly as provided, so pass an accessor when consumers should react to changes.

from wybthon import component, create_context, create_signal, html, use_context

Theme = create_context("light")


@component
def ThemedButton():
    theme = use_context(Theme)
    return html(t'<button class="btn-{theme()}">Hi</button>')


@component
def App():
    theme, set_theme = create_signal("dark")
    return Theme(theme, ThemedButton())

docs.title: Patterns checklist
docs.text:
• Declare inputs on a Props class with plain annotations; annotate callbacks Callable[...]; use prop(default_factory=...) for mutable defaults.
  • Subclass ParentProps for components that render children; pass children with the <{Card}> tag form, item syntax, or the children keyword.
  • Write expressions directly in the markup ({count() * 2}, {props.title}); the compiler keeps them reactive.
  • Seed local state with untrack(lambda: props.x); derive with create_memo.
  • Forward attributes with omit and merge.
  • Give nodes a key when identity should force a remount.
  • Use For for lists with a keyed strategy that matches your data: {For(todos(), todo_row)} in a template, or For(todos, todo_row) in Python code (pass the accessor, not a plain list).
  • Write signals from event handlers, actions, or the apply stage of a split effect, never inside a memo or hole.
  • Use on_settled for DOM-dependent setup and return a cleanup from it.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read Templates, The compiler, Components, and Lifecycle and Ownership.
  • Browse the Authoring patterns example for a complete module.
  • See the reactivity API for merge, omit, children, and friends.

docs.title: Demo apps
docs.text:
Wybthon's demo applications live in standalone repositories under the wybthon GitHub organization. Each is a complete static site: Python in the browser via Pyodide, no JavaScript build step, and each installs Wybthon from PyPI the same way your own app would.

Repository What it shows demo-template A minimal starter: index.html, a Pyodide bootstrap.js, and an app/ package ready to edit. Fork or clone it to begin a new app. reactive-profiler An interactive visualization of run-once components and fine-grained reactive holes, including a live profiler that tallies signal writes and DOM mutations. Live at profiler.wybthon.com. data-lab Explore, analyze, visualize, and export data entirely in the browser. A larger app exercising forms, stores, flow control, and async data. photo-lab Resize, compress, convert, and strip image metadata privately in the browser. Demonstrates file handling and JS interop.

Versions

The demos are separate repositories with their own release cadence, so they may target an earlier Wybthon API than the one these docs describe. A demo that builds markup with element helpers (div(...), p(...)) or declares Prop[T] fields predates Engine v4, which removed both: on the current release, markup is written as html templates and props are plain annotations. Use wyb init for a starter that matches the installed version's API.

docs.title: Running a demo locally
docs.text:
A demo that contains a wybthon.toml is a Wybthon project, so the workflow is the same as for your own app:

git clone https://github.com/wybthon/demo-template.git
cd demo-template
pip install wybthon
wyb dev --open

wyb dev builds the project, serves it, and reloads the page when a source file changes; see the dev server guide. A demo that ships its own index.html and bootstrap.js without a wybthon.toml is a plain static site, so serve it with any static file server (python -m http.server) and follow its README.

docs.title: How a project boots
docs.text:
Wybthon projects follow the same pattern:

  • wybthon.toml names the entry function (entry = "app.main:app"), the mount selector, and the routes to prerender.
  • wyb build runs the app/ package through Wybthon's compiler, packages it with Wybthon into archives, and writes a bootstrap that loads Pyodide and the archives concurrently, then imports the entry.
  • app/main.py returns the root view from its entry function, typically wrapping the tree in Errored and Loading boundaries around a Router from wybthon.router. The bootstrap renders it, or hydrates the prerendered HTML.
  • Folders under app/ mirror routes and components, and route pages are often loaded with lazy so the initial import stays small.

The Pyodide guide covers the runtime details, and the Deployment guide covers the build.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Start from the demo-template for your own app.
  • Explore the Examples for individual feature walkthroughs.
  • See the Dev server guide for the local feedback loop.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
wyb build creates a static application bundle from a project containing wybthon.toml. wyb preview serves the result with client-route fallback and the configured base path.

entry = "app.main:app"
mount = "#app"
app-dir = "app"
base = "/"
pyodide-version = "314.0.6"
packages = []
wheels = []
prerender = ["/"]
crawl = true

[chunks]
charts = ["app/charts/**"]

The entry function returns the root view (it can be async); the bootstrap renders it into mount, or hydrates it when the page was prerendered. Projects require Python 3.14, matching the Pyodide 314 runtime. index.html must contain exactly one <!-- wyb:bootstrap --> marker. Files in public/ are copied beside the output HTML; public/assets/ is reserved for generated content.

wyb build --base /dashboard/
wyb preview --dir dist --port 8000

Deploy the contents of dist/, configure missing extensionless routes to serve 200.html, and serve the app beneath /dashboard/ in this example. Use long-lived immutable caching for hashed assets and revalidate the HTML files and manifest.json. The preview server demonstrates that policy; use your static host for production serving.

docs.title: What the page loads
docs.text:
The build replaces the <!-- wyb:bootstrap --> marker with the tags that start the application, so every page it writes (index.html, 200.html, and each prerendered route) carries them:

  • A <link rel="modulepreload"> for Pyodide's pyodide.mjs, and a <link rel="preload" as="fetch" crossorigin> for the runtime archive and the application archive. The browser starts downloading all three while the page parses, instead of after the bootstrap has run.
  • The manifest, inlined as <script type="application/json" id="wyb-manifest">, so the bootstrap doesn't spend a round trip fetching it. manifest.json is still written at the root of the output, and the bootstrap falls back to fetching it when a page doesn't carry the inline copy.
  • The bootstrap module itself.

docs.title: Production mode
docs.text: wyb build writes a production build: the bootstrap calls set_dev_mode(False) before the application imports, so production apps skip the development checks (such as unknown-prop validation and write-in-scope errors) and print no development warnings. The manifest's dev field records the mode. wyb dev builds the same project with dev mode on. From Python, build_app builds for production by default; pass dev=True for a development build. Read the current mode with is_dev_mode().

docs.title: Reproducible output
docs.text: Builds sort files and normalize archive timestamps, so identical inputs produce identical assets. A complete build is prepared before the destination is replaced. Existing nonempty output must contain the .wyb-build marker; source directories can't be used as output. Build validation failure leaves the previous output available.

docs.title: Prerendering
docs.text:
prerender lists routes to render to HTML at build time, and crawl = true adds every in-app link those pages contain. Each route is written to <route>/index.html with the markup placed between the <!-- wyb:app --> and <!-- /wyb:app --> markers in index.html. The browser shows the page immediately and hydrates it once Pyodide is ready. Prerendering imports the application in a separate CPython process, after Wybthon, so the import hook compiles its templates; browser-only imports must be guarded there, and the build reports the failing import otherwise. wyb dev prerenders the same routes on every rebuild.

The client-only shell is also written to 200.html. Serve it for routes that weren't prerendered.

docs.title: Compiled templates
docs.text: wyb build runs every application module through Wybthon's compiler before packaging it. A malformed template fails the build with its file and line. Each html(t"...") call gets its dynamic expressions wrapped in getters and its parse tree and mount function emitted as ordinary module code, so a production page never parses a template or generates code at run time.

docs.title: Bytecode
docs.text: When the interpreter running the build has the same Python version as the pinned Pyodide runtime (Python 3.14 for Pyodide 314), the archives include precompiled bytecode, so the browser doesn't compile Wybthon or the application at startup. Application bytecode is the compiler's output, and the import hook that import wybthon installs uses it as is. The manifest's bytecode field records whether it was included. Set bytecode = false to ship source only; the import hook then compiles each application module's templates in the browser as it's imported.

docs.title: Runtime and dependencies
docs.text:
The bootstrap loads Pyodide and the runtime/application archives concurrently (the preload hints have usually started all three already), then unpacks and imports Python. It doesn't fetch every Python module separately. packages names packages in the pinned Pyodide distribution. wheels accepts exact name==version requirements or explicit wheel URLs compatible with the selected runtime. Set pyodide-url to host that runtime yourself.

Pin dependencies and keep the runtime version deliberate. Browser Python code is public, including bundled configuration. Keep application secrets on a server.

docs.title: Explicit lazy chunks
docs.text:
from wybthon import lazy

Chart = lazy(lambda: ("app.charts.main", "Chart"), chunk="charts")

The matching files are excluded from the main archive. Rendering Chart inside Loading fetches its archive once before importing the module. Hover preloading through a Link from wybthon.router can warm a lazy route, and Chart.preload() warms it on any user intent. load_chunk("charts") from wybthon.assets is available for explicit preloading.

Chunk groups mustn't overlap, and the entry module must stay in the main bundle. This is explicit packaging, not automatic dependency analysis: keep shared imports in the main application, and don't eagerly import a chunk module. Concurrent chunk requests share one fetch; a failed fetch is evicted so a later attempt can retry. Call Chart.retry() to restart a failed lazy load and let its error boundary recover.

docs.title: Startup measurements
docs.text:
window.__WYB exposes startup status, errors, the runtime, and timings for runtime loading, archive loading, unpacking, application startup, readiness, and the next frame opportunity. Concurrent phases overlap; don't add them as if they were sequential. These values include network/cache conditions and differ from warmed update benchmarks.

The production browser test builds a starter, boots a deep link beneath a base path, clicks a real counter, and verifies that its lazy chunk isn't fetched until requested.

docs.title: Dev server
docs.text:
wyb dev builds a Wybthon project in development mode, serves the build, rebuilds when a source file changes, and reloads connected pages over Server-Sent Events (SSE). It serves projects only: a directory with a wybthon.toml (create one with wyb init).

pip install wybthon
wyb init my-app
cd my-app
wyb dev --open

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
• Builds the project with dev mode on, including any routes listed in prerender, so you develop against the same server-rendered pages you'll deploy. Production builds (wyb build) turn dev mode off; see Deployment.
  • Runs application modules through Wybthon's compiler, as wyb build does, so a malformed template fails the rebuild with its file and line instead of failing in the browser.
  • Serves the build under the configured base path with client-route fallback to 200.html. Requests outside the base path return 404.
  • Watches the application directory (app-dir), public/, index.html, and wybthon.toml. A change, including a new or deleted file, triggers a rebuild and then a reload. Change detection polls modification times about every 0.5 seconds.
  • Reports a failed build in the terminal and keeps serving the previous output, so a typo doesn't take the page down.
  • Binds to the requested port or the next available one, up to 20 ports higher, and prints the project, the watched paths, and the URL it serves.
  • Sends Cache-Control: no-store on every response, so the browser never reuses a stale build.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• --dir: the project directory (default .).
  • --host (default 127.0.0.1) and --port (default 8000).
  • --open: open the default browser to the app after the server starts.
  • --open-path: open this path instead of the app's base path, for example /about.

To expose the server on your LAN or from a container, use --host 0.0.0.0 and open the page via your machine's IP.

docs.title: How reloads work
docs.text: Each page the dev build writes includes a small script that subscribes to GET /__sse and reloads on a reload event. After a successful rebuild, the server sends that event to every connected page. A full page reload means Pyodide boots again, so expect a short delay between saving a file and seeing the change.

docs.title: Embedding the server
docs.text:
serve is the function behind wyb dev:

from wybthon.dev import serve

serve("my-app", host="127.0.0.1", port=8000, open_browser=True, open_path=None)

It raises ValueError when the directory has no wybthon.toml.

docs.title: Not for production
docs.text: The dev server is built on Python's http.server and is intended for development only. Use wyb build and a static host for production, and wyb preview to check a production build locally. See the Deployment guide.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• "has no wybthon.toml." The dev server only serves projects. Run it from the project directory, pass --dir path/to/project, or create a project with wyb init. To try a single script with its templates compiled, use wyb run script.py instead.
  • Auto-reload isn't firing. Confirm GET /__sse shows an open EventSource connection in the browser's Network panel, and check the terminal for a build error. Only the application directory, public/, index.html, and wybthon.toml are watched. Behind a proxy, pass /__sse through unbuffered (Nginx: proxy_buffering off; and X-Accel-Buffering: no).
  • A page shows 404. Requests must fall under the configured base path. Open the URL the server prints.
  • Port is already in use. The server picks the next free port and prints a notice. If you need the exact port, stop the conflicting process (macOS: lsof -i :8000, then kill <PID>).
  • The browser didn't open. --open relies on the system default browser; some headless or remote setups block it. Copy the printed URL instead.
  • Exposing on the network. Use --host 0.0.0.0 and allow inbound traffic to the selected port through your firewall.

See also the general troubleshooting page.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• See the dev API reference for the underlying server.
  • Read the Deployment guide for production builds and hosting.
  • Browse Examples for components to try in a starter project.

docs.title: Migrating from React
docs.text:
Wybthon will feel familiar to React developers, but the underlying model is intentionally different. The key shift: components run once, not on every render, and updates flow through signals into small reactive expressions in the tree.

This guide maps common React idioms to Wybthon equivalents and calls out the pitfalls people hit most often.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text: React Wybthon const [count, setCount] = useState(0) count, set_count = create_signal(0) useEffect(fn, deps) create_effect(compute, apply); dependencies are whatever compute reads useMemo(() => fn, deps) create_memo(fn) useContext(Ctx) / <Ctx.Provider value> use_context(Ctx) / Ctx(value, *children) useRef() Ref() ref={el => ...} A callback ref: ref={remember}, where remember(el) receives the element useId() create_unique_id() <Suspense fallback={...}> Loading(children, fallback=...) useTransition / useOptimistic action / create_optimistic <ErrorBoundary> Errored(children, fallback=...) lazy(() => import('./X')) lazy(loader) createPortal(children, node) Portal(children, mount=...) useReducer create_signal plus plain functions, or a create_store with draft mutations {cond && <A/>} / ternaries {Show(cond(), A(), fallback=B())} with Show, or Switch / Match items.map(item => <Row key={item.id}/>) {For(items(), row, keyed=...)} with For function Card({ title }: CardProps) A Props class and def Card(props: CardProps) props.children ParentProps and props.children JSX An html template: html(t'<div class="card"><p>{message}</p></div>') {expression} in JSX {expression} in the template; the compiler keeps calls, attribute reads, and subscripts live, as Solid's does className, htmlFor, onClick class, for, onclick (onClick works too) <Card title="Hi">...</Card> <{Card} title="Hi">...</{Card}>, or {Card(title="Hi")[...]} for full type checking <input {...attrs} /> <input {attrs}> {`Count: ${count}`} Count: {count()} inside the template

docs.title: Components run once
docs.text:
The single biggest change. In React, your component function runs on every render, and useState and useEffect work because of hook rules. In Wybthon:

from wybthon import component, create_signal, html


@component
def Counter():
    count, set_count = create_signal(0)
    print("Counter body running")

    def increment():
        set_count(lambda n: n + 1)

    return html(t"<button onclick={increment}>count: {count()}</button>")

You'll see "Counter body running" exactly once, no matter how many clicks. {count()} in the template becomes a reactive hole, so only that text node updates. Handlers may take the event or, as here, no arguments. Read Mental model for the formal definition.

docs.title: JSX becomes templates
docs.text:
Markup is an HTML template written as a Python 3.14 template string: html(t"..."). It's the counterpart of JSX, and Wybthon's compiler plays the role of the JSX transform: it turns every dynamic expression in the markup into a getter, and turns each literal into a native template ahead of time. Each instance is a clone of that template, so a template costs about what the markup inside it costs. You don't run the compiler yourself: it runs in wyb dev and wyb build, in an import hook that import wybthon installs, and under pytest. See Templates for the full syntax.

  • Attribute names are HTML names: class, for, aria-label, tabindex. Handlers are onclick={save}; onClick and on:click work too.
  • {expression} works in a child, an attribute, part of an attribute (class="btn btn-{kind()}"), an event, a ref, and a spread (<input {attrs}>).
  • Write expressions as you would in JSX: {count() * 2}, {user().name}, class={"on" if active() else ""}. An expression with a call, an attribute access, or a subscript stays live; a name or a constant is a value. Event handlers are never wrapped.
  • Use a component with a tag, <{Card} title={user().name}>...</{Card}>, or call it in an interpolation, {Card(title=user().name)}. Either way the component receives a getter for each dynamic prop. The call form is fully type-checked; the tag form's props are checked at run time in dev mode.
  • Markup the browser would silently fix is an error instead: put <tr> inside a <tbody>, and don't nest a <div> in a <p>.

If you need to build markup in code, h(tag, props, *children) is the programmatic layer, like React.createElement.

docs.title: Implications
docs.text:
• No dependency arrays. Effects subscribe to whatever signals they read while running.
  • No useCallback, useMemo, or React.memo for stability; closures aren't re-created because the body doesn't re-run.
  • No stale-closure bugs from missing deps.
  • if/else in the body runs once. Use Show or Switch for conditions that should follow state.

docs.title: State and effects
docs.text:
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
useEffect(() => {
  document.title = `count ${count}`;
}, [count]);

becomes

from js import document

from wybthon import create_effect, create_signal

count, set_count = create_signal(0)


def set_title(value: int, prev: int | None) -> None:
    document.title = f"count {value}"


create_effect(count, set_title)

The split form create_effect(compute, apply) is the closest analogue to useEffect's deps-then-body structure: compute runs tracked and declares the dependencies (here the count accessor itself), and apply runs untracked with the value. apply may return a cleanup, like useEffect's return value. Effects run after the DOM commit, and the first run happens after the component mounted.

Signal writes are staged: after set_count(1), count() still returns the old value until the graph flushes at the end of the event handler. That's why the counter above uses set_count(lambda n: n + 1), the equivalent of React's setCount(n => n + 1), and it composes the same way.

docs.title: Props
docs.text:
In React, props are a frozen object per render, typed with an interface. In Wybthon, props are declared on a Props class with plain annotations, and the component takes one parameter annotated with it. Reading props.name returns the parent's current value and tracks it, as in Solid: place it in the markup, or read it inside a memo or effect.

type GreetProps = { name: string; excited?: boolean; onWave?: () => void };

function Greet({ name, excited = false, onWave }: GreetProps) {
  return <p onClick={onWave}>Hello, {name}{excited ? "!" : "."}</p>;
}

becomes

from collections.abc import Callable

from wybthon import Props, component, html


class GreetProps(Props):
    name: str
    excited: bool = False
    on_wave: Callable[[], None] | None = None


@component
def Greet(props: GreetProps):
    return html(t"<p onclick={props.on_wave}>Hello, {props.name}{'!' if props.excited else '.'}</p>")
  • Every field is reactive. When the parent writes <{Greet} name={user().name}>, the child gets a getter and {props.name} follows it, without re-running the body.
  • A field annotated Callable[...] is returned exactly as the parent passed it, so on_wave is the function itself.
  • Defaults are ordinary = value defaults; use prop(default_factory=list) for mutable ones.
  • Pyright and mypy check every call against the class, the way TypeScript checks JSX props.

Destructuring a prop into a local (name = props.name) at the top of the body freezes it at mount and loses reactivity; dev mode warns about it when the parent passed something reactive. When you really want a one-time read (to seed local state, for example), write untrack(lambda: props.name).

There's no {...rest} catch-all: a component reads only what it declares. To forward attributes, declare them and spread the remainder with omit (attrs = omit(props, "title"), then <div {attrs}>); merge covers {...defaults, ...props}.

docs.title: Children
docs.text:
Subclass ParentProps to accept children, and place props.children in the markup. Callers pass children as nested markup in the tag form, with item syntax, or with the children keyword:

from wybthon import ParentProps, component, html


class CardProps(ParentProps):
    title: str = ""


@component
def Card(props: CardProps):
    return html(t'<section class="card"><h3>{props.title}</h3>{props.children}</section>')


html(t'<{Card} title="Hello"><p>Body text</p></{Card}>')
Card(title="Hello")[html(t"<p>Body text</p>")]
Card(title="Hello", children=html(t"<p>Body text</p>"))

To inspect or reorder children, resolve them with children: kids = children(lambda: props.children), then kids.to_array().

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
const ThemeCtx = createContext("light");
<ThemeCtx.Provider value={theme}><App/></ThemeCtx.Provider>
const theme = useContext(ThemeCtx);

becomes

from wybthon import component, create_context, create_signal, html, use_context

Theme = create_context("light")


@component
def Consumer():
    theme = use_context(Theme)  # the accessor, exactly as provided
    return html(t"<p>Theme: {theme()}</p>")


@component
def Root():
    theme, set_theme = create_signal("dark")
    return Theme(theme, Consumer())  # the Context object is its own provider

Pass an accessor as the value and consumers update without unmounting.

docs.title: Lists
docs.text:
{items.map(item => <Row key={item.id} item={item} />)}

becomes

from wybthon import For, html


def row(item, index):
    return Row(item=item)


html(t"<ul>{For(items(), row, keyed=lambda i: i['id'])}</ul>")

With a key function, item is an accessor. Row declares an ordinary field (item: dict[str, Any]), which unwraps the accessor on read, so the row stays live as its data changes.

For runs the callback once per row and caches the result; reorders move DOM nodes instead of re-rendering. With a key function, the callback receives accessors for the item and the index; with the default keyed=True, rows match by identity and the callback gets the raw item and an index accessor. In a template, {For(items(), row)} hands For a getter for the list. In Python code, pass the accessor itself (For(items, row)), not a plain Python list.

docs.title: Conditional rendering
docs.text:
{isLoaded ? <Profile/> : <Spinner/>}

becomes

from wybthon import Show, html

html(t"<main>{Show(is_loaded(), Profile(), fallback=Spinner())}</main>")

Show tracks only the truthiness of when, so the branch re-renders when the condition flips, not on every value change. For several branches, use Switch(Match(cond, children), ..., fallback=...). The built-ins work as calls in an interpolation ({Show(ready(), panel)}) or with the tag form (<{Show} when={ready()}>...</{Show}>).

docs.title: Refs and DOM access
docs.text:
const ref = useRef(null);
useEffect(() => { ref.current.focus(); }, []);
return <input ref={ref} />;

becomes

from wybthon import Ref, component, html, on_settled


@component
def AutoFocus():
    ref = Ref()
    on_settled(lambda: ref.current.element.focus())
    return html(t"<input ref={ref}>")

on_settled is the "after mount" hook: it runs once after the flush that mounted the component, and it may return a cleanup. ref.current is an Element; .element is the raw DOM node. A callback ref (ref={remember}) receives the Element instead, like React's ref={el => ...}. To forward a ref, declare it as a field (ref: Ref | None = None) and pass it down (<input ref={props.ref}>); there's no forwardRef.

docs.title: Async data
docs.text:
React with Suspense is similar in spirit, but Wybthon is more direct: any create_memo with an async def body is an async computation, and Loading shows a fallback until it produces its first value:

from js import fetch

from wybthon import Loading, component, create_memo, html


@component
def Title():
    async def fetch_data():
        resp = await fetch("/api/data")
        return (await resp.json()).to_py()

    data = create_memo(fetch_data)

    return Loading(html(t"<span>{data()['title']}</span>"), fallback=html(t"<p>Loading</p>"))

Later recomputes run as transitions, holding the dependent UI on the previous state until the new value lands, so the boundary doesn't flash and nothing tears; is_pending tells you when that's happening. For mutations, action and create_optimistic cover what useTransition and useOptimistic do in React:

from wybthon import action, create_optimistic, refresh

shown, set_shown = create_optimistic(likes)


@action
async def like():
    set_shown(lambda n: n + 1)  # instant UI
    await api_like()
    await refresh(likes)  # reverts to real data when the action settles

See Async and Loading.

docs.title: Error boundaries
docs.text:
from wybthon import Errored, html
from wybthon.router import current_path


def failed(err, reset):
    return html(t"<div><p>{str(err())}</p><button onclick={reset}>Retry</button></div>")


Errored(Dashboard(), fallback=failed, reset_on=current_path)

The fallback receives err, an accessor for the caught error, and reset, which re-renders the children. reset_on clears the error when the given accessor changes, here on every navigation.

docs.title: Things you can stop doing
docs.text:
• useCallback and useMemo for identity stability. Closures aren't re-created.
  • React.memo. Components don't re-render.
  • Hook rules and exhaustive-deps lints. Creating state or an effect is just a function call, anywhere in the body.
  • batch-style wrappers. Every write batches until the next flush.
  • key by index. For keys rows for you; pick the strategy that fits.

docs.title: Things to watch out for
docs.text:
• Don't read props or signals at the top level of the body. props.name there freezes the value (and warns). Read it in the markup, or inside a memo or effect.
  • Don't expect a write to be visible immediately. set_x(1); x() returns the old value until the flush. Use functional updates to compose writes.
  • Don't write signals inside a memo or a hole. Dev mode raises WriteInScopeError. Write from event handlers, actions, or the apply stage of an effect.
  • Annotate callbacks as callables. A callback field (on_save: Callable[[], None] | None = None) returns the function the parent passed; any other field unwraps an accessor or getter to its value.
  • Parenthesize inline handlers. Python doesn't allow a bare lambda in a t-string interpolation, so onclick={lambda: save()} is a SyntaxError; write onclick={(lambda: save())}, or name the handler.
  • Keep templates in compiled modules. A template in a module imported after wybthon is compiled automatically. A script you run directly with python isn't, and dev mode raises TemplateError when one of its dynamic expressions was evaluated only once; run it with wyb run script.py.
  • Define components at module scope. Creating one inside a body doesn't cause re-renders, but it does create a new component identity on every hole re-run, which forces a remount.

docs.title: Cheat sheet
docs.text:
from wybthon import (
    Errored,
    For,
    Loading,
    Match,
    ParentProps,
    Portal,
    Props,
    Ref,
    Repeat,
    Show,

    action,
    children,
    component,
    create_context,
    create_effect,
    create_memo,
    create_optimistic,
    create_signal,
    create_store,
    html,
    lazy,
    merge,
    omit,
    on_cleanup,
    on_settled,
    prop,
    untrack,
    use_context,
)
from wybthon.router import Link, Route, Router, navigate
from wybthon.testing import fire, render

docs.title: Migrating from Solid
docs.text:
Wybthon is SolidJS for Python, and it tracks SolidJS 2.0 semantics: async-first reactivity, automatic batching, actions and optimistic state, draft-first stores, and the For plus Repeat flow components. Nearly every primitive has a direct equivalent, and the mental model is identical: components run once, signals drive fine-grained updates, the ownership tree manages cleanup, and a compiler turns the dynamic expressions in your markup into getters.

Solid 2.0 hasn't had a stable release yet. Release candidate 17 (RC.17) is the latest, and it's the version Wybthon targets.

The differences are mostly surface: Python instead of JavaScript, t-string templates instead of JSX, a Props class instead of a props interface, snake_case names, and a small number of deliberate semantic choices listed at the end.

docs.title: API mapping
docs.text:
The table follows Solid 2.0 RC.17.
