NotReadyError NotReadyError createStore(initial) (draft setter) create_store(initial) reconcile(value, key) reconcile(value, key="id"); key may be a string, a function, or None createProjection(fn, initial) create_projection(fn, initial) createSelector(source) (removed in 2.0) A projection: create_projection(lambda: {} if sel() is None else {sel(): True}), then is_selected.get(key) unwrap(store) snapshot(store) mapArray(list, fn, { fallback }) map_array(list, fn, fallback=...) indexArray(list, fn) map_array(list, fn, keyed=False) repeat(count, fn, { from, fallback }) repeat(count, fn, start=..., fallback=...) <Loading fallback> (was Suspense) Loading(children, fallback=...) <Reveal order collapsed> (was SuspenseList) Reveal(children, order=..., collapsed=...) <Errored fallback={(err, reset) => ...}> Errored(children, fallback=lambda err, reset: ...); err is an accessor, so call err() <Show when fallback> {Show(when, children, fallback=...)} <For each> {For(each, children)} (keyed by identity) <For each keyed={fn}> {For(each, children, keyed=lambda item: ...)} <For each keyed={false}> (was Index) {For(each, children, keyed=False)} <Repeat count> {Repeat(count, children)} <Switch> / <Match when> {Switch(...)} / Match(when, children) dynamic(source) dynamic(source), called like a component <Portal mount> Portal(children, mount=...) lazy(() => import(...)) lazy(loader) lazyModule(() => import(...)) lazy_module(loader): a cached async import with preload() and peek() createContext(default) create_context(default) <Ctx value> Ctx(value, *children): the context object is the provider useContext(Ctx) use_context(Ctx) interface CardProps / props: CardProps A Props subclass: class CardProps(Props) and def Card(props: CardProps) props.title (getter) props.title: returns the value, tracked isStatic(props, key) is_static(props, "key") ParentProps<T> ParentProps merge(a, b) merge(a, b) omit(props, ...keys) omit(props, *keys) omit(props, predicate) omit(props, lambda key: ...) children(() => props.children) children(lambda: props.children) children(...).toArray() children(lambda: props.children).to_array() flatten(children) flatten(children): the unmemoized form of children createUniqueId() create_unique_id() renderToString(fn) render_to_string(view) renderToStream(fn) render_to_stream(view): iterate it for chunks await renderToStream(fn) (replaces renderToStringAsync) await render_to_stream(view) returns the complete HTML hydrate(fn, el) hydrate(view, container) isServer is_server() isHydrating() is_hydrating() onHydrationEnd(fn) on_hydration_end(fn) <NoHydration> NoHydration(*children) <Hydration> Hydration(*children) (a passthrough; a NoHydration region stays static as a whole) getRequestEvent() get_request_event() httpStatus(code) http_status(code) httpHeader(name, value) http_header(name, value) clientOnly(() => import(...)) client_only(children, fallback=...) createMemo(fn, { ssrSource }) create_memo(fn, ssr_source="server" \| "hybrid" \| "client") ref={el => ...} A callback ref: ref={remember} (or ref={(lambda el: ...)}), which receives an Element let el; <input ref={el} /> ref = Ref() and ref={ref}; read ref.current.element in on_settled JSX, or html from solid-js/html html(t"...") templates, compiled like JSX (below) {expr} {expr}: the compiler makes it a getter when it contains a call, attribute access, or subscript <Card title={user().name}>...</Card> <{Card} title={user().name}>...</{Card}>, or {Card(title=user().name, children=...)} <div {...attrs}> <div {attrs}> h(tag, props, ...children) h(tag, props, *children)

Solid 1.x primitives that 2.0 removed (createResource, on, createComputed, createSelector, produce, createMutable, splitProps, mergeProps, Index, path-based store writes, useTransition, renderToStringAsync) don't exist here either. The table above covers their 2.0 replacements. Solid 2.0's createDeferred isn't 1.x's idle-time deferral: it's the async memo in the table, and that's what create_deferred mirrors.

createAsync was never part of Solid 2.0's core API: it came from @solidjs/router 0.x and was removed in router 2.0. In Solid 2.0 you read async data with createMemo, and that's what create_memo with an async def mirrors.

docs.title: JSX becomes templates
docs.text:
function Greeting(props) {
  return <p class="greeting">Hello, {props.name}{props.excited ? "!" : "."}</p>;
}

from wybthon import Props, component, html


class GreetingProps(Props):
    name: str
    excited: bool = False


@component
def Greeting(props: GreetingProps):
    return html(t'<p class="greeting">Hello, {props.name}{"!" if props.excited else "."}</p>')
  • html takes a Python 3.14 template string, and Wybthon's compiler does the two jobs Solid's JSX compiler does. It turns each literal's static markup into a native <template> that the kernel clones for every instance, and it turns every dynamic expression into a getter. It runs when wyb build and wyb dev build your app, in an import hook that import wybthon installs, under pytest, and for scripts run with wyb run script.py. See Templates.
  • The rule is Solid's: an interpolation that contains a call, an attribute access, or a subscript is dynamic, so {props.name}, {count() * 2}, {row["label"]}, and class={"on" if active() else ""} become getters, and each updates only its own text node or attribute. A name, a constant, or a lambda is a value. A signal placed directly ({count}) is still bound reactively, so {count} and {count()} both work.
  • Event handlers, refs, spreads, and nested html(t"...") templates are never wrapped. Prefer a named handler (onclick={increment}); Python forbids a bare lambda in an interpolation, so an inline one needs parentheses: onclick={(lambda: set_open(False))}.
  • A call in a child position is decided when the template is created. A component ({Card(title=user().name)}, {Show(...)}, {For(...)}) is built with a getter for each dynamic argument, exactly like <Card title={user().name} />. Any other call ({badge(user())}, {str(total())}) becomes one reactive hole, as a function call in JSX does.
  • Attributes are HTML names (class, for, aria-label) and take interpolations the same way: class={row_class(id)}, href="/users/{user_id()}" (one binding for the whole value), disabled={add.pending()}.
  • Event handlers are onclick={handler}; onClick and on:click work too. A handler may take no arguments or receive a DomEvent with e.target, e.key, e.prevent_default(), and friends.
  • A component tag is written <{Card} title={user().name}>...</{Card}> (like <${Card}> in Solid's html), or self-closed as <{Card} />. Attributes become keyword props and the content becomes children. Type checkers can't see a tag's attributes, so dev mode checks its props at run time; the call form ({Card(title=user().name)}) is checked statically, and the compiler still passes getters.
  • Show, Loading, Errored, Link, and context providers work as calls in an interpolation ({Show(ready(), panel)}) or with the tag form (<{Show} when={ready()}>...</{Show}>), which calls each the way its signature takes children.
  • Markup the browser's parser would rewrite is an error instead of a silent change: put <tr> in a <tbody>, and don't nest a <div> in a <p>. The compiler reports it as a SyntaxError with the file and line.
  • A template that reaches html() without being compiled (a REPL, exec) has already evaluated its dynamic expressions once, so dev mode raises TemplateError instead of rendering markup that would never update.
  • h(tag, props, *children) is the programmatic layer, the counterpart of Solid's h, for markup built by code. Its props take Python names (class_, html_for, on_click) or HTML names. SVG works in a template.

docs.title: Components and props
docs.text:
Solid types props with an interface (props: CardProps); Wybthon declares them on a Props class with plain annotations, and the component takes one parameter annotated with it. Pyright and mypy check every call against the class with no plugin.

interface CardProps extends ParentProps {
  title: string;
  body?: string;
  onClose?: () => void;
}

function Card(props: CardProps) {
  return (
    <div class="card">
      <h2>{props.title}</h2>
      <p>{props.body ?? ""}</p>
      {props.children}
      <button onClick={() => props.onClose?.()}>Close</button>
    </div>
  );
}

<Card title={user().name} onClose={() => setOpen(false)}><p>Body</p></Card>

from collections.abc import Callable

from wybthon import ParentProps, component, create_signal, html


class CardProps(ParentProps):
    title: str
    body: str = ""
    on_close: Callable[[], None] | None = None


@component
def Card(props: CardProps):
    def close():
        if props.on_close is not None:
            props.on_close()

    return html(t"""
      <div class="card">
        <h2>{props.title}</h2>
        <p>{props.body}</p>
        {props.children}
        <button onclick={close}>Close</button>
      </div>
    """)


@component
def App():
    user, set_user = create_signal({"name": "Ada"})
    open_, set_open = create_signal(True)

    def close():
        set_open(False)

    return html(t"<{Card} title={user()['name']} on_close={close}><p>Body</p></{Card}>")
  • Props work as they do in Solid: reading props.title returns the value and tracks it, like reading a getter on Solid's props object. In markup, {props.title} is dynamic, so the compiler makes it a getter and the text updates when the parent's value changes. {props.body or "No details."} is one expression and one binding.
  • The parent may pass a value, a compiler getter (what title={user()["name"]} becomes), or an accessor such as a signal. Getters and accessors are unwrapped when the prop is read, unless the field is annotated as callable (Callable[...] or Accessor[...], alone or in a union with None): then the value is returned exactly as passed, which is how callbacks work.
  • Passing a prop through stays reactive: <{Child} title={props.title}> hands the child a getter, as in Solid.
  • Optional props take ordinary defaults (body: str = ""). Use prop(default_factory=list) for a mutable default.
  • Assigning title = props.title at the top of the body reads once and freezes, as destructuring does in Solid; dev mode warns when the value is reactive. Use untrack(lambda: props.title) when a one-time read is what you mean.
  • is_static(props, "title") says whether the parent passed a plain value, as Solid 2.0's isStatic does.
  • merge and omit match Solid 2.0's helpers. Their views read like props (view.title is the tracked value), and you can spread them onto elements: attrs = omit(props, "title", "children"), then <div {attrs}>. There's no **rest; a component reads only what it declares.
  • Children arrive as the children prop. Pass them as nested markup in the tag form, with the children= keyword, or with item syntax in Python code (Card(title="Hi")[...]). Inside a template, {Card(...)[...]} is a subscript rather than a call, so it becomes one reactive hole instead of a component built with getters.
  • Every component accepts key=. A component with no props takes no parameters.

docs.title: Signals and effects
docs.text:
from wybthon import create_effect, create_signal, flush

count, set_count = create_signal(0)


def log(value: int, prev: int | None) -> None:
    print("count =", value)


create_effect(count, log)
set_count(1)
flush()

The split form is Solid 2.0's createEffect(compute, apply): compute runs tracked, apply runs untracked with the value and previous value, and may return a cleanup. Effects run after the DOM commit; the first run happens on the flush after the component mounted. The single-function form create_tracked_effect(fn) also works.

Signal semantics that carry over:

  • Automatic batching. All writes in one turn coalesce into one flush; there's no batch().
  • Glitch-free propagation. An effect that reads several memos derived from the same signal runs once per flush and never sees an inconsistent pair.
  • Lazy memos with equality short-circuit. create_memo recomputes when read after a source changed and doesn't notify if the value is equal under equals.
  • Async-first. An async def passed to create_memo is an async computation. Reading it before the first value raises NotReadyError (which Loading catches); later recomputes run as transitions that hold the dependent UI on the previous state until the new value lands.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
from wybthon import For, Match, Show, Switch, create_signal, create_store, html

user, set_user = create_signal(None)
status, set_status = create_signal("loading")
store, set_store = create_store({"todos": [{"id": 1, "title": "Write docs"}]})


def greeting(u):
    return html(t"<p>Hello, {u()['name']}</p>")


def todo_row(todo, i):
    return html(t"<li>{todo()['title']}</li>")


loading = html(t"<p>Loading...</p>")
ready = html(t"<p>Ready</p>")
unknown = html(t"<p>Unknown</p>")

html(t"""
  <main>
    {Show(user, greeting, fallback=html(t"<p>Sign in</p>"))}
    <ul>{For(store.todos, todo_row, keyed=lambda t: t["id"])}</ul>
    {Switch(Match(status() == "loading", loading), Match(status() == "ready", ready), fallback=unknown)}
  </main>
""")

These are calls in a child position, so the compiler builds them like JSX components: status() == "loading" and store.todos arrive as getters, and Match inside Switch is prepared the same way. Show passes the truthy value to a one-argument callback as an accessor, like Solid's <Show> with a function child; with keyed=True it passes the value itself. For mirrors Solid's unified For: with keyed=True (the default) rows match by identity and the callback receives (item, index_accessor); with keyed=False it receives (item_accessor, index); with a key function it receives (item_accessor, index_accessor). Type checkers infer these from the call (see Typing). In a template, {For(todos(), row)} passes a getter; in Python code, pass the accessor (For(todos, row)) or a store list, because a plain list renders once. Repeat(count, lambda i: ...) matches Solid 2.0's Repeat.

These are native regions, not wrapper components: Show and Switch are one branch computation each, and when a hole re-renders a tree containing one, the new condition or source is pushed into the mounted region instead of remounting it.

docs.title: Boundaries
docs.text:
from wybthon import Errored, Loading, html
from wybthon.router import current_path


def failed(err, reset):
    return html(t"<div><p>{str(err())}</p><button onclick={reset}>Retry</button></div>")


Errored(
    Loading(Dashboard(), fallback=html(t"<p>Loading...</p>")),
    fallback=failed,
    reset_on=current_path,
)

Loading and Errored match their Solid 2.0 namesakes. The error fallback receives (err, reset), where err is an accessor for the caught error, as in Solid 2.0; reset_on re-mounts when the given accessor changes. Reveal coordinates multiple boundaries like SuspenseList.

docs.title: Stores
docs.text:
from wybthon import create_store, reconcile, snapshot

state, set_state = create_store({"count": 0, "items": []})


def update(s):
    s.count += 1
    s["items"].append({"id": 3, "title": "new"})


set_state(update)
set_state(reconcile({"count": 5, "items": fetched_items}, key="id"))
raw = snapshot(state["items"])

Setters are draft-first, as in Solid 2.0. Reads are tracked at the leaf, only leaves that changed notify, and reconcile preserves identity by key so For rows keep their DOM. create_projection and create_optimistic_store match their Solid 2.0 namesakes.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
from wybthon import component, create_context, create_signal, html, use_context

Theme = create_context("light")


@component
def Root():
    theme, set_theme = create_signal("dark")
    return Theme(theme, Page())


@component
def Page():
    theme = use_context(Theme)
    return html(t"<p>Theme: {theme()}</p>")

There's no .Provider: calling the Context object with a value and children returns the provider node. use_context returns the value exactly as provided, so an accessor stays an accessor.

docs.title: Async, actions, and optimistic state
docs.text:
from js import fetch

from wybthon import Loading, action, create_memo, create_optimistic, html, is_pending, refresh


async def fetch_user():
    resp = await fetch("/api/user")
    return (await resp.json()).to_py()


user = create_memo(fetch_user)

Loading(
    html(t"<p>{user()['name']}<span>{' (refreshing)' if is_pending(user) else ''}</span></p>"),
    fallback=html(t"<p>Loading...</p>"),
)

shown, set_shown = create_optimistic(likes)


@action
async def like():
    set_shown(lambda n: n + 1)
    await post_like()
    await refresh(likes)

Everything here has the same name and shape as Solid 2.0, with await in place of promise chaining. like.pending() is tracked, so it works directly as disabled={like.pending()}.

The transition model is Solid 2.0's too. A change that makes an async memo recompute holds the UI that depends on it until the new value lands, so a header reading user_id and a body reading user never disagree; is_pending reports the hold and latest reads ahead of it. An action's writes are staged into the same transaction and reveal together when it settles, while optimistic writes reveal now and revert on settle. Loading(on=...) names the inputs whose change should show the fallback again instead of holding, and Errored heals when the failing computation's inputs change.

docs.title: Server rendering
docs.text:
import asyncio

from wybthon import Loading, NoHydration, RequestEvent, component, create_memo, html, http_status
from wybthon.server import render_to_stream, render_to_string


@component
def NotFound():
    http_status(404)
    return html(t"<h1>Not found</h1>")


@component
def Page():
    async def load():
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        return "Ada"

    name = create_memo(load)
    greeting = Loading(html(t"<p>Hello, {name()}</p>"), fallback=html(t"<p>Loading...</p>"))
    footer = NoHydration(html(t"<footer>Static footer</footer>"))
    return html(t"<div>{greeting}{footer}</div>")


async def main():
    event = RequestEvent(url="/missing")
    markup = render_to_string(NotFound(), event=event)
    assert event.response.status == 404

    markup = await render_to_stream(Page(), url="/")  # complete HTML, data embedded
    async for chunk in render_to_stream(Page(), url="/"):  # out-of-order streaming
        print(chunk)


asyncio.run(main())

As in Solid 2.0, awaiting render_to_stream replaces renderToStringAsync: it waits for every async memo the page reads and returns the complete HTML. Iterating it streams the shell first, then each Loading boundary as its data arrives. A stream is single use: iterate it or await it, once. http_status and http_header are tied to the scope that declared them, so a branch that's disposed before the response head is committed (an error boundary recovering, say) retracts its status. NoHydration keeps a region as static server HTML that the browser adopts without mounting.

docs.title: What's intentionally different
docs.text:
• Naming. snake_case across the API; component names stay PascalCase.
  • Component calls are recognized at run time. In JSX, <Card /> and badge() look different; in a template, {Card(title=...)} and {badge(...)} are both calls. The compiler checks the callee when the template is created: a component gets getters for its props, and anything else becomes one reactive hole. A naming convention can't tell Card(...) from Decimal(...), so Wybthon doesn't use one.
  • Callable props are declared. Solid's props getters return whatever the parent passed. Wybthon unwraps accessors the parent passes, unless the field's annotation is callable (Callable[...] or Accessor[...]), so a callback or an accessor you mean to keep must be annotated as one.
  • A virtual DOM under the reactive graph. Solid compiles JSX to direct DOM operations. Wybthon's compiler also emits each template's parse tree and mount code ahead of time, but changes are applied in batches through a small JS kernel, so every update crosses from Python to JavaScript once. You still get fine-grained holes as the unit of update, and each template instance mounts with one native clone.
  • Callback refs receive a wrapper. A function ref gets an Element; its .element is the raw DOM node.
  • Staged writes. After set_x(1), x() returns the old value until the flush (end of the handler, or flush()). Solid 2.0 leans the same way; Wybthon makes it strict. Use functional updates (set_x(lambda v: v + 1)) to compose writes, and create_signal's returned setter gives back the staged value if you need it.
  • Writes are forbidden inside tracking scopes. Writing a signal from a memo body, a hole, or a single-function effect raises WriteInScopeError in dev mode. Write from handlers, actions, on_settled, or the apply stage.
  • Equality. The default equals (is_equal) is Python == with an identity fast path, not ===. Pass equals=lambda a, b: a is b for identity-only, equals=False to always notify.
  • .peek(). Every accessor has .peek(), a one-read untrack.
  • on_settled instead of onMount. The name reflects when it runs: after the flush that mounted the component committed to the DOM. It may return a cleanup.
  • Python 3.14. Template strings (PEP 750) stand in for JSX, and the framework's own generics (Accessor[T], Memo[T]) are meant to be written in your code.
  • JS interop through Pyodide. from js import fetch, pyodide.ffi.create_proxy for callbacks, .to_py() for JS objects. See the Pyodide guide.

docs.title: What carries over directly
docs.text:
• The mental model: components run once, reactivity is fine-grained, ownership handles cleanup.
  • The compiler's contract: calls and member accesses in markup become getters, and props are values read through getters.
  • The 2.0 async story: async memos, deferred memos, transitions, Loading, Reveal, is_pending, latest, resolve, refresh, actions as transactions, optimistic state, affects, until, error boundary healing.
  • Draft-first stores, reconcile, projections.
  • Flow components, boundaries, context, lazy components and modules, portals.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Read Mental model to see the formal definitions of holes and scopes, and The compiler for exactly what it rewrites.
  • Explore Authoring patterns; most should look familiar.
  • Browse the API reference for the full set of primitives.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Wybthon keeps fine-grained dependency tracking and a Virtual DOM that batches native mutations into one bridge crossing per flush. Python execution, serialization, bridge calls, native DOM work, and browser rendering have different costs. Measure the operation you intend to improve.

docs.title: Start with startup
docs.text:
Loading and initializing Pyodide takes over a second even with a warm cache, before any Wybthon code runs. For most applications that wait matters more than anything else on this page.

  • Prerender the pages users land on. Server rendering puts their content on screen at first paint, and the page hydrates once Python is ready.
  • Ship bytecode. Build with the same Python version as the Pyodide runtime so the archives include precompiled bytecode and the browser doesn't compile Wybthon or your application at startup (see Deployment).
  • Let the build start downloads early. wyb build inlines the manifest into the page and emits preload hints for Pyodide's module and both archives, so the browser starts fetching them while the page parses instead of after the bootstrap runs.
  • Keep the first import small. Load routes and heavy components with lazy, and move rarely used code into explicit chunks.

Production builds also turn dev mode off, so they skip the development checks and warnings.

docs.title: What the engine does for you
docs.text:
Rendering cost in Wybthon is mostly Python bookkeeping, not browser DOM work, so the engine's fast paths target the Python side.

  • Templates are compiled ahead of time. Wybthon's compiler parses and validates each html(t"...") literal when its module is compiled, and writes the literal's parse tree and mount functions into the module as ordinary Python. wyb build turns that into bytecode with the rest of your app, so a production build never parses a template or generates code at run time. On first use, a template rebuilds its slot plan from the stored tree. The static markup becomes a native <template>, and each instance mounts with one fused CLONE command that clones it, fills its text slots, marks its delegated listeners, and inserts it. No VNode tree is built for static parts. See Templates.
  • Bindings that read nothing cost nothing. The compiler's rule is syntactic, so {item["label"]} or {props.title} becomes a getter even when it reads nothing reactive. Before allocating a computation, the renderer runs such an expression (one that makes no calls) under a lightweight probe. If it reads nothing reactive, the value is applied and no computation exists; if it returns an accessor without reading it, the binding targets that accessor directly. Any other hole or attribute binding that finishes its first run without reading anything reactive (and without creating children, cleanups, or async work) is disposed immediately, keeping only the DOM it produced.
  • Bindings keep their state in slots. A hole or attribute binding is a small computation that holds its node, name, and last value in slots and applies changes with a method, instead of a closure with its cells. A node with one delegated handler stores it directly in the handler table. Fewer objects per row means less work for the garbage collector, which matters most in Pyodide.
  • Components cost what their markup costs. A component can only receive new props when a reactive hole re-renders a tree that contains it (or render runs again into the same container). Everywhere else (another component's output, a list row, a Show branch, a template slot), a prop passed as a constant subscribes to nothing, and a prop passed as an expression subscribes the reader to what that expression reads.
  • Native control flow. Show, For, Repeat, and Switch mount as regions the reconciler manages directly, with no component, props object, or wrapper memo. When a hole re-renders one of them, the new condition or source is pushed into the mounted region instead of remounting it.
  • Rows are cheap. A list row is its own owner and its own index accessor. Its index is a plain integer until something reads index() in a tracking scope; only then is a signal created for it, so a row that never reads its index allocates nothing for it.
  • Keyed matching skips what didn't change. Matching a new list against the mounted rows first skips the common prefix and suffix by identity, without calling into each row. A replacement that only swapped two rows is detected the way Solid's reconcileArrays detects it, and becomes two native moves. Only what's left goes through a key table.
  • Native disposal. Removing a range or a subtree releases every node inside it in the JavaScript kernel, which walks the removed nodes natively. Python releases its own registrations (handlers, reactive bindings, refs) without visiting every node. Clearing a For list is one range removal plus disposal of each row's owner.
  • Bulk replacement. When a keyed list reuses none of its rows, the old rows go in one DISPOSE_RANGE command and the new rows mount as one splice, instead of reconciling every unrelated pair.
  • Text placeholders. A hole whose neighbors aren't text uses a text-node placeholder, so a text result is a plain nodeValue write rather than a node replacement.
  • Lighter computations. Async state lives outside each computation until a computation actually runs async work, so an ordinary render binding doesn't allocate it.

docs.title: Templates and h()
docs.text:
Templates and h share one set of prop appliers, so they behave the same; they differ in what happens before mounting.

  • A template is prepared by the compiler. Each call costs a cached lookup and one clone, and its structure is fixed by the literal.
  • An h() tree is built as VNodes on every call and mounts on the generic path, with no template to clone.

Use templates for markup you write by hand, and especially for list rows. Use h() where markup is built by code.

docs.title: Use the incremental paths
docs.text:
• Bind values where they're shown. Write the read where it's used (<b title={role()}>{name()}</b>), and only that attribute or text node updates. A hole that returns a subtree re-runs as a whole: a template from the same literal is patched slot by slot, but anything else is rebuilt. A plain function called in markup ({user_card(user())}) is such a hole, so make it a component instead: {UserCard(name=user().name)} mounts once and receives a getter, so a change updates only the text that reads props.name.
  • Keep holes small. A hole around a single text node patches one node.
  • Pass a store list directly through a For accessor. Local draft edits can use its change records. A list comprehension creates a replacement list that needs generic matching.

  • Select rows with a projection. Each row reads its own key, so a selection change notifies only the old and new rows, not every row:

    from wybthon import For, component, create_projection, create_signal, html


@component
def Rows():
    rows, set_rows = create_signal([{"id": i, "label": f"Row {i}"} for i in range(1000)])
    selected, set_selected = create_signal(None)
    is_selected = create_projection(lambda: {} if selected() is None else {selected(): True})

    def row(item, index):
        def select():
            set_selected(item["id"])

        return html(t"""
          <li class={"danger" if is_selected.get(item["id"]) else ""} onclick={select}>{item["label"]}</li>
        """)

    return html(t"<ul>{For(rows, row)}</ul>")

    is_selected.get(key) is tracked per key and returns None when the key is absent. Each row mounts with one clone command, and a selection change sends one command per affected row.

  • Use Repeat(count, row) for integer slots. Growing it mounts only the new slots.

  • Keep component setup stable. Place dynamic reads in the markup, memos, or effects. Components don't rerun for ordinary state updates.
  • Virtualize large collections. Use VirtualFor for large scrollable collections with fixed row heights. Offscreen rows are disposed, so store durable row state outside the row component.
from wybthon import create_signal, html
from wybthon.virtual import VirtualFor

records, set_records = create_signal([{"name": f"Record {i}"} for i in range(10_000)])


def record(item, index):
    return html(t"<p>{item['name']}</p>")


VirtualFor(records, record, row_height=32, height=400, overscan=4)

map_cooperative(items, fn, budget_ms=8) from wybthon.scheduling yields between chunks of expensive Python work, and yield_to_browser() provides an explicit cooperative yield. A single expensive callback still blocks until it returns; these helpers don't preempt Python or replace a worker.

docs.title: Measure work as well as time
docs.text:
from wybthon import create_root, create_store, flush
from wybthon.diagnostics import profile, runtime_stats

store, edit = create_root(lambda dispose: create_store({"rows": []}))

with profile() as measured:
    edit(lambda draft: draft["rows"].append({"id": 1}))
    flush()
print(measured.as_dict())
print(runtime_stats())

Profiling is opt-in. Reports include computation runs, rows created, list entries scanned, edit records, commits, DOM commands, serialized bytes, and serialization and kernel time when those operations occur. template_clones counts template instances mounted by cloning. inspect_graph(owner) reports ownership and dependencies without evaluating values.

The repository's benchmarks/check_work.py gates command counts in CI: appending 1,000 rows must create 1,000 rows with one template clone command each, and selection and swap must each emit at most two commands. Work counts are deterministic, so they make better regression gates than timings.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
uv sync --locked --group dev
uv run playwright install chromium
uv run python benchmarks/browser_bench.py --mode signal --json
uv run python benchmarks/browser_bench.py --mode store --json

The browser benchmark builds the benchmark app (an ordinary project in benchmarks/app) with wyb build, serves it, and drives ordinary delegated button events. Each scenario restores its own baseline, warms up, checks that the DOM actually changed, and reports separate synchronous commit and input-to-frame samples. Append starts from 10,000 rows and verifies 11,000 afterward. Selection toggles between distinct rows.

Run comparisons serially on the same browser, runtime, hardware, and cache conditions. Use repeated samples and operation counts; don't turn a single local timing into a universal threshold. CI gates deterministic work contracts and saves browser measurements as artifacts. Production startup is measured separately by the generated loader.

benchmarks/compare_browser.py --baseline /path/to/baseline alternates identical operations between isolated checkouts, building each one, with five measured samples by default. It measures direct Python operations separately from delegated event dispatch. Use --mode store for store comparisons and --profile for additional, untimed CPU profiles.

benchmarks/row_bench.py times the same table operations in plain CPython against any checkout's sources, reporting Python's share of the work and the commands each operation sends. With the compiler, its rows are compiled the way an application's modules are, with no hand-written lambdas.

Recorded measurements, with the hardware and versions they were taken on, live in benchmarks/results/; engine-v4.md compares this engine with the previous release, and engine-v3.md the one before it. In Engine v4, a mounted template row keeps about half as many objects tracked by the garbage collector as before, and swapping two rows is two native moves.

A general store splice can rebuild a persistent sequence. Arbitrary replacement lists still require linear matching. Removing a row shifts following indices. Virtualization is the appropriate tool when mounting the entire collection is the dominant cost.

docs.title: Diagnose pending publication
docs.text:
Use diagnostics.inspect_transitions() to see which computations and actions hold each dependency group. diagnostics.inspect_graph(owner) includes read modes, group IDs, and provisional owners. An ordinary consumer of two pending results joins their groups; a separate latest() or is_pending() binding can publish during the hold. See Runtime contracts for the read and ownership rules.

A transition that remains open retains the values and resources still used by the visible UI. Dispose unused scopes and ensure application actions can finish or be canceled. The native async benchmark reports independent publication at increasing widths; its times exclude browser and network costs.

docs.title: Pyodide
docs.text: Wybthon runs in the browser through Pyodide, a CPython distribution compiled to WebAssembly. Most of the framework is plain Python; Pyodide-specific concerns surface only at the boundaries: module loading, async and event-loop integration, and JS interop.

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
• Wybthon requires Python 3.14, so in the browser it needs Pyodide 314 or newer. wyb init pins Pyodide 314.0.6, the version the framework's own browser test suite runs on.
  • wyb build packages Wybthon and your application into archives that its generated bootstrap loads, so a project doesn't install Wybthon at runtime. Templates are compiled at build time, so the browser never parses one. See Deployment.
  • Use micropip to install other Python packages from PyPI at runtime, or list them under packages and wheels in wybthon.toml.
  • Bridge to the browser with the js module and pyodide.ffi. Wybthon doesn't re-export js; import it yourself where you need it.

A project's entry function returns the root view, and the generated bootstrap renders it into the mount element (or hydrates it when the page was prerendered):

from wybthon import component, create_signal, html


@component
def App():
    count, set_count = create_signal(0)

    def increment():
        set_count(lambda n: n + 1)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <h1>My Wybthon app</h1>
        <button onclick={increment}>Count: {count()}</button>
      </div>
    """)


def app():
    return App()

Outside a project, install Wybthon with micropip and render yourself. import wybthon installs an import hook that compiles the templates in every module imported after it, so keep components in a module and import them:

import micropip

await micropip.install("wybthon")

from wybthon import render

from app.main import App  # compiled by the import hook as it's imported

render(App(), "#app")

Code typed straight into a Pyodide console or passed to runPython isn't compiled. A template there whose dynamic expressions ({count() * 2}) were evaluated only once raises TemplateError in dev mode rather than silently never updating; see The compiler.

docs.title: The Pyodide event loop
docs.text:
Pyodide ships with a single-threaded event loop integrated with the browser's microtask queue. A few practical implications:

  • There are no native threads in WebAssembly. Anything that blocks the main thread freezes the page. Prefer async APIs (asyncio.sleep, await fetch(...)) over busy loops.
  • Use asyncio for cooperative concurrency. asyncio.create_task, asyncio.gather, and asyncio.sleep work as you'd expect.
  • await JavaScript promises directly. Pyodide adapts Python coroutines to JS Promises and vice versa. From Python you can await fetch(...); from JavaScript you can await pyodide.runPythonAsync(...).
  • Wybthon flushes on microtasks. Signal writes are staged and applied on the next microtask (queueMicrotask) and at the end of every event handler. You never call flush in browser code; it exists for tests and scripts without an event loop.
  • Long computations should yield. If you have a slow synchronous routine, break it up with await asyncio.sleep(0) inside an async memo or action, or move it to a Pyodide web worker (advanced; outside the scope of this guide).
from js import fetch

from wybthon import create_memo


async def fetch_user() -> dict:
    response = await fetch("/api/users/u-1")
    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(f"HTTP {response.status}")
    return (await response.json()).to_py()


user = create_memo(fetch_user)

Async memos and actions integrate with Pyodide's event loop automatically: await inside them runs on the same loop as the browser's microtask queue, so awaiting fetch(...) or any JS promise just works. create_memo with an async def body raises NotReadyError on reads before the first value (which Loading boundaries catch to show fallbacks) and runs later recomputes as transitions that hold the dependent UI until the new value lands. Use is_pending and latest to observe in-flight state, resolve to await the next settled value, and refresh to recompute quietly.

docs.title: JavaScript interop tips
docs.text:
• Convert Python collections to JS objects with pyodide.ffi.to_js(...) when calling JS APIs that expect plain objects (for example JSON.stringify or fetch request bodies).
  • Convert JS objects to Python with .to_py(); most JS values returned by await calls have this method.
  • Wrap Python callbacks in create_proxy when handing them to JS APIs that keep them (setInterval, addEventListener). Wybthon already does this internally for its delegated event handlers and its popstate listener. Destroy the proxy in a cleanup:
from wybthon import component, create_signal, html, on_settled


@component
def Clock():
    now, set_now = create_signal("")

    def start():
        from js import Date, clearInterval, setInterval
        from pyodide.ffi import create_proxy

        proxy = create_proxy(lambda: set_now(Date().toLocaleTimeString()))
        handle = setInterval(proxy, 1000)
        return lambda: (clearInterval(handle), proxy.destroy())

    on_settled(start)
    return html(t"<div>{now()}</div>")
  • For imperative DOM work, Ref gives you an Element whose .element is the raw node. Event handlers receive a DomEvent built from a payload (no bridge crossing to read e.target.value); e.raw is the native event when you need it.

docs.title: Lazy imports and module loading
docs.text:
lazy uses Python's regular import system, so the only requirement is that the target module is reachable on sys.path at import time:

  • In a wyb build project, the application archive is unpacked before your entry runs, so imports like "app.about.page" resolve. Modules in an explicit [chunks] group are fetched the first time a lazy component in that chunk renders; see Deployment.
  • For third-party packages, use an async loader that awaits micropip.install(...) before importing.
  • Python imports are synchronous, but fetching files into the Pyodide filesystem is asynchronous on the JS side. Copy or preload modules before invoking lazy loaders, or call the lazy component's .preload() method on user intent (link hover) to warm the import.
  • Attribute resolution defaults to Page, then default, then the first callable export; otherwise pass the export name explicitly.
from wybthon import lazy
from wybthon.router import Link

About = lazy(lambda: ("app.about.page", "Page"))


async def load_charts():
    import micropip

    await micropip.install("app-charts")
    import app_charts

    return app_charts.Chart


Chart = lazy(load_charts)

Link("About", href="/about", on_mouseenter=lambda: About.preload())

docs.title: Dev mode
docs.text:
Pyodide takes over a second to load and initialize. Server rendering shows prerendered HTML during that time, and the page hydrates once Python is ready.

Wybthon's dev-mode diagnostics (prop validation, write-in-scope errors, and warnings) are on by default, and wyb dev keeps them on. Production builds from wyb build call set_dev_mode(False) before the application imports, so you don't need to. Outside a project build, call it yourself at startup. is_dev_mode() reads the current mode.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Wybthon's reactive core, VDOM, reconciler, and event delegation are plain Python, so components can be tested in CPython with pytest, no browser required. wybthon.testing renders a view into an in-memory DOM through the real reconciler, kernel protocol, scheduler, and delegated events, then lets you query and interact with it the way a user would. Browser-specific behavior (real layout, Pyodide itself) is covered by a Playwright suite.

Three rules cover most of what's different about testing reactive code:

  1. Writes are staged. After set_count(1), count() still returns the old value until the graph flushes. In the browser that happens on a microtask; in a test, fire flushes for you, and flush does it explicitly.
  2. Effects run after commit. create_effect's first run is deferred to the next flush, so assert after a flush.
  3. Templates are compiled. Wybthon's compiler turns each dynamic interpolation into a getter before a module runs. The pytest plugin compiles your test modules, so templates written in a test behave exactly as they do in an application (see Compiling templates in tests).

docs.title: Rendering components
docs.text:
render mounts a view into a fresh container, flushes it, and returns a Screen:

from wybthon import Props, component, create_signal, html
from wybthon.testing import fire, render


class CounterProps(Props):
    label: str


@component
def Counter(props: CounterProps):
    count, set_count = create_signal(0)

    def increment():
        set_count(lambda n: n + 1)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <p>{props.label}: {count()}</p>
        <button onclick={increment}>+</button>
      </div>
    """)


def test_counter_increments():
    with render(Counter(label="Clicks")) as screen:
        assert screen.get_by_text("Clicks: 0")
        fire.click(screen.get_by_role("button", name="+"))
        assert screen.get_by_text("Clicks: 1")

render accepts any node: a component call, an html template, or a tree built with h. The compiler checks each template's markup when it compiles the module, so a template the browser would rewrite fails the test module with a SyntaxError that names its file and line.

Use render as a context manager to unmount when the block ends, or call screen.unmount() yourself. screen.html() returns the container's inner HTML without Wybthon's comment markers, and screen.text() returns its text with whitespace collapsed:

from wybthon import html
from wybthon.testing import render

with render(html(t"<ul><li>a</li><li>b</li></ul>")) as screen:
    assert screen.html() == "<ul><li>a</li><li>b</li></ul>"
    assert screen.text() == "ab"

docs.title: Cleaning up between tests
docs.text:
cleanup unmounts every view that render mounted and that's still mounted. An autouse fixture in your conftest.py makes every test start from a clean slate, even when a test fails before it unmounts:

import pytest

from wybthon.testing import cleanup


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def _unmount_views():
    yield
    cleanup()

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
Queries come in three forms, as in Testing Library:

Form No match One match Several matches get_by_* Raises LookupError Returns it Raises LookupError query_by_* Returns None Returns it Raises LookupError get_all_by_* Raises LookupError Returns a list Returns a list Query Finds get_by_text(text, exact=True), query_by_text, get_all_by_text The deepest elements whose text matches. With exact=False the match is a case-insensitive substring; pass a compiled regular expression to search. get_by_role(role, name=None), query_by_role, get_all_by_role Elements with an explicit role or an implicit one (button, link, textbox, checkbox, heading, list, ...). name matches the accessible name: aria-label, then the text content (or placeholder for inputs). get_by_label_text(text), query_by_label_text The form control a <label> names (through for or by nesting), or the element with that aria-label. get_by_test_id(id), query_by_test_id, get_all_by_test_id Elements whose data-testid matches. Write data-testid="save" in a template, or data_testid="save" in h() props.

Queries return TestNodes. Read .text_content, .attributes (a dict of strings), .value, .checked, and .tag, or use .classList.contains(name):

import re

from wybthon import html
from wybthon.testing import render

form = html(t"""
  <div>
    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input id="email" type="email" placeholder="you@example.com">
    <p data-testid="status">Saved 3 items</p>
    <button class="primary">Save</button>
  </div>
""")

with render(form) as screen:
    assert screen.get_by_label_text("Email").attributes["type"] == "email"
    assert screen.get_by_text(re.compile(r"Saved \d+ items"))
    assert screen.get_by_test_id("status").text_content == "Saved 3 items"
    assert screen.get_by_role("button", name="Save").classList.contains("primary")
    assert screen.query_by_text("Deleted") is None

docs.title: Firing events
docs.text:
fire dispatches an event through Wybthon's delegated handlers, then flushes, so the next assertion sees the settled DOM:

Helper What it does fire.click(node) Dispatches click. fire.input(node, value) Sets the control's value, then dispatches input. fire.change(node, value=None, checked=None) Sets the value or checked state, then dispatches change. fire.submit(form) Dispatches submit. fire.key_down(node, key) Dispatches keydown with key. fire.focus(node), fire.blur(node) Dispatch focus and blur. fire(node, "dblclick", **payload) Dispatches any event type. Keyword fields become event fields (shift_key=True is e.shift_key). 
from wybthon import component, create_signal, html
from wybthon.testing import fire, render


@component
def Mirror():
    text, set_text = create_signal("")

    def update(e):
        set_text(e.target.value)

    return html(t"""
      <div>
        <input aria-label="Name" value={text()} oninput={update}>
        <p>Hello, {text()}</p>
      </div>
    """)


def test_input_updates_text():
    with render(Mirror()) as screen:
        fire.input(screen.get_by_label_text("Name"), "Ada")
        assert screen.get_by_text("Hello, Ada")

docs.title: Props and parents
docs.text:
To drive a prop from the test, render the component from a template that reads a signal, then flush after writing it. The compiler passes name={name()} to the component as a getter, so the component body runs once and only the bound text updates:

from wybthon import Props, component, create_signal, flush, html
from wybthon.testing import render


class GreetingProps(Props):
    name: str


runs: list[int] = []


@component
def Greeting(props: GreetingProps):
    runs.append(1)
    return html(t"<p>Hello, {props.name}</p>")


def test_prop_updates_without_rerunning_body():
    name, set_name = create_signal("Ada")
    with render(html(t"<{Greeting} name={name()} />")) as screen:
        set_name("Grace")
        flush()
        assert screen.text() == "Hello, Grace"
        assert runs == [1]

{Greeting(name=name())} works the same way and is type-checked. Passing the signal itself in Python, Greeting(name=name), works at run time too, but type checkers reject it when the field is annotated name: str. Callback fields (annotated Callable[...]) are returned as passed, so a test can pass a recording function and assert on its calls after firing events.

docs.title: Async components
docs.text:
Async memos, actions, and Loading boundaries need an event loop. Run the test body with asyncio.run (or a plugin such as pytest-asyncio), and use wait_for to wait for an observable result. It flushes between checks and raises TimeoutError if the condition never holds:

import asyncio

from wybthon import Loading, component, create_memo, html
from wybthon.testing import render, wait_for


@component
def UserCard():
    async def load():
        await asyncio.sleep(0)
        return {"name": "Ada"}

    user = create_memo(load)
    return Loading(html(t"<p>User: {user()['name']}</p>"), fallback=html(t"<p>Loading...</p>"))


def test_loading_shows_fallback_then_content():
    async def main() -> None:
        with render(UserCard()) as screen:
            assert screen.text() == "Loading..."
            await wait_for(lambda: screen.query_by_text("User: Ada") is not None)

    asyncio.run(main())

tick drains ready asyncio continuations and flushes, for when you want to step instead of wait. resolve awaits an async memo's next settled value: assert await resolve(user) == {"name": "Ada"}.

docs.title: The reactive core, no DOM
docs.text:
Signals, memos, effects, and stores need no rendering at all. reactive_scope owns the computations created inside it and disposes them when the block ends:

from wybthon import create_effect, create_memo, create_signal, flush
from wybthon.testing import reactive_scope


def test_memo_and_effect():
    with reactive_scope():
        count, set_count = create_signal(0)
        doubled = create_memo(lambda: count() * 2)
        seen: list[int] = []

        create_effect(doubled, lambda value, prev: seen.append(value))
        flush()  # first effect run
        assert seen == [0]

        set_count(1)
        set_count(lambda n: n + 1)  # functional updates compose
        assert count() == 0  # still staged
        flush()
        assert count() == 2
        assert seen == [0, 4]  # one effect run per flush

docs.title: Stores, router, and forms
docs.text:
• Store writes are staged like signal writes. Python doesn't allow assignment inside a lambda, so write draft functions with def, pass them to the setter, and flush before asserting on reads.
  • Outside a browser, navigate only updates the current_path signal. Flush afterward. Path matching (resolve in wybthon.router) is pure and needs no rendering.
  • Drive form bindings with fire.input, fire.change, and fire.submit against the rendered controls.

docs.title: Dev-mode diagnostics
docs.text: Dev-mode warnings print to stderr; capture them with pytest's capsys. Warnings are deduplicated per process, so call wybthon._warnings._reset_warning_dedupe() at the start of a test that asserts on one. A write inside a memo raises WriteInScopeError when the memo is read (pytest.raises(WriteInScopeError) around the read); a write inside a single-function effect surfaces through the effect's error= handler on the next flush. Calling a component with an unknown or missing prop raises TypeError at the call.

docs.title: Compiling templates in tests
docs.text:
Installing Wybthon registers a pytest plugin (through the pytest11 entry point) that adds the compiler to pytest's assertion rewriting, so every test module and conftest.py is compiled before it runs. Its cached bytecode gets a tag of its own, so a test module cached without the compiler is never reused. Helper modules that your tests import are compiled by the import hook that import wybthon installs. There's nothing to configure; disable the plugin with -p no:wybthon.

Two cases need a step of your own:

  • Scripts. A template in a script run with python script.py isn't compiled, and in dev mode html() raises TemplateError when one of its dynamic expressions has already been evaluated once. Run the script with wyb run script.py instead; it compiles the script and everything it imports.
  • Templates built at run time. A test that builds a module's source as a string (to check compiler output, for example) compiles it with compile_source before running it:
from typing import Any

from wybthon import create_signal, flush
from wybthon.compiler import compile_source
from wybthon.testing import render

SOURCE = """
from wybthon import html

def view(count):
    return html(t"<p>{count() * 2}</p>")
"""


def test_generated_template():
    namespace: dict[str, Any] = {}
    exec(compile_source(SOURCE, "<generated>"), namespace)
    count, set_count = create_signal(1)
    with render(namespace["view"](count)) as screen:
        set_count(2)
        flush()
        assert screen.text() == "4"

docs.title: Framework tests
docs.text:
Wybthon's own unit tests under tests/ also use a lower-level wyb fixture from tests/conftest.py. It installs stub js and pyodide modules, reloads the browser-facing modules (kernel, dom, events, and reconciler), and installs a kernel.PythonBackend over the same in-memory document wybthon.testing uses; root_element provides a fresh container. Use it when a test needs to inspect kernel commands or reconciler internals. For component behavior, prefer wybthon.testing.

Run the unit suite with:

uv run pytest -q

docs.title: Browser E2E suite (Playwright and Pyodide)
docs.text:
The e2e job in CI runs the browser suite under tests/e2e/. All tests carry the e2e pytest marker and exercise the real Pyodide runtime (314.0.6) in headless Chromium against a feature fixture app: an ordinary wybthon.toml project in tests/e2e/ with one route per framework feature (reactivity, holes, props, events, context, flow control, forms, stores, loading, error boundaries, lifecycle, portal, lazy loading, router, hydration, and production builds). Each per-feature test module (tests/e2e/test_*.py) drives that route and asserts through stable data-testid selectors.

Design choices that keep the suite fast and deterministic:

  • Boot Pyodide once. The session-scoped fixture starts wyb dev --dir tests/e2e and boots the app a single time; tests navigate between features with the History API router instead of reloading the page.
  • Isolation between tests. The goto_feature helper bounces through a /blank route first, forcing the previous feature's tree to unmount.
  • Stable selectors. Components expose data-testid attributes (see the tid helper in tests/e2e/app/testkit.py).
  • Fail fast on boot errors. The bootstrap records its status on window.__WYB.status, and the readiness wait surfaces a boot error as a test error instead of a timeout. The page's Pyodide instance is window.__WYB.pyodide, and the app mounts into #app.

Run locally:

uv sync --group dev
uv run playwright install chromium

# full browser suite
uv run pytest -q -m e2e tests/e2e

# a single feature module
uv run pytest -q -m e2e tests/e2e/test_errors.py

Notes:

  • The default pytest configuration excludes the browser suite from the fast unit run; pass -m e2e to opt in. Pyodide's cold start can take a while in CI, so the tests use generous timeouts.
  • The fixture app under tests/e2e/app/ is Pyodide-runtime code (it uses absolute app.* imports that only resolve inside the built bundle), so it's excluded from mypy and never imported by the CPython unit tests.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
pytest-cov is in the dev group, and CI fails below 80% coverage:

uv run pytest -q --cov=wybthon --cov-branch --cov-report=term-missing --cov-fail-under=80

docs.title: Typing
docs.text: Wybthon requires Python 3.14. Its accessors, components, actions, and stores carry type information that both pyright (including Pylance) and mypy understand with no plugin or extra configuration.

docs.title: Component props
docs.text:
Components declare their inputs on a Props subclass with plain annotations. Props is a PEP 681 dataclass_transform base, so a type checker treats each props class as a keyword-only constructor and checks every component call against it:

from collections.abc import Callable

from wybthon import Props, VNode, component, create_signal, html, prop


class GreetingProps(Props):
    name: str
    copies: int = 1
    tags: list[str] = prop(default_factory=list)
    on_wave: Callable[[], None] | None = None


@component
def Greeting(props: GreetingProps) -> VNode:
    def wave() -> None:
        if props.on_wave is not None:
            props.on_wave()

    return html(t"<p onclick={wave}>{props.name * props.copies}</p>")


name, set_name = create_signal("Ada")
Greeting(name="Ada")
Greeting(name="Ada", copies=2, on_wave=lambda: print("hi"))
html(t"<div>{Greeting(name=name(), copies=2)}</div>")
  • Inside the component, a field reads as its annotation: props.name is a str, and props.copies is an int. The read is tracked, so {props.name * props.copies} updates when either changes.
  • A caller passes values of the declared types. In a template, {Greeting(name=name())} type-checks as name: str, and the compiler still passes a getter, so the prop stays reactive. In Python code outside a template, Greeting(name=name) passes the accessor itself, which works at run time (the read unwraps it) but is a type error, because an Accessor[str] isn't a str.
  • A missing required prop, a value of the wrong type, and an unknown keyword are all type errors:
Greeting(name=42)  # incompatible type
Greeting()  # missing "name"
Greeting(name="Ada", typo=1)  # unexpected keyword "typo"

At run time, dev mode raises TypeError for the same unknown and missing props, so code that isn't type checked still fails loudly.

docs.title: Callable fields
docs.text:
A field annotated as callable, with Callable[...] or Accessor[T], alone or in a union with None, is returned exactly as the parent passed it. That's how callbacks work: reading props.on_wave never calls it, so props.on_wave() calls the parent's function. Every other field unwraps an accessor the parent passes, so a field that should hold a function must be annotated as one.

Annotate a field Accessor[T] when the component needs the accessor itself, for example to hand it to For:

from wybthon import Accessor, For, Props, VNode, component, html


class TagListProps(Props):
    items: Accessor[list[str]]


def tag(item: str, index: Accessor[int]) -> VNode:
    return html(t"<li>{item}</li>")


@component
def TagList(props: TagListProps) -> VNode:
    items = props.items  # the accessor itself
    return html(t"<ul>{For(items, tag)}</ul>")

Reading a callable field returns what the parent passed without calling it, so reading it once at the top of the body freezes nothing. The parent passes the accessor by name, {TagList(items=tags)}; an expression such as tags() would hand the component a getter, which every read unwraps, even for a callable field.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text: Defaults work as in a dataclass (copies: int = 1, on_wave: ... = None). Use prop(default_factory=list) for a mutable value; the factory runs once per component instance. prop(default=value) also works, but type checkers only recognize a field specifier's default when it's passed by keyword, so a positional prop(0) isn't accepted.

docs.title: Children
docs.text:
ParentProps declares children: Any. Both the children keyword and item syntax are checked:

from wybthon import ParentProps, VNode, component, html


class CardProps(ParentProps):
    title: str


@component
def Card(props: CardProps) -> VNode:
    return html(t"<div><h2>{props.title}</h2>{props.children}</div>")


Card(title="Hi")[html(t"<p>a</p>"), html(t"<p>b</p>")]
Card(title="Hi", children=html(t"<p>a</p><p>b</p>"))

Positional children (Card(html(t"<p>a</p>"), title="Hi")) work at run time, but checkers reject them because the props constructor is keyword-only.

docs.title: What a component call returns
docs.text:
@component is typed so that calling a component looks like constructing its props class; that's how the checker validates the keywords. At run time the call returns a VNode. Every child position, in a template interpolation or in h, accepts the props type, so this mismatch only shows if you inspect the result yourself: an isinstance check sees a VNode. A component with no parameters is typed as a function returning VNode.

Under mypy --strict, annotate component functions with -> VNode, as above; html and h return VNode.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
A template's interpolations are ordinary Python expressions, so the checker sees them like any other code, before the compiler turns the dynamic ones into getters. What's checked depends on where a value appears:

In a template Checked {expression} in any position Statically, as ordinary code: an undefined name, a wrong attribute, or a bad call is reported. {Card(title=user().name)} Statically, with full prop checking, like any component call. The checker sees user().name as a str; the compiler passes a getter. <{Card} title={user().name}>...</{Card}> The expression user().name is checked as code, but not against Card's props. An unknown or missing prop raises TypeError at run time, in dev mode, when the template renders. The HTML markup itself When the module is compiled: markup the parser would rewrite is a SyntaxError with the file and line (or a TemplateError for a template compiled at run time).

Type checkers can't see inside the template's static text, so a component tag's attributes aren't checked against its props class. Use the call form inside an interpolation when you want the checker's help with a component's props, and the tag form when passing nested markup as children reads better.

html() is annotated to take a string.templatelib.Template, so passing a plain string is a type error, and it raises TypeError at run time:

from wybthon import html

html("<p>Hello</p>")  # error: expected "Template", got "str"

docs.title: Control flow
docs.text:
For and Show have generic overloads, so their callbacks are checked against the data you pass. With For, the keyed strategy decides which arguments are accessors:

Call Callback arguments For(items, fn) (the default, keyed=True) (item: T, index: Accessor[int]) For(items, fn, keyed=False) (item: Accessor[T], index: int) For(items, fn, keyed=lambda item: ...) (item: Accessor[T], index: Accessor[int]) 
from typing import TypedDict

from wybthon import Accessor, For, VNode, create_signal, html


class Todo(TypedDict):
    id: int
    title: str


todos, set_todos = create_signal([Todo(id=1, title="Write docs")])


def row(todo: Todo, index: Accessor[int]) -> VNode:
    return html(t"<li>{todo['title']}</li>")


def slot(todo: Accessor[Todo], index: int) -> VNode:
    return html(t"<li>{index}: {todo()['title']}</li>")


For(todos, row)
For(todos, slot, keyed=False)
For(todos, lambda todo, i: html(t"<li>{todo['title']}</li>"))  # todo: Todo
For(todos, lambda todo, i: html(t"<li>{todo['titel']}</li>"))  # error: no key "titel"
html(t"<ul>{For(todos(), row)}</ul>")  # in a template, the compiler passes a getter

A lambda's parameters are inferred from the overload, so the fourth call is reported even though nothing is annotated. In a template, For(todos(), row) checks the same way: the checker sees a list[Todo].

Show passes the truthy value to a one-argument callback as an Accessor, or as the value itself with keyed=True. Either way, None is narrowed away, because the branch only renders when the value is truthy:

from typing import TypedDict

from wybthon import Show, create_memo, create_signal, html


class User(TypedDict):
    name: str


users, set_users = create_signal([User(name="Ada")])
user = create_memo(lambda: next(iter(users()), None))  # Memo[User | None]

Show(user, lambda u: html(t"<p>{u()['name']}</p>"))  # u: Accessor[User]
Show(user, lambda u: html(t"<p>{u['name']}</p>"), keyed=True)  # u: User
Show(user, html(t"<p>Signed in</p>"), fallback=html(t"<p>Sign in</p>"))

The callback's type comes from when, so pass the accessor itself (Show(user, ...)) when the callback takes the value. {Show(user(), panel)} works the same at run time, but a checker sees a plain User | None there and accepts only a zero-argument callback or a node.

Repeat's callback receives an int index. Switch and Match take their children untyped.

docs.title: Accessors, setters, and memos
docs.text:
• Accessor[T] is readable: call it for a tracked read, or .peek() for an untracked one.
  • Setter[T] accepts a value or an updater function T -> T.
  • Memo[T] is a disposable derived accessor. An async def passed to create_memo produces a Memo of the awaited type.
from wybthon import Accessor, Memo, create_memo, create_signal

count, set_count = create_signal(0)
doubled: Memo[int] = create_memo(lambda: count() * 2)
reader: Accessor[int] = count
set_count(lambda n: n + 1)

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An @action keeps its parameters and result type. An async action returns an asyncio.Future[T], which supports cancellation, and the action object has .pending().

from wybthon import action


@action
def save(name: str) -> int:
    return len(name)


length: int = save("Ada")

docs.title: Stores
docs.text:
create_store returns a Store[S] (a read-only mapping) or a StoreList[T] (a read-only sequence), and setters receive the matching draft type. A store keeps its schema as a type parameter, but reads of individual keys (store.name, store["name"]) are typed Any, because a mapping proxy can't express per-key types without a checker plugin. Annotate where you read when the type matters:

from typing import TypedDict

from wybthon import create_store


class Person(TypedDict):
    name: str
    age: int


person, write = create_store(Person(name="Ada", age=36))
name: str = person.name
age: int = person["age"]
write(lambda draft: setattr(draft, "name", "Grace"))

Mapping method names stay methods, so read a data key that collides with one (items, keys, get) with []. A TypedDict annotation isn't runtime validation.

docs.title: Running the checkers
docs.text:
No plugin is needed. A minimal configuration:

[tool.mypy]
python_version = "3.14"
strict = true

[tool.pyright]
pythonVersion = "3.14"
typeCheckingMode = "strict"

The repository's tests/typing fixtures check valid calls and expected errors (missing, mistyped, and unknown props, an accessor passed where a value is declared, a mistyped component call inside a template, a mistyped For row, and a plain string passed to html()) as part of the unit test gate.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Welcome! This page is a quick orientation for contributors. The full and authoritative guidelines live in the repository's CONTRIBUTING.md; please skim it before opening a pull request.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/wybthon/wybthon.git
cd wybthon
uv sync --group dev --group docs

uv creates .venv and installs the framework, the dev tooling, and the docs site dependencies. Prefix commands with uv run to use that environment, for example uv run pytest -q or uv run mkdocs serve.

docs.title: Where to make changes
docs.text: Want to change... Look here Framework code src/wybthon/ Demo apps Standalone repos under the wybthon organization, e.g. demo-template Documentation site docs/ Tests tests/ Lint / format / typing config pyproject.toml

docs.title: Coding standards
docs.text:
• Source code targets Python 3.14 with type hints throughout.
  • Docstrings use the Google style documented in the docs style guide. The Ruff pydocstyle ruleset enforces this.
  • Format with uv run ruff format . and lint with uv run ruff check . before pushing.
  • Run uv run mypy and uv run pytest -q to verify types and tests. CI requires 80% coverage.
  • ./scripts/check.sh runs everything CI's unit job runs, in the same order.

docs.title: Updating documentation
docs.text:
• Author new pages under docs/ and add them to mkdocs.yml.
  • Build the site locally with mkdocs serve (or mkdocs build --strict to fail on warnings the way CI does).
  • Cross-reference Python symbols with [label][wybthon.symbol] syntax; see the style guide for details.
  • Write examples in the current style (templates, plain-annotation props) and check them by running them with uv run wyb run example.py, which compiles their templates the way an application's are.

docs.title: Filing a pull request
docs.text:
1. Open an issue first for non-trivial changes so we can align on the approach.
  2. Keep PRs focused: one logical change per PR makes review easier.
  3. Add or update tests when changing behavior.
  4. Update the relevant docs page(s) so the framework stays self-explanatory.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Skim the docs style guide before writing prose.
  • Browse open issues at github.com/wybthon/wybthon/issues for ways to help.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text: Quick answers to the questions we get most often. If yours isn't here, check the troubleshooting guide or open an issue.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
Is Wybthon production ready?

Not yet. The framework is pre-1.0 and the public API may shift between minor releases (old APIs are removed outright rather than shimmed). We recommend it for prototypes, internal tools, and learning projects today, and we'll relax this guidance as the API stabilizes.

Does it work outside the browser?

Everything except the real browser. Signals, memos, effects, async computations, actions, stores, forms, context, flow control, and VDOM construction run in plain CPython. wybthon.testing renders components into an in-memory DOM through the real reconciler and event delegation, so you can test them with pytest (see the testing guide), and wybthon.server renders them to HTML for prerendering and server rendering.

Which Python version do I need?

Python 3.14. Template strings (PEP 750) are part of the component API, and server rendering, tests, and tooling run on the same Python version as the browser. In the browser that means Pyodide 314 or newer; wyb init pins 314.0.6.

Why Python in the browser?

Wybthon lets data scientists, researchers, and tooling teams build interactive UIs without switching to TypeScript. Pyodide makes the scientific Python stack (NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, and friends) available client-side, so you can render results without a server round-trip.

Why is there a virtual DOM if this is 'SolidJS for Python'?

Every DOM call crosses the Python-to-JavaScript bridge, so Wybthon batches mutations instead of making them one at a time. The VDOM is that batching layer, not a re-render model: each reactive hole diffs only its own subtree, and the reconciler sends the resulting mutations to a JavaScript kernel in one bridge crossing. The static parts of an html template never become VNodes at all. Wybthon's compiler turns each template literal into a native <template> that's cloned with one command, and its dynamic expressions into getters, which is the job Solid's compiler does for JSX. The reactive model is fine-grained; a signal change re-runs the holes that read it, never whole components.

Do I need to wrap expressions in lambdas to keep them reactive?

No. Wybthon's compiler does what Solid's does for JSX: an interpolation that contains a call, an attribute access, or a subscript ({count() * 2}, {props.title}, {row["label"]}, class={"on" if active() else ""}) becomes a getter, so it updates when what it reads changes. Names, constants, and lambdas are passed as they are, and event handlers and refs are never wrapped. The compiler runs when a module is imported after wybthon, in wyb build and wyb dev, under pytest, and for scripts run with wyb run script.py. See The compiler.

You still can't write a bare lambda in an interpolation: Python's grammar treats its : as the start of a format spec. Name an inline event handler, or wrap it in parentheses: onclick={(lambda: set_open(False))}.

Why does html() say my template wasn't compiled?

In dev mode, a template that reaches html without passing through the compiler raises TemplateError when one of its dynamic expressions has already been evaluated, because the markup would silently stop updating. This happens in a script run with python script.py (use wyb run script.py), at a REPL, or in code built with exec. See the troubleshooting entry.

What happened to the element helpers (div(...), p(...))?

RFC 0004 removed them, along with wybthon.elements and wybthon.svg. A helper evaluates its arguments before Wybthon sees them, so it can't benefit from the compiler. html templates are the way to write markup (including <svg>), and h(tag, props, *children) is the programmatic layer, like h in Solid: use it for markup that code builds, such as generated forms, recursive trees, or a computed tag. h() props take Python names (class_, html_for, on_click) as well as HTML names.

docs.title: Pyodide and runtime
docs.text:
Which Pyodide version should I target?

Pin a single version per deployment with pyodide-version in wybthon.toml. Wybthon requires Pyodide 314 or newer (Python 3.14). Building with the same Python version as the runtime also lets wyb build ship precompiled bytecode.

How do I install Python packages from PyPI?

Use micropip inside Pyodide:

import micropip


async def setup():
    await micropip.install("httpx")

The package must be pure Python or available as a Pyodide-compatible wheel. See the Pyodide guide for details.

How do I call a JavaScript API from Python?

Import names from the js module yourself (Wybthon doesn't re-export it):

from js import fetch, window

window.alert("hello!")


async def load_users():
    response = await fetch("/api/users")
    return await response.json()

Convert Python objects with pyodide.ffi.to_js(...) when handing them to JS APIs that expect plain objects. For DOM nodes Wybthon rendered, prefer Ref and Element over document.querySelector.

docs.title: Building and shipping apps
docs.text:
Do I need a bundler or a build step?

There's no JavaScript bundler, but there is a build step. wyb build packages Wybthon and your application into archives with a generated bootstrap, prerenders the routes you list, and turns dev mode off; any static host can serve the result. wyb dev runs the same build in development mode and reloads on change. See the deployment guide.

Can I lazy-load route components?

Yes; see lazy. It's backed by an async memo, so it integrates with Loading for declarative loading UIs and with Errored for load failures, and each lazy component has a .preload() method for warming the cache early.

docs.title: Components and props
Reactivity
docs.text:
Why didn't my component re-run after a signal changed?

Because components run once by design. A read in the component body captures the value at setup time. To stay reactive, read it in the template, where the compiler turns the expression into a getter (<span>{count()} items</span>, <h2>{props.title}</h2>), or derive it with create_memo. In dev mode Wybthon warns when a signal, memo, or prop is read at the top level of a component body; use untrack (untrack(lambda: props.initial)) when a one-time read is what you want.

Why does my signal still show the old value right after I set it?

Writes are staged. set_count(1) records the new value, and count() keeps returning the committed value until the next flush: a browser microtask, the end of an event handler, or an explicit flush. Functional updates see the staged value, so set_count(lambda n: n + 1) twice in one handler adds two. In tests and plain scripts, call flush() after your writes before asserting.

How do I batch multiple signal updates?

You don't need to; everything batches. Consecutive writes in one handler (or one synchronous block) coalesce into a single flush, so an effect that reads both fields runs once:

set_first("Ada")
set_last("Lovelace")
flush()  # the name effect runs once, not twice

There is no batch() function.

Why didn't my effect run when I created it?

create_effect runs its first time on the next flush, after the DOM has been committed, so an effect created in a component body sees the mounted DOM. If you need code to run immediately during setup, just run it; if you need something after mount, use on_settled. create_render_effect runs immediately, but it's meant for rendering primitives.

How do I fetch data?

Write an async def and pass it to create_memo. Reads before the first value raise NotReadyError, which the nearest Loading boundary turns into fallback UI; later refetches run as transitions that hold the dependent UI on the previous state until the new value lands. Use is_pending for a refresh hint, latest to peek without suspending, and refresh or resolve to drive it imperatively. Mutations go through action, optionally with create_optimistic for instant UI.

How do I highlight the selected row without re-running every row?

Use a projection keyed by the selection. Each row reads only its own key, so a change notifies the old and new rows:

from wybthon import create_projection, create_signal

selected, set_selected = create_signal(None)
is_selected = create_projection(lambda: {} if selected() is None else {selected(): True})
# In a row: html(t"<tr class={'active' if is_selected.get(row_id) else ''}>...</tr>")
Why don't I see dev warnings in production?

wyb build turns dev mode off before your application imports, so production builds skip development checks and warnings. wyb dev keeps them on. Check the mode with is_dev_mode().

docs.title: Documentation style guide
docs.text: This page describes how Wybthon's documentation and source-level docstrings are written. Follow it when authoring new code or revising existing pages so the site renders consistently and help() reads cleanly inside a Pyodide REPL.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
• Use Google-style docstrings everywhere (modules, classes, functions).
  • Let type hints carry the types. Don't repeat them inside docstrings.
  • Use Material admonitions (!!! tip "Title") for callouts in Markdown, not plain > blockquotes.
  • Cross-link API symbols using mkdocstrings autorefs: [`create_signal`][wybthon.create_signal].
  • Comments explain why, not what (the code already says what).

docs.title: Grammar and punctuation
docs.text:
We follow the Chicago Manual of Style (17th edition) for prose. Highlights:
