  • Control flow is built from components. Show creates a component context, a RawProps mapping with its own signals, a truthiness memo, two owners, a branch computation, and six kernel commands.
  • Component children get a throwaway placeholder. In a compiled shape, a component child mounts before a comment placeholder that's then disposed, so one dashboard mount sends 173 CREATE_COMMENT and 169 DISPOSE commands it doesn't need.
  • A render computation is large. Computation has 39 slots and about 1 KB per binding once its closure and edges are counted. In Pyodide, live object count drives the cyclic collector, which the engine v2 evaluation identified as the dominant cost of large browser timings.

Components that cost fourteen times an element quietly push authors away from factoring their UI, which is the opposite of Solid's mental model.

docs.title: Python already has Solid's compiler
docs.text:
Solid's speed comes from its compiler: JSX's static structure becomes a template cloned once per instance, and only the dynamic parts run code. RFC 0002 compiled shapes at run time, but every instance still builds its whole VNode tree and is checked node by node against the shape before it can use the compiled mount.

PEP 750 template strings remove both costs. A t-string literal's strings tuple is a constant of the code object, so it's the same object on every evaluation:

def row(i, label):
    return t"<tr class={i}><td>{i}</td><td><a>{label}</a></td></tr>"

row(1, "x").strings is row(2, "y").strings  # True

That identity is exactly what JavaScript tagged templates provide, and what lit-html and Solid's buildless solid-js/html rely on. Building that t-string costs 0.36 µs; building the same row with the element helpers costs 2.84 µs, before any shape matching. The literal guarantees its own structure, so there's nothing to match.

Template strings are also the most Pythonic way to write HTML that Python has: HTML templating is the motivating example of PEP 750, and the markup reads like the HTML it produces instead of nested calls with renamed attributes (class_, html_for, input_).

docs.title: Two props systems
docs.text: RFC 0002 replaced the props-as-mapping model with typed Props classes and listed Props.raw as removed. Every built-in component still runs on that model, renamed RawProps: Show, For, Switch, Loading, Errored, Reveal, Portal, the context provider, dynamic, lazy, the router, and virtual lists. That's a second props implementation with its own signals, and the reason built-ins are expensive.

docs.title: 1. html(): compiled t-string templates
docs.text:
from wybthon import Prop, Props, Show, component, create_memo, create_signal, html


class CounterProps(Props):
    label: Prop[str]


@component
def Counter(props: CounterProps):
    count, set_count = create_signal(0)
    doubled = create_memo(lambda: count() * 2)

    def increment():
        set_count(lambda n: n + 1)

    return html(t"""
      <div class="counter">
        <p>{props.label}: {count} (doubled: {doubled})</p>
        <button onclick={increment}>+</button>
        {Show(lambda: count() > 5, html(t"<p>That's a lot of clicks.</p>"))}
      </div>
    """)

html(template) returns a node usable anywhere a node is accepted. The template is HTML with interpolations in these positions:

Position Example Behavior Child <p>{value}</p> Same as a child of an element helper: text, a node, a list, None, or a reactive expression (an accessor or zero-argument function), which becomes a hole. Attribute value <a href={url}> Same as an element helper prop: a static value is applied once; a reactive expression becomes its own binding. Part of an attribute <div class="card card-{kind}"> The parts form one string; reactive parts make the whole attribute one binding, like a t-string attribute. Event <button onclick={handler}> onclick, onClick, and on:click all bind a delegated click handler. A capture suffix (onClickCapture) and event(...) options work as with helpers. Spread <input {attrs}> A mapping of props applied to the element, like **attrs on a helper. Component tag <{Card} title="Hi">...</{Card}> Calls the component with the attributes as keyword props (class and for become class_ and html_for) and the content as children, one child per top-level node. A self-closing <{Card} /> passes no children. Built-ins that are plain functions (Show, Loading, Link, context providers) are called the way their signatures take children.

The rules follow HTML, with a few JSX conveniences:

  • Attribute names are HTML names (class, for, aria-label, data-id, tabindex). Static values are written into the compiled markup.
  • Any element may self-close (<div />); void elements may be written either way.
  • Whitespace follows JSX: text that spans lines is trimmed line by line and joined with single spaces, and whitespace-only text containing a newline is dropped. <pre> keeps its text verbatim.
  • Character references (&,  ) are decoded in static text and attribute values.
  • <!-- comments --> are dropped.
  • <script>, <style>, and <textarea> take static content only.

A template with several top-level nodes returns a fragment. A template with no elements (html(t"Hello, {name}!")) is text and holes.

Compilation. The first call with a given strings tuple parses the template into a small tree, validates it, and compiles it:

  • the static skeleton, serialized once and registered with the kernel as a native <template>;
  • the pre-order offset of every dynamic slot, with its kind (attribute, event, ref, spread, child, component);
  • the delegated event types per offset, so cloning marks listeners natively, as in RFC 0002.

Compiled templates are cached in a dictionary keyed by the strings object's identity (holding a reference so the identity can't be reused), with a structural fallback for templates built by hand. Templates are code, so the cache is bounded by the size of the program.

Mounting takes one CLONE command, as a compiled shape does today, then walks the slot plan with the instance's values. No VNode tree is built for static parts, and there are no per-node guards: the literal is the guarantee.

  • A child slot keeps its placeholder as a permanent anchor. A text value is written into the clone command itself when the placeholder is a text node, so a row's label costs no extra command. A node is mounted in front of the placeholder, and nothing is disposed.
  • Attribute, event, and ref slots use the same appliers as element helpers, so semantics can't drift between the two authoring styles.

Re-rendering. When a hole returns a template from the same literal again, the instance is patched slot by slot, comparing each value with the previous one by identity, as lit-html does. A changed text is one nodeValue write; an unchanged slot costs one comparison.

Validation. The compiler rejects markup the browser's parser would rewrite, with an error that names the template and the fix, rather than silently falling back: an unclosed or mismatched tag, <tr> directly inside <table> (add <tbody>), block content inside <p>, interactive content nested in itself (<a> inside <a>), interpolation inside raw-text elements, and attribute names that aren't valid identifiers for a component tag.

Other renderers. Server rendering, hydration, SVG, and MathML expand a compiled template into ordinary VNodes and mount those, so their output is identical to the element helpers'. A template containing <svg> or <math> always expands; its children still benefit from compilation elsewhere.

Typing. Interpolations are ordinary Python expressions, so pyright and mypy check them. Calling a component inside an interpolation ({Card(title="Hi")}) keeps full prop checking. The <{Card}> tag form is checked at run time in dev mode, like any component call, and is meant for passing nested markup as children.

Element helpers stay. div(...), h(...), and element(...) remain the programmatic layer, the counterpart of Solid's h. They keep RFC 0002's runtime shape compilation. They move from wybthon.html to wybthon.elements and are still exported from wybthon.

docs.title: 2. Zero-cost components
docs.text:
Constant props cost nothing. A component can only receive new props when a hole re-renders a tree that contains it. Components mounted anywhere else (another component's output, a list row, a Show branch, the inside of a template) are never patched. The renderer records which case applies when it mounts a component:

  • A patchable component's Prop reads track one version signal per props instance, created on the first tracked read. A patch that changes any reactive field bumps it. That replaces one signal per field.
  • A fixed component's Prop reads track nothing for a constant value. A value that's an accessor or zero-argument function is still called, so the reader subscribes to it directly.

Inert bindings are dropped. When a hole or reactive attribute binding finishes its first run without reading a reactive source, and without creating children, cleanups, or async work, it can never run again. The renderer disposes it immediately and keeps only the DOM it produced. Together with constant props, a component whose props never change costs about what its markup costs.

Native control flow. Show, For, Repeat, and Switch return region nodes the reconciler mounts directly. There's no component context, props object, or truthiness memo. (client_only, NoHydration, and dynamic need an owner at mount time, so they stay components, with typed internal Props.)

  • Show and Switch are one branch computation that re-mounts only when the selected branch changes.
  • When a hole re-renders a region of the same kind, the new condition or source is pushed into the mounted region instead of remounting it. That's the only part that was ever reactive.

No throwaway placeholders. In compiled helper shapes, a component child with a static node after it mounts in front of that node; only a component followed by another dynamic child keeps a placeholder.

docs.title: 3. A leaner reactive core
docs.text:
The plan was for Computation and Owner to keep their hot fields as slots, and to move the fields most instances never set to class defaults, stored per instance only when written:

  • Computation: the error handler, laziness, the unobserved callback, the name, preparation owners, the readiness signal, the publication and landing transitions, the apply cleanup and apply owner, and the deferral and eager flags.
  • Owner: async tasks, the context map, and the error handler.

It was implemented and reverted. It cut a computation from 328 to 216 bytes, but CPython 3.14 doesn't specialize attribute reads that fall back to a class default on these instances, which keep a __dict__ slot. Reading one of those fields was 3.5 times slower than reading a slot, and every apply, settle, child attachment, and disposal reads several of them. Every field stays a slot. The bindings that this RFC removes outright (constant props, inert bindings, control-flow wrappers) save far more memory than the slimming did.

docs.title: 4. One props system, one in-memory DOM
docs.text:
RawProps is removed. Built-in components (Loading, Reveal, Errored, Portal, the context provider, dynamic, lazy, the router, and virtual lists) declare internal Props classes. An internal class can accept undeclared keys, for components that forward attributes (Link) or props (dynamic).

A non-component callable used as a tag (h(fn, props)) receives the props dictionary unchanged. A function that wants typed, reactive props uses @component.

tests/conftest.py builds on wybthon.testing's DOM instead of carrying a copy, and the void-element and raw-text sets live in one module.

docs.title: 5. Typed control flow
docs.text:
For and Show get generic overloads, so callbacks are checked (Repeat takes an (int) -> node callback):

  • For(todos, lambda todo, i: ...) infers todo: Todo and i: Accessor[int] with the default matching.
  • With keyed=False, it infers todo: Accessor[Todo] and i: int.
  • With a key function, both are accessors.
  • Show(user, lambda u: ...) infers u: Accessor[User].

docs.title: 6. Housekeeping
docs.text:
• wybthon.html (the element helper module) becomes wybthon.elements. wybthon.html is the template function.
  • wyb build inlines the manifest into the page and emits modulepreload and preload hints for Pyodide and both source archives, so they download while the page parses instead of after the bootstrap has fetched the manifest.
  • An @action can be an event handler directly: its wrapped function decides whether it receives the event.
  • wybthon._template (RFC 0002's shape compiler) becomes wybthon._shapes.
  • The browser benchmarks build the benchmark app with wyb build and serve its dist, like compare_startup.py already does. benchmarks/_serve.py and its /__manifest endpoint are removed.
  • DEV_MODE leaves wybthon._warnings.__all__, and is_dev_mode() is the only reader.
  • Two class-name normalizers become one.
  • Dead functions, unused noqa directives, and stale configuration are removed:
  • the functions are _nearest_component, _accessor_of, and the shape-kind constants;
  • the configuration is the per-file-ignores entries for directories that don't exist, and the one-entry CI matrix.
  • The documentation and examples move to templates. Examples drop lambdas the runtime never needed: boundaries take nodes, handlers take no event, and store lists are passed directly.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
Removed or changed Replacement wybthon.html module (element helpers) wybthon.elements; the helpers are still exported from wybthon wybthon.html attribute Now the template function: from wybthon import html RawProps (internal) Typed Props classes A plain function used as a component tag received RawProps A function whose only parameter is the props receives the props dictionary, and is re-run when patched with changed props; use @component for typed props A hole that re-renders Show, For, Repeat, or Switch patched a wrapper component The region is patched in place; only its condition or source updates, as before wybthon._template (internal) wybthon._shapes benchmarks/_serve.py and /__manifest Benchmarks build each checkout with wyb build DEV_MODE in wybthon._warnings.__all__ is_dev_mode()

Patchable and fixed components behave identically for every prop that's passed as an accessor or that changes through a patch; the difference is only in what's allocated.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
A build-time AST compiler for element helpers. Deferred again. It would let div(...) trees skip VNode construction too. But it must prove that div is the helper and not a local name, it needs the same transform in tests, the dev server, and the build, and code would behave differently depending on whether it was transformed. T-strings give the same compile-once property with a guarantee from the language, and no transform.

Templates as the only markup syntax. Rejected. The helpers are a good programmatic API, many Python developers prefer call-style markup (htpy, FastHTML), and the runtime shape compiler already makes them reasonably fast. Two styles share one set of prop appliers, so their semantics can't drift.

Typed component tags in templates. Not possible without a type checker plugin: checkers don't see inside template strings. Component calls inside interpolations remain fully typed, and dev mode validates tag-form props at run time.

Remounting patched components instead of tracking a version signal. Simpler, but it would discard component state whenever a re-rendering hole passes a changed constant. The version signal keeps today's semantics and costs one signal per patchable instance, allocated only when it's read.

A separate, minimal render-binding class. Considered for the reactive core. The scheduler, transitions, and error routing all operate on Computation, so a second node type would duplicate their protocol. Moving rare fields out gets most of the memory benefit without a second implementation.

Do nothing. Components stay fourteen times the cost of their markup, and markup stays nested calls with renamed attributes.

docs.title: Drawbacks and risks
docs.text:
• Templates put markup in strings. Editors don't highlight HTML inside t-strings by default, and formatters don't format it. Python expressions inside interpolations are highlighted and checked as code.
  • Two authoring styles exist. The documentation leads with templates and presents helpers as the programmatic layer.
  • The patchable/fixed distinction depends on the reconciler knowing where a component mounts. A component mounted somewhere new that can be patched, without being marked patchable, would miss prop updates. Tests cover every mount path: hole results, render into an existing root, template slots, rows, branches, and boundaries.
  • Dropping inert bindings relies on the computation's dependency set after its first run. A binding that reads a non-reactive global and expected to re-run never did, so nothing changes.
  • The template compiler is new parsing code. Its error paths and HTML edge cases (void elements, raw text, entities, whitespace, tables) need direct tests.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Unit tests:
  • template parsing, compilation, caching, and every validation error;
  • every interpolation position, multi-root and text-only templates, and component tags with and without children;
  • slot-wise patching through re-rendering holes;
  • mixing templates with helpers, and templates inside For, Show, Loading, and Errored;
  • server rendering and hydration of templates;
  • patchable and fixed components, inert binding disposal, native regions patched by holes, typed control-flow overloads (in the typing fixtures), and teardown with no leaked handlers or bindings.
  • Existing suites: reactivity, transitions, async, stores, boundaries, router, forms, server rendering, and hydration pass, ported to the renamed modules.
  • Browser tests: the Playwright suite runs against the fixture project, with template-based pages added.
  • Work gates: benchmarks/check_work.py keeps one command per appended row, gates a template row at one command, and gates Show at two commands per toggle.
  • Benchmarks: native and browser comparisons against v0.37.0. Targets:
  • creating rows with templates at least 1.8 times faster;
  • mounting a component tree at least 2 times faster;
  • Show within 1.5 times the cost of a raw hole;
  • retained memory per binding lower;
  • updates no slower.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The engine v3 evaluation measured the implementation against v0.37.0. The machine was under heavy unrelated load, so it leads with deterministic work measures and reports process CPU time from alternating runs.

  • Template rows run 44% fewer function calls than helper rows and send one command per row. By CPU time they create rows 1.25 to 1.39 times faster than v0.37.0's helper rows, short of the 1.8 times target.
  • Constant props are free. Mounting 100 components with three constant props runs a third fewer calls and creates no signals or computations, where v0.37.0 created 300 of each.
  • Show runs 42% fewer calls and costs about 1.5 times a raw hole, meeting that target.
  • The dashboard (237 component instances in v0.37.0) mounts 1.24 times faster and unmounts 1.27 times faster. It creates 1 signal instead of 407 and 350 computations instead of 554, and sends 692 commands instead of 799. That's short of the 2 times target.
  • Memory: a helper row retains 23% less memory. A template row with a selection binding retains 3% more than a sealed helper row, because it keeps its values for slot patching.
  • Updates are no slower.
  • The leaner reactive core (part 3) was reverted. Moving rare fields to class defaults made a computation 112 bytes smaller, but slot-free reads of those fields aren't specialized by CPython 3.14 and were 3.5 times slower on every binding's hot path.
  • Validation:
  • 798 unit tests pass with 87% branch coverage, including typing contracts under mypy and pyright.
  • 82 browser tests pass on Pyodide. Eleven of them cover templates in the real HTML parser and JavaScript kernel, including checks that the validation rules match Chromium's parser.

The largest remaining costs per row are now one object each: the row's owner and index signal, the label's computation, and the delegated handler records. Further gains need cheaper reactive nodes rather than less tree work.

docs.title: Unresolved questions
docs.text:
• Head management (Title, Meta, useHead), server functions, an ASGI adapter, and a router data layer (query, revalidate, URL-bound actions). They belong to a full-stack RFC built on this engine.
  • Editor support for HTML inside t-strings (highlighting and completion), and a wyb check command that validates component tags against their Props classes statically.
  • Whether a future build step should precompile template skeletons into the production bundle, removing the first-call parse.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Accepted on 2026-10-08. Wybthon is pre-1.0 and has no production users yet, so the breaking changes ship without a compatibility layer.

docs.title: RFC 0004: Engine v4: the Wybthon compiler, Solid-style props, and leaner bindings
docs.text:
• Status: Implemented
  • Author: Owen Carey
  • Created: 2026-10-21

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Give Wybthon the one part of Solid it still lacks: a compiler. Solid's compiler does two jobs. It turns static markup into templates, which Wybthon already does at run time with t-strings (RFC 0003), and it turns every dynamic expression in the markup into a getter, so {count() * 2} stays reactive without the author wrapping it. Python can do the second job too. A t-string's interpolations are separate nodes in the module's syntax tree, so a small AST transform can defer each dynamic one before the module runs.

With that in place, the rest of the engine follows Solid more closely, and costs less:

  1. The compiler. wybthon.compiler rewrites html(t"...") calls. Dynamic interpolations become getters, component calls receive getters for their props, and each literal's parse tree and mount function are emitted as ordinary Python, so a production build never parses a template or generates code at run time. It runs in wyb build, wyb dev, an import hook, and a pytest plugin.
  2. Solid-style props. Fields are plain annotations (title: str = "Hi"), and props.title is a tracked read that returns the value. Prop[T] goes away.
  3. Leaner bindings and faster lists. A binding that reads nothing reactive never allocates a computation; bindings keep their state in slots instead of closures; a list row is its own owner and allocates its index signal only when something reads it; keyed lists match unchanged and swapped runs without per-row work.
  4. Solid 2.0 RC.17 alignment. Add create_deferred, is_equal, is_static, flatten, lazy_module, and on_hydration_end.
  5. Removals. The element helpers (div(...) and friends, wybthon.elements, wybthon.svg), the runtime shape compiler, Prop[T], and t-strings outside html(). h() stays as the programmatic layer.

The Virtual DOM stays as the batching layer between Python and the browser.

docs.title: The last gap in the mental model is the compiler
docs.text:
Solid's migration story is "components run once, reactivity is fine-grained, the compiler takes care of the rest." Wybthon matches the first two. For the third, the migration guide says Solid's compiler wraps expressions in effects for you, and that Python can't. That gap is the reason for most of what's unusual about writing Wybthon today:

  • inline expressions must be wrapped, and Python's grammar forces parentheses: {(lambda: count() * 2)}. That pattern appears 50 times in the documentation and tests;
  • props are accessors, so components read props.step() and use props.initial.peek() for a one-time read;
  • Prop[T] exists only to tell the runtime which props are reactive;
  • passing a prop through to a child stays reactive only if the author remembers not to call it.

Solid doesn't have any of these, because its compiler decides which expressions are dynamic. The decision is syntactic: an expression containing a call or a member access might read a signal, so it becomes a getter; anything else is a value. Python's syntax tree supports exactly the same rule, and t-strings keep their interpolations as separate nodes in it, so the decision can be made before the module runs, with no change to the language.

docs.title: Startup pays for templates twice
docs.text:
RFC 0003 compiles each template literal the first time it runs. Profiling that compilation natively shows where its time goes, per template:

Phase Native CPython Parse, normalize, and validate 120 to 170 µs Build the slot plan and skeleton 40 to 50 µs Generate the mount function (compile and exec) 1,070 to 1,280 µs

Generating the mount function is 85% of the cost, and every page pays it again for every template it renders, in WebAssembly, where Python runs two to three times slower. A compiler that already parses each literal can emit that function as ordinary module code, which wyb build turns into bytecode like the rest of the application.

docs.title: Creating and removing rows costs a few dozen objects each
docs.text:
The browser benchmark's update paths are fast: selecting a row among 10,000 commits in under a millisecond. Creating and clearing aren't, and the profile is flat; no function dominates. What dominates is object count. A mounted template row with a selection binding keeps 43 objects the cyclic collector tracks:

Objects per row Count Cells 11 Dictionaries 8 Functions 7 Tuples 6 Computations, VNodes, and handler records 2 each The row, its owner, its index signal, its projection key, a list 1 each

Many of those are closures: each attribute binding and each hole keeps its apply function, the cells it closes over, and the closure tuple. In Pyodide the collector's work grows with the live object count, which is why clearing 10,000 rows took 449 ms in the browser against 212 ms natively, and why RFC 0003 concluded that "further gains need cheaper reactive nodes rather than less tree work."

Keyed list matching also walks every row in Python. Swapping two rows of 10,000 calls a row update 10,000 times; natively it takes 22 ms, and 93 ms in the browser.

docs.title: Solid 2.0 kept moving
docs.text: Solid 2.0 isn't stable yet; 2.0.0-rc.17 is the current release candidate. Since RC.14, which RFC 0002 aligned with, it added createDeferred, isStatic, lazyModule, and made onHydrationEnd public, and its documented exports include isEqual and flatten.

docs.title: What it rewrites
docs.text: The compiler rewrites every call of Wybthon's html whose argument is a t-string literal. It resolves html through the module's imports (from wybthon import html, from wybthon.templates import html, an alias of either, or wybthon.html through import wybthon), so a module that defines its own html is left alone. Nothing else in the module changes.

docs.title: Which expressions become getters
docs.text:
An interpolation's expression is dynamic when it contains a call, an attribute access, or a subscript, ignoring the bodies of lambdas inside it. Everything else (a name, a constant, a lambda, an f-string of names) is static. This is Solid's rule: a name can't change by itself, but a call or a member access can read a signal, a store, or a prop.

Position Dynamic expression Static expression Child: <p>{count() * 2}</p> A getter: a reactive hole The value, as today Attribute: class={row_class(id)} A getter: a reactive binding The value Part of an attribute: class="card {kind()}" A getter for that part The value Component tag attribute: <{Card} title={user().name}> A getter the component reads through its props The value Spread: <input {omit(props, "x")}> Evaluated once, when the template is created The value Event handler (onclick), ref Never wrapped: handlers and refs are values The value Nested html(t"...") Never wrapped: it's markup, compiled in place

Existing code keeps working. A signal or memo placed directly ({count}) is still an accessor, a lambda is still a reactive expression, and the runtime still treats both the way it does today.

Calls in child position. {Show(...)}, {Card(title=user().name)}, and {badge(user())} are all calls, but they mean different things. In JSX the difference is syntactic (<Card> against badge()); in Python it isn't, and a naming convention can't tell Card(...) from Decimal(...). So a call whose callee is a name or a dotted name is dispatched at run time:

__wybthon__.call(Card, lambda: Card(title=user().name), (), {"title": getter(lambda: user().name)})
  • When the callee is a component (an @component, a lazy or dynamic component, a context, or a built-in such as Show, For, Loading, or Link), it's called with the prepared arguments: each dynamic argument is a getter, exactly what <{Card} title={user().name}> passes. Arguments are prepared recursively, so Errored(Loading(...)) builds its inner component the same way.
  • Any other callee (badge, str, Decimal) gets the deferred call back as one getter, so the whole expression is a reactive hole, which is what Solid does with a function call in JSX.

A built-in that takes a callback (For's row function, Show's children, a keyed function) unwraps a getter it receives once, untracked, so For(rows(), make_row(kind)) behaves as it reads.

Captured names. A getter evaluates its expression later, possibly after a loop variable has moved on. The compiler captures every name the expression reads from an enclosing function scope, by value, when the template is created, as keyword-only defaults of the getter's lambda. Python's late binding never shows through a template, and templates in class bodies can read class-level names.

Conversions and format specs. {price():.2f} and {name()!r} fold into the getter, so the hole renders the formatted text.

Expressions it doesn't wrap. An expression containing await, yield, or an assignment expression can't move into a lambda without changing its meaning, so it stays eager.

docs.title: Precompiled templates
docs.text:
The compiler parses and validates each literal with the same code html() uses at run time, so a malformed template is an error when the module is compiled, with the file and line. It then emits, at the top of the module:

  • the literal's normalized parse tree, as a tuple of constants;
  • one mount function per compiled element, as an ordinary def (the code wybthon.templates previously generated with exec);
  • an entry object holding both, created lazily on first use.

The call becomes html(t"...", __wybthon_t0__). On first use, the entry rebuilds the slot plan from the tree (no parsing, no regular expressions, no validation) and installs the precompiled mount functions. A production build never runs the template parser or exec.

The generated names (__wybthon__, __wybthon_t0__, __wybthon_m0__) are dunder names, which Python never mangles inside classes and applications don't define.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text:
• wyb build and wyb dev compile application sources through the compiler before writing bytecode into the archives.
  • An import hook, installed by import wybthon (or explicitly with wybthon.compiler.install()), compiles candidate modules imported after it. A candidate is a source file outside the standard library that mentions both wybthon and html and contains a t-string. Compiled code is cached next to the normal bytecode under its own tag (*.opt-wyb1.pyc), so a cached plain compile is never mistaken for a compiled one. An unchecked-hash bytecode file that wyb build wrote is used as is.
  • A pytest plugin (registered through the pytest11 entry point) compiles test modules alongside pytest's assertion rewriting, and gives their cached bytecode its own tag.
  • wyb run script.py runs a script with its own templates compiled, for scripts and quick experiments.
  • Prerendering imports the application after Wybthon, so the hook compiles it.

docs.title: Templates that weren't compiled
docs.text: html() still compiles a literal at run time when it's called without an entry: in a REPL, in exec'd code, or in a __main__ script run directly. Such a template has already evaluated its dynamic expressions once, so in dev mode, html() checks each interpolation's source text (Interpolation.expression) and raises TemplateError when a dynamic expression arrived as a plain value, naming the expression and how to compile the module. Code can't silently behave differently depending on whether it was compiled.

docs.title: 2. Solid-style props
docs.text:
from collections.abc import Callable

from wybthon import ParentProps, component, html, prop


class CardProps(ParentProps):
    title: str
    body: str = ""
    tags: list[str] = prop(default_factory=list)
    on_close: Callable[[], None] | None = None


@component
def Card(props: CardProps):
    def close():
        if props.on_close is not None:
            props.on_close()

    return html(t"""
      <div class="card">
        <h2>{props.title}</h2>
        <p>{props.body or "No details."}</p>
        {props.children}
        <button onclick={close}>Close</button>
      </div>
    """)
  • Fields are plain annotations. prop(default=...) and prop(default_factory=...) are the field specifier for defaults that need one; ordinary defaults work as in a dataclass.
  • Reading a prop returns its value, tracked. In a template, {props.title} is dynamic, so the compiler makes it a getter, and the text updates when the parent's value changes. props.body or "No details." is one expression and one binding.
  • The parent may pass a value, a compiler getter, or an accessor. A getter is always unwrapped on read. An accessor (a signal, a memo, or a zero-argument function) is unwrapped too, unless the field's annotation is callable (Callable[...] or Accessor[...], alone or in a union): a callback is returned as the parent passed it. For the same reason, a value field reads through an accessor a getter returns (<{Card} title={store.title}>, where store.title is a signal), as a binding of the same expression would.
  • Reading a prop whose value is reactive at the top level of the component body warns in dev mode, as Solid does: the read happens once. Wrap it in untrack(lambda: props.initial) when a one-time read is what you want. A constant can't change, so reading one doesn't warn.
  • Type checkers see title: str, so {Card(title=user().name)} is checked against the field types inside an interpolation, and the compiler still passes a getter.
  • is_static(props, "title") reports whether the parent passed a plain value, as Solid 2.0's isStatic does.
  • merge(...) and omit(...) return views that read like props: view.title is the tracked value. Spreading a view onto an element (<div {omit(props, "title")}>) binds each key reactively.

Patchable components (those mounted directly in a reactive hole's result, or passed to render) keep RFC 0003's single version signal per props instance, so reading a constant prop costs nothing anywhere else.

docs.title: 3. Leaner bindings and faster lists
docs.text:
A static probe before a computation. A hole or attribute binding first runs its expression under a lightweight observer. If the expression reads nothing reactive, creates nothing, and returns synchronously, the result is applied and no computation exists. The probe stops at the first reactive read, and the binding then runs as a computation as it does today. A probe that returns an accessor without reading anything ({row["label"]} returning a signal) re-targets the binding at that accessor, so a signal in a data structure still binds directly. This replaces RFC 0003's special cases for constant props.

Bindings keep state in slots. Attribute bindings and holes are small Computation subclasses that hold their node, name, and last value in slots and implement their apply stage as a method, instead of a closure with its cells.

Rows. A list row is its own owner and its own index accessor. Its index is a plain integer until something reads index() in a tracking scope, which is when the signal behind it is created.

Handlers. A node with one delegated handler stores it directly in the handler table, without a per-node dictionary.

Keyed matching. Matching a new list against the mounted rows skips the common prefix and suffix by identity without calling into each row, detects swapped ends the way Solid's reconcileArrays does, and only then falls back to a key table for what's left.

docs.title: 4. Solid 2.0 RC.17 alignment
docs.text: Solid 2.0 RC.17 Wybthon createDeferred(fn, options) create_deferred(fn, ...): an async memo that, after its first value, never holds the rest of the UI; readers keep the last value while a refetch runs isEqual(a, b) is_equal(a, b): the default equality (== with an identity fast path) isStatic(props, key) is_static(props, key) flatten(children) flatten(children): resolves nested accessors and lists to rendered values lazyModule(fn) lazy_module(fn): a cached async import with preload() and peek() onHydrationEnd(callback) on_hydration_end(callback)

docs.title: 5. Removals
docs.text:
• The element helpers. div(...), p(...), and the rest of the tag functions, element(), wybthon.elements, and wybthon.svg are removed. Templates are the way to write markup, and h(tag, props, *children) is the programmatic layer, the counterpart of Solid's h. A helper can't benefit from the compiler: it evaluates its arguments before Wybthon sees them.
  • The runtime shape compiler (wybthon._shapes). It existed to make helper trees mount like templates. h() trees mount on the generic path.
  • Prop[T], prop() returning a Prop, and accessor-typed props.
  • t-strings outside html(). A t-string as a child of h(), as a hole's result, or as an attribute value is no longer formatted implicitly. Pass it to html().

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text: Removed or changed Replacement Prop[T] fields and Prop Plain annotations: title: str; read with props.title props.title() and props.title.peek() props.title; untrack(lambda: props.title) for a one-time read prop(default=...) returning a Prop prop(default=...) / prop(default_factory=...) for plain fields, or an ordinary default merge(...) / omit(...) attribute access returned accessors Returns values; item access (view["title"]) still returns accessors for spreading Element helpers: a, div, p, span, ... and element() html(t"..."), or h(tag, props, *children) wybthon.elements, wybthon.svg Templates (<svg> works in a template), or h() wybthon._shapes (internal) Removed t-string children and attribute values outside html() html(t"...") render_template, template_getter in wybthon.vnode Removed Dynamic interpolations were evaluated once unless wrapped in a lambda They're getters; dev mode rejects uncompiled templates that relied on the old behavior A plain function call in a template's child position ran once It's a reactive hole, as in Solid

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Keep Prop[T] and add only the compiler. The compiler would remove the lambdas from templates, but components would still call their props, and a prop passed through to a child would still depend on the author not calling it. Solid's props are values read through getters, and the compiler makes that possible here.

Decide component calls by capitalization. Simple, and it's JSX's rule, but in Python it misreads Decimal(price()), Path(...), and any other class called in a template. Dispatching on the callee at run time costs one call and is exact.

Evaluate Interpolation.expression at run time instead of compiling. html() could re-evaluate each dynamic expression's source text in its caller's frame. The value has already been computed once by then, closures and comprehensions make the frame's names unreliable, and eval on every re-run is slow.

Rewrite functions in @component. The decorator could recompile its own function's source. It can't reach templates outside components (row functions, helpers), needs the source at run time, and has to rebuild closures.

Keep the element helpers. They're a pleasant programmatic API, but a helper's arguments are evaluated before the compiler or the runtime sees them, so they'd keep the old, wrap-it-yourself reactivity next to templates that don't need it. h() covers programmatic markup.

Compile the reactive core to a native extension (mypyc or Cython) for Pyodide. It may be two to four times faster, but it needs a WebAssembly wheel per Pyodide release and a larger download, and it doesn't change the API. It's worth revisiting once the engine's shape stops changing.

Do nothing. Wybthon stays the framework where markup needs lambdas and props need calls, and every page compiles every template in the browser.

docs.title: Drawbacks and risks
docs.text:
• An import hook is global. It's scoped narrowly: only html() calls on t-string literals change, standard-library modules are never read, and compiled bytecode has its own cache tag. pytest's assertion rewriting is the precedent.
  • Two compilation paths. Compiled templates and the runtime fallback share the parser, validation, slot plan, and mount code generation; only where the result is stored differs.
  • The dynamic rule is syntactic. {item.name} on a plain object becomes a getter that reads nothing; the static probe applies it without allocating a computation, so it costs a lambda.
  • Error tracebacks point into getters the author didn't write. Each getter keeps the interpolation's source position, so the traceback names the right line.
  • Breaking every component. Every component, document page, and test changes. Wybthon is pre-1.0 with no production users, so it's the right time.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• Compiler unit tests: each position's wrapping rule; captured names in loops and comprehensions; format specs; nested templates; dispatch to components, built-ins, and plain callables; unresolved and shadowed html; errors with file and line; precompiled entries matching runtime compilation; the import hook's cache and candidate rules; the pytest plugin; wyb run; and the dev-mode error for uncompiled templates.
  • Props: reads, tracking, defaults and factories, callable fields, getters and accessors from the parent, top-level-read warnings, patchable components, merge, omit, and is_static.
  • Bindings and lists: the static probe (inert, reactive, re-targeted, async, raising), slot-based bindings through transitions and error boundaries, lazy row indices, and keyed matching for swaps, reversals, prefix and suffix edits, and duplicates.
  • RC.17 additions: one test module each.
  • Existing suites, ported to templates and plain props: reactivity, transitions, async, stores, boundaries, router, forms, server rendering, and hydration.
  • Browser tests on Pyodide, with the fixture app built by wyb build.
  • Work gates: benchmarks/check_work.py keeps one command per appended row and two per selection.
  • Benchmarks, native and browser, against v0.38.0. Targets: at most 20 tracked objects per template row; creating rows at least 1.3 times faster; clearing 10,000 rows at least 1.5 times faster; swapping and removing in 10,000 rows at least 3 times faster natively; updates no slower; no runtime template parsing or code generation in a production build.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
The engine v4 evaluation measured the implementation against v0.38.0 on a heavily loaded machine, so it leads with deterministic work measures.

  • Objects: a mounted template row keeps 20 objects the cyclic collector tracks, down from 42 (13 from 32 without a selection binding), and retains 3,856 bytes instead of 6,082.
  • Templates: a precompiled template's first use costs about 83 µs natively instead of 1,870 µs. The browser tests check that a production build never compiles a template at run time.
  • CPU time, native, by the median of alternating rounds:
  • creating rows: about 1.1 times faster (1.38 times by minimum without a selection binding);
  • clearing: 1.2 to 1.4 times faster;
  • swapping two rows of 10,000: 2.65 to 2.92 times faster;
  • removing the first of 10,000: 1.56 to 2.45 times faster;
  • updates: no slower.
  • Targets: the object and production targets were met. Creation and swapping were partly met, and clearing 10,000 rows missed its 1.5 times target.
  • Plain computations: bindings stay plain Computations with one extra slot. Subclasses that held their state in slots allocated as little but created rows about 8% slower than v0.38.0, because CPython 3.14 stopped specializing the reactive core's hottest attribute reads once they saw several types.
  • Probing: only expressions without calls are probed. Probing every getter evaluated reactive expressions twice up to their first read; a store read ends a probe at once.

docs.title: Unresolved questions
docs.text:
• Editor support for the HTML inside t-strings, and a wyb check command that type-checks component tags against their Props classes.
  • The router's data layer, server functions, and an ASGI adapter. Server functions will need the compiler to split server code from the client bundle, so they build on this RFC.
  • Whether the compiler should also hoist static h() trees.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Accepted on 2026-10-21. Wybthon is pre-1.0 and has no production users yet, so the breaking changes ship without a compatibility layer.
